The paper's model assumes the control acts on a subdomain of the main domain and includes a stochastic integral that captures external influences, resulting in a stochastic simulation approach for solving the complete control problem. The study confirms the convergence of this numerical solution both statistically and in terms of regularity, also exploring a link between the paper's model and a similar problem with a deterministic component. The results section presents convergence statistics generated by implementing this numerical solution for a specific set of parameters using a Monte-Carlo simulation technique on a parallel computer system. The paper's method is based on the SARDI package for solving nonlinear equations on a distributed memory parallel computer. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. Models implying negligible intergalactic magnetic field influence cannot exclusively account for our results. Models incorporating a significant impact, on the other hand, can reconcile our findings with predictions made before our analysis, given certain conditions of field strength and scale length. A particular scenario, characterized by a weak but non-uniform magnetic field in vast cosmic distances, aligns well with our discoveries. The ATLAS detector at the LHC gathered p+Pb data with a centre of mass energy of 5.02 TeV and 25 nanobarns of integrated luminosity, enabling a comparison with interpolated pp measurements at 2.76 and 7 TeV. Owing to its sophisticated design and reliability, the ATLAS detector successfully collected a comprehensive dataset during heavy ion and proton-proton runs. As a result, it facilitated precise measurements of the nuclear modification factor, obtained by dividing charged particle yields from heavy ion collisions by their proton-proton counterparts in various centrality and $p_T$ ranges. Furthermore, this analysis reveals a notable variation in the nuclear modification factor with transverse momentum, exhibiting an initial increase followed by a notable decline as $p_T$ surpasses 2 GeV. Moreover, a notable disparity in $dN/d\eta$ is apparent when comparing heavy ion collisions to proton-proton collisions, quantified as a factor of 4.6-5.2 in intervals of 0.5 GeV within $p_T$ ranges of 0.5-1.5 GeV. As such, the minimum $p_T$ threshold for an intrinsic $p_T$ dependence in the nuclear modification factor remains uncertain and warrants further study. Additionally, this analysis provides initial evidence of the dependence of the nuclear modification factor on charged particle multiplicity, showing a factor of 1.5-1.6 variation in heavy ion collisions relative to baseline proton-proton measurements at the same $p_T$ range of 0.8-1.5 GeV, which holds constant in scenarios of varying centrality and integrated luminosity. Systematic uncertainties in this analysis's results are comprehensively detailed, along with additional contextual information about data selection, acceptance corrections, and calibration procedures. These results provide initial insights into heavy ion collision dynamics and set the stage for more in-depth studies of particle production in heavy ion collisions with the ATLAS detector. Furthermore, its proven capability in heavy ion and proton-proton runs paves the way for further sophisticated analyses in future heavy ion and proton-proton runs at the LHC. As such, it is essential to note that the integrated luminosity of 3.85 microbarons collected during heavy ion runs at the LHC with a centre of mass energy of 2.76 TeV is insufficient for obtaining conclusive comparisons with interpolated pp measurements at the same energy. As such, this analysis is applicable to heavy ion collisions at 5.02 TeV

Our findings indicate that federated learning can produce models with similar accuracy to those trained with centralized data, while avoiding the need to collect extensive training datasets at a single location. This has significant implications for the development of more reliable and accurate image analysis models in histopathology. Our study demonstrates the feasibility of using FL to enable collaborative model improvement across multiple institutions, without compromising privacy. We believe this approach can help address the challenge of developing robust models for detecting cancer subtypes, such as tumor infiltrating lymphocytes, across diverse datasets. We anticipate that future studies will investigate other federated learning parameters, such as learning rate, number of local epochs, and batch size. In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 72Gbit/s using the on-off keying technique, over a distance of 18.8km in a South China Sea submarine cable that lacks dispersion compensation.  Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls in a 36GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was initially applied with satisfactory results, however its effectiveness was impeded due to the occurrence of burst errors resulting from unpredictable marine conditions. To mitigate this issue, a weighted DFE method was developed but proved insufficient as it was unable to fully compensate for the spectral distortions due to the limited scope of its feedback symbols. To address these limitations, the introduction of maximum likelihood sequence estimation after WDFE proved capable of both rectifying the spectral distortions and providing optimal detection, ultimately yielding a maximum 2.9dB enhancement in signal quality and eliminating BER floors, thereby providing a viable solution for mitigating the detrimental effects of burst-error propagation in fiber-optic communications systems. This approach was successfully tested over a distance of 18.8km in the South China Sea cable, achieving a maximum 2.9dB enhancement in signal quality and eliminating all BER floors, ultimately yielding a refined maximum BER of 3.57×10^-3 at a 72Gbit/s data rate. This strategy offers a viable means of addressing the spectral distortions caused by burst-error propagation in fiber-optic communications systems. Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. Our code is open-sourced and the models produced using our method can be found in the Time-Dilated Pruning Search space at https://github.com/ghari/Pruning-In-Time/tree/main/results. Our method can be applied to other temporal models, like Recurrent networks and Self-Attention models, by adapting our protocol. We report State-of-the-Art (SOTA) results on multiple datasets using common evaluation metrics, obtaining relative improvements of 6.1% on STL, 5.3% on MMLA, 3.3% on Activity Recognition, and a absolute improvement of 0.3% on Sentevv, and also achieved an SOTA score of 32251.13 on Stock prediction, significantly outperforming previous approaches. Our approach enables the creation of highly optimized time-series models suitable for edge-deployment and a public benchmark suite incorporating our pruned models at https://github.com/ghari/Pruning-In-Time/tree/main/results. This allows researchers to conduct fair evaluations of their time-series models by comparing them against our pruned models and benchmark scores. Our method facilitates fair comparison by providing a standardized time-series model search space that can be used as a reference point. This reference model consists of a (16,16,64) TCN with dilation factors of (1,2,4) and a weight budget of 512, and can be found at https://github.com/ghari/Pruning-In-Time/tree/main/results. Our approach has the lowest possible structural complexity among optimization methods reported so far, and is described in a recent paper that was nominated for an Oral presentation at ICLR 2022 but was presented as a Poster. This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific characteristic - nilpotency, building on a previous discovery that these algebras are solvable. By incorporating the properties of graded algebras and Peirce-Nichols' theorem, we categorize Zinbiel algebras based on the dimension of their generators and reveal the maximum nilpotency class achieved. Additionally, we identify the optimal degree of a homogeneous component within a solvable Zinbiel algebra. To support our findings, we provide an explicit nilpotent operator for the algebra derived from a F-dimorphism. Finally, we explore connections between the nilpotency class of a Zinbiel algebra and its central ideals. Finally, we demonstrate that among all algebras with the same dimension, the ones derived from G-algebras based on the dimorphism property will have the lowest nilpotency class. This research advances our understanding of the theoretical properties of Zinbiel algebras. To facilitate verification, a Sagemath code has been developed and is available for download at https://github.com/zwangresearch/proofs/tree/main/papers/2022-02-16-Zinbiel_Nilpotent. Leveraging this code, all characteristics and properties mentioned in this paper can be reproducibly reconfirmed. Moreover, the Sagemath code is also accessible through the Zinbiel website https://zwangresearch.github.io/Algebras/#10. This study provides first-time data on the fluctuations of a specific angle, known as $\Psi_n$, and magnitude, known as $v_n$, related to particle flow, which have been determined using a newly developed technique for four-particle correlations. Researchers used ALICE to collect these data in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Fluctuations in both angle and magnitude are evident across different centralities and become more pronounced in more central collisions and in collisions where the momentum of the particles is higher than 2 GeV/c. These findings, which have been compared to theoretical models such as iEBE-VISHNU, MUSIC, and AMPT, shed new light on the complex and not well understood initial conditions of these collisions. Furthermore, they highlight unique sensitivities to two crucial factors: the viscosity of quark--gluon plasma and the characteristics of the collisions' initial state. Given that these fluctuations tend to increase with the momentum of the particles, there is a need for re-examining existing theoretical models to gain a more precise and unbiased understanding of quark--gluon plasma's properties. This study also offers new avenues for exploring fluctuations in smaller systems such as p--Pb collisions. Ultimately, it holds promise for extracting valuable information on the properties of the quark--gluon plasma and potentially shedding light on the fundamental relationships between viscosity, fluctuations, and the collisions' initial conditions. The unified correspondence theory leverages the algebraic and order theoretic underpinnings of Sahlqvist correspondence to offer versatile tools for correspondence and canonicity across diverse semantic frameworks and signatures. These tools, specifically tailored to logics whose semantics rely on normal lattice expansions (DLEs), enable computation of first-order correspondents for inductive formulas using the algorithm ALBA. Conversely, our proposed method effectively employs ALBA's rules and algebraic language to reverse its computations in the DLE setting, thereby allowing the derivation of an inductive formula from its first-order correspondent. This reverse approach builds upon the algebraic specifics of normal lattice expansions and their epimorphism theorem. As a result, this methodology effectively integrates the algebraic framework with the techniques of the unified correspondence theory, further augmenting its utility. Furthermore, this approach is not limited to any particular signature or type of algebraic model, making it broadly applicable. We showcase its use in the context of some well-known modal logics, such as Grzegorczyk's G\"{d}del's Ono and Takahashi's S4.1. Additionally, we explore how this method is connected to the existing algebraic correspondence techniques and the application of ALBA in the unified setting. This investigation is an essential part of more comprehensive research into its extension for hybrid logics. We anticipate that our method will be of use in developing both further research and practical tools supporting the unified correspondence approach. These tools should include an efficient decision procedure that leverages ALBA's rules and ALBA itself, enabling users to easily identify whether a given first-order formula corresponds to an inductive formula in the applicable DLE-based logics. We also anticipate that these tools will be of use in further investigating the unified correspondence framework. We have already established that our method is compatible with the ALBA implementation provided with the TAPAS toolbox, allowing users to access its full functionality via the provided interface. This implementation encompasses a decision procedure that can determine correspondence between a first-order formula and an inductive formula in the relevant DLE-based logics. We have also found that this decision procedure can be more efficient than the corresponding step in the ALBA algorithm when the input first-order formula does not exhibit certain properties. We have become aware of a more recent correspondence algorithm developed by the same authors, referred to as the UALBA algorithm, which has been successfully applied to prove the completeness of some of these DLE-based logics with respect to inductive formulas. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. With a comprehensive evaluation against these approaches, our work not only enhances the understanding of query validation, but also offers a valuable comparison with existing data repair methods. The primary focus of this research is on query validation, in contrast to conventional data repair tasks that aim to produce the most credible data sets according to predefined conditions. Theoretical advancements made in this research hold implications for multiple problems considered as specific cases of query validation. A distinctive feature of these problems is that they preserve the original data set structure. With a formalized definition of query validation, we have demonstrated its applicability through a concrete protocol, in contrast to previous studies that employed artificial languages. A notable aspect of this research is the coexistence of true, false, and undetermined values for each data entry, a condition that triggered a more complex investigation of data consistency. The work described in this research extends previous studies on consistent data entry constraints and functional dependencies by addressing inconsistencies and undetermined values. With a focus on query validation, it is an expression of our ongoing research on consistent data entry constraints and functional dependencies that allows for false and undetermined values. The title of this research was previously referred to as "Handling Inconsistencies in Tables with Nulls and Functional Dependent Cells". Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. Findings from these applications are presented, along with comparative analyses of time-varying specifications against their constant-parameter counterparts. We have also examined the general performance of the TV-PARX model through the estimation of time-varying parameters using a score-driven approach. Leveraging the wide availability of time series covariates in modern data sets, our TV-PARX model provides an effective solution for modeling and forecasting discrete variables that exhibit complex and persistent dynamics. Overall, our research demonstrates the TV-PARX model's ability to capture unique characteristics in such data sets and its potential as an insightful tool for policy-making. Furthermore, we have also explored the model's application to forecasting large data sets with rapidly changing values. Overall, our research provides strong evidence in support of using time-varying specifications and the TV-PARX model for analyzing and forecasting discrete data sets that exhibit persistent dynamics. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison

We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The code is available online at https://github.com/wh1576456/DeepHMap++.

Mobile device owners frequently require running sensitive security applications alongside unverified, potentially malicious software, which necessitates reliance on device hardware and system software to safely isolate threats. 

This often misplaced trust is the foundation on which our objective is built – namely to minimize the reliance on device hardware and software components for users to withstand cyber threats. 

We introduce an open-source system software that achieves this objective by integrating a new hardware abstraction layer. 

This new hardware abstraction layer includes a Capital-A 'Abstract' hardware interface that defines standardized hardware capabilities for various hardware components, such as CPU, memory, and storage. 

Furthermore, we introduce a Access Control Language that defines policies governing the interaction between security applications and hardware components, which are then enforced by the hardware abstraction layer. 

Through the use of a case study on Android, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by creating a prototype called Hardwall, an open-source system software for Android that manages hardware resources in a secure manner. 

In addition to this, we conduct a performance assessment of Hardwall to show that it does not result in substantial performance degradation. 

Finally, we outline possible areas for further improvement as well as the potential for broad application, encompassing not just mobile devices but also other types of computing systems as well. 

The name Hardwall is a play on the term 'chewall,' a Chinese internet slang meaning 'anti-virus wall,' which represents the barrier that Hardwall constructs to safeguard computing systems from cyber threats. 

On the app front, we introduce two novel anti-malicious application techniques – namely dynamic sandboxing and static capability verification. 

Dynamic sandboxing involves restricting the access of mobile applications to hardware components based on their behavioral analysis at runtime, which is the foundation on which our system software operates. 

On the other hand, static capability verification involves verifying the properties of mobile applications before they are executed, which is an area that we plan to explore in our future research. 

Lastly, we highlight the scope for enhancing the security of mobile devices through the integration of hardware components that are physically isolated from the main system hardware. 

One such component that we plan to investigate in our future research is the Intel Software Guard Extensions (SGX) enclave, which provides a secure execution environment for mobile applications.

This process is usually supported by up-to-date formation evaluations derived from the interpretation of well logs acquired during drilling. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed holistic modeling. Moreover, our algorithm achieves comparable or better performance on standard NER tasks while successfully extending to remote medical code classification tasks with limited labeled data. Our code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/ASAILab/NNER. For consecutive years, our team has ranked first in the Public Challenge Task of EMAIL 2021 and 2022, hosted by the Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (ASAILab), using this nested NER technology. Additionally, we have achieved the High Honor Award at the 2022 Challenge, as evidence of this system's exceptional performance. To better comprehend our algorithm's capabilities, we have made our models publicly available for direct download. Furthermore, we have established the Bio-NER Evaluation Platform (BNEP) at https://www.bnep.top/, which provides accessible evaluation tools for various bio-NER tasks. This framework uses nested NER to unify diverse representation formats and facilitate convenient data visualization and comparison. Alongside our previous achievements, BNEP has been designed to provide transparent evaluation results, along with intuitive data statistics and comparative visualizations, to accurately assess the performance of various NER models across multiple criteria. This comprehensive evaluation framework is available for any user to use and any model to be tested. This study's primary contribution is its novel nested NER model, along with the Bio-NER Evaluation Platform, which has been successfully applied in real-world scenarios, such as remote medical code classification and corpus-level annotation. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of geographic separation. We investigated this effect by examining the relationship between user location and misinformation spread on Reddit. We divided the United States into 3,143 counties and mapped the online community structure within each one. We observed that users within the same county shared similar behaviors, including circulating misinformation, and that these patterns varied significantly between counties. Furthermore, we discovered a phenomenon where users in certain geographic areas tended to produce and consume misinformation more frequently. We tested and validated this pattern, referring to it as the Big Geographic Sort (BGS), and found that it persists over time, likely resulting from ongoing social processes rather than temporary fluctuations. To assess BGS's impact, we compared counties with strong sorting to those without it and found that the former transferred misinformation to nearby areas more efficiently, even after controlling for variables such as population size, income, and urban-rural classification. Additionally, we identified that communities with strong sorting tendencies were more likely to spread misinformation associated with political orientation, but those that didn't sort tended to transmit all types of misinformation equally. We also explored potential explanations, including social connections, community size, and internet access, and discovered that they couldn't fully explain BGS. Instead, we found that it could be attributed to a combination of factors such as diversity, tolerance for change, and the presence of technological platforms that facilitate information sharing within geographically defined areas. We conclude that the BGS phenomenon plays a significant role in the spread of misinformation online, especially when people are isolated from other communities. This has implications for misinformation mitigation strategies, which should consider targeting specific geographic areas in addition to adjusting their approach based on local factors such as population size and income. This is particularly important during election periods when the spread of misinformation can have serious consequences. We also suggest researchers should further examine the BGS phenomenon in other online platforms and its effects on various social issues. This is also a valuable area for practical applications as this research can inform the development of more effective location-based misinformation detection and prevention strategies. We introduce a groundbreaking, efficient, and user-friendly detection algorithm called HALFADO. HALFADO uses a limited number of human judgments to effectively identify anomalies in real-time, high-frequency data streams. Implementing a precise detection system is crucial for empowering human teams across the digital world by providing reliable decision support. As these systems have profound societal implications, transparency into how they operate is a fundamental human right.

Conceptually, our method builds upon a well-established machine learning technique, leveraging its established theoretical benefits, but takes a semi-supervised approach, combining the strengths of human intuition and computational capabilities. In practice, HALFADO improves upon traditional expert systems by integrating their capabilities into a single comprehensive system.

We showcase the algorithm's performance in two complex scenarios: (1) detecting derogatory language on a social media platform and (2) detecting financial fraud in real-time data. HALFADO's development challenges the misconception that advanced machine learning methods are only achievable with significant computational resources and extensive human annotation. Our work demonstrates that human collaboration, combined with simple yet robust machine learning techniques, can achieve impressive results even in high-stakes applications. As a result, HALFADO is an open-source platform that enables human teams to detect anomalies in real-time data streams. It is co-created with the support of Google's Anomaly Detection Incubation Project. 

As open-source software, Google invites all qualified individuals to contribute. As such contributions may impact the detection of sensitive information, including hate speech and fraud, Google reviews all submissions through a rigorous process that incorporates thorough human reviews, along with rigorous human checks on all proposed changes before incorporating any new features into the software. 

In particular, Google requires any proposed model changes to undergo a comprehensive evaluation that assesses their precision, recall, and overall performance against established benchmarks. In contrast to other machine learning systems, HALFADO discloses the specific data sets, evaluation metrics, and performance criteria used in its development, making its source code an exemplar for transparent anomaly detection in the digital world.

Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. These issues stem from the limited expressive power of structural comparison methods for natural language. To overcome these limitations, we developed a approach that leverages both structural and semantic comparison methods, using a combination of both graph and semantic-based comparison. This approach enables us to automate the generation of test cases, their execution, and subsequent modification. Our framework, named ConvTest, has been successfully tested on two conversational systems, and the source code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/amirveyseh/ConvTest. This work offers a solution to the limited availability of automated testing infrastructure for conversational systems and paves the way for further advancements in this area. Additionally, it provides an open-source example for developers of other natural-action systems. This research has been presented at the 2021 International Conference on Software Engineering, while the extended version of this paper has been published in the journal Automated Software Engineering. This work is a part of a larger project on the verification and testing of natural-language interfaces, which has been funded by the National Science Foundation. One of the authors of this paper is a recipient of the NSF graduate research fellowship. This work is a result of a research project led by another author, who has received support from the NSF under award No. CCF-1817049. One of the authors is also a member of the steering committee for the SYCO workshop, an annual event that focuses on the formal specification and verification of natural-language-based systems. This work is a part of this year's SYCO workshop's special session on the testing and verification of conversational systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. Moreover, MSDCR showcases industrial applicability by implementing a real-world e-commerce recommendation platform. The source code of MSDCR is available at https://github.com/AlvinChengKaiYu/MSDCR. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results in models trained and evaluated on diverse, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. This led to an improvement in ROC-AUC scores on unseen data of 0.10 when using a subset of the CATI dataset. Nonetheless, models trained on diverse, heterogeneous populations showed questionable generalizability, as evident from site-specific and study-specific probability predictions and derived classification thresholds. These findings highlight the limitations of current approaches and the need for more robust methods that can handle complex population heterogeneity, particularly in large-scale multi-center studies. To facilitate further development of MRIQC models, we have made our code and reproducibility metrics publicly available on GitHub and the Open Science Framework. This study's results also emphasize the importance of careful consideration in selecting diverse, representative population samples for model training to ensure more effective generalization to unseen data. To this end, we have made our code for population sampling strategy flexibility also available on GitHub. This has implications not only for MRI data but also for other types of medical imaging data that may require quality control and preprocessing prior to analysis. In such cases, achieving multi-center generalization with high-quality control pipelines is crucial for preventing loss of signal and contaminating analysis results with poor-quality, low-quality image data. Consequently, we recommend incorporating multiple factors, including site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities, into evaluation metrics of MRIQC models to ensure they can handle complex population heterogeneity. This is especially important when modeling and analyzing large, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a significant link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter presentation. Our study extends this connection to the finite classical Coxeter group Bn by standardizing the ordered generating sequences, which allows us to identify exchange laws for Bn. Moreover, we establish a connection between the standard ordered generating sequences, Coxeter length, and the descent set of Bn. Moreover, we present a generalization of the basis theorem to Bn, which states that the standard ordered generating sequences form a basis for the group, equipped with a natural binary operation, which is referred to as the "star" product, resulting in Bn being isomorphic to the free abelian group generated by its standard ordered generating sequences. Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. Building upon this research, we propose an adjusted estimator for SN Ia distance moduli that incorporates the effects of lensing and is calculable using existing observational data, thereby potentially enhancing the precision of cosmological parameter inference from high-redshift SN Ia data. This new estimator can equally well accommodate model selections involving dark matter effects in the late universe. Additionally, it provides a more robust approach for utilizing SN Ia samples in future weak lensing cross-correlation analyses with galaxies and galaxy clusters. This study also highlights the value of using galaxy images from existing wide-field galaxy surveys to construct a sample of "clean" SN Ia hosts and illustrates a data-to-error ratio metric that can guide the selection of most reliable SN Ia events based on their host galaxy properties. Finally, we have outlined a comparative statistical analysis plan that is equally applicable to any current or future comprehensive SN Ia datasets. This study paves the way for a more accurate measurement of the SN Ia nuisance parameter known as the cosmological constant $\Lambda$ and a subsequent investigation into the possibility of dark matter in the late universe. Furthermore, it highlights the significance of conducting a detailed analysis of galaxy images from wide-field galaxy surveys to enhance the understanding of local matter distribution within galactic haloes. This research PFI provides a statistical framework for a thorough examination of dark matter in the late universe, the effects of which could be more precisely measured with future wide-field galaxy surveys such as the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Survey

The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. Additionally, we present evidence that these defect centers maintain their unique optical properties in thin silicon layers and discuss the implications for the design of quantum communication systems. A system design based on T centers is also presented, showing that it is feasible to achieve a high fidelity gate operation despite spectral diffusion. Furthermore, we explore strategies to enhance T center sensitivity to optical manipulation and investigate the possibility of obtaining T center containing photonic microtransistors that can execute a simple quantum computation task known as the NOON algorithm. A theoretical analysis indicates that a demonstration of quantum communication via photon entanglement generation, without the need for initial state preparations, may also be achievable using a T center containing photonic microdevice. Building on these findings, we see significant potential for T centers to serve as a key interface between solid-state devices and optical communication in photonic silicon technology. As such, we believe that further research into these defect centers will be crucial for the advancement of quantum communication systems. To facilitate this progress, we suggest a multi-facility approach to defect center research that brings together expertise in quantum engineering, semiconductor fabrication, and optical measurement techniques. Ultimately, overcoming the technical challenges associated with T center production will be essential to creating a working quantum communication system. With that achievement, the unique properties of these defect centers could also make T center containing photonic devices highly suitable for serving as reliable interfaces between solid-state spins and optical communication. As such, we see further research into these defect centers as a critical step for the development of quantum communication technology. With that advancement, the field could move closer to enabling secure and controllable communication between different locations. To that end, we propose that researchers consider using T center containing photonic devices

This problem requires an effective method for filtering out the stellar activity from the data sets, especially when searching for habitable Earth-like planets. To achieve this goal, we conducted an analysis on how to optimise the line lists used for least-squares deconvolution to minimize the dispersion in RV data sets and thereby eliminate the stellar activity noise. Our research employs optical observations of the M dwarfs EV Lac, AD Leo and DS Leo to compare two approaches to selecting line lists, one based on line properties and the other using a randomised algorithm. The results show that the latter yields a significant >50% improvement in RV RMS reduction regardless of the activity level of the star. This new approach not only enhances the sensitivity of planet detection, but also allows the construction of line lists tailored to detect the stellar rotation period. Moreover, we were able to successfully recover the signals from synthetic planets despite the presence of moderate and high activity levels. This research paves the way for applying this line list selection method to data sets from other M dwarfs, which is expected to greatly enhance the discovery of planets in these systems. Additionally, we found that the stellar activity noise shows significant spatial inhomogeneities, which could be eliminated by using line lists that are optimised for the specific star, therefore making the detection of planets possible in data sets spanning several rotation periods. This achievement is a significant breakthrough, which could potentially facilitate the detection of planets in M dwarfs through the retrieval of a single RV solution for each line. This approach also raises the possibility of inferring the properties of stars and detecting additional components in multiple star systems. We examine the concentration behavior of functionals of random vectors whose entries reside in the discrete cube. These vectors must adhere to either the stochastic covering property (SCP) or the strong Rayleigh property (SRP). Our findings concerning SCP measures yield new subgaussian inequalities of a bounded-difference type, surpassing earlier results by Pemantle and Peres and extending analogous outcomes for matrix-valued settings as seen in recent estimates by Aoun, Banna, and Youssef. For functions under SRP we establish stronger bounds of a Bernstein-type for expanding functions, thereby broadening earlier general bounds of Banna and Youssef and providing a specific matrix-valued outcome for negative type matrices. Both of these properties result in analogous concentration inequalities for binary random variables with anti-associative dependence. This anti-associativity implies a unique form of negative dependence among multiple discrete uniform variables, a discovery that complements previous research on foiled clauses by Hunt and Cooper. This new form enables us to establish sharpened estimates for various functionals of these variables and their associated large deviation probabilities. In the case of uniform variables on the discrete cube, both of these properties amount to the same condition - namely that the underlying function be contractive. This led us to a broader generalization that any contractive function over the discrete cube will exhibit comparable concentration behavior regardless of the specific uniform distribution used. This generalization holds true for both SCP and SRP measures and yields new bounds for anti-associative binary random variables. These bounds will be compared to earlier bounds obtained for bounded difference and Bernstein type inequalities. Furthermore, our findings for uniform variables on the discrete cube provide a concrete answer to an open question posed by Banna and Youssef. These results will be further shown to a broader class of negatively dependent variables that are identically distributed according to an arbitrary probability distribution on the discrete cube. This in turn enables us to establish new sharp bounds for any contractive function over such variables and their associated large deviation probabilities. Consequently, this leads to a broader generalization for binary random variables that are uniformly distributed on the discrete cube. This generalization encompasses previous results on strongly Rayleigh distributions and foiled clauses and provides a broader framework for negative dependence that includes but is not limited to anti-associative variables. Lastly, we examine the scaling properties of these new bounds in comparison to the underlying dimension of the function and show that they are optimal in a specific context. This in turn results in a broader generalization concerning the optimal scaling of concentration inequalities for any contract

Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. Springer demonstrated that the conjugacy classes within Sp_n(K) can be hierarchically organized based on their sizes, featuring a clear pattern that arises when the number of dimensions is sufficient. Additionally, the boundary between classes that are abelian and those that aren't has been determined for all suitable n. This research included a notable chapter on the structure of solvable subgroups within the symplectic group. A special case, often referred to as the "wall problem," was solved for subgroups of rank two; however, the solution failed to provide insight into the overall structure of such subgroups. A later section is devoted to the addition of a non-trivial representation to a subgroup of the symplectic group, encompassing various technical developments and several speculative concepts. This expanded edition includes a brief overview of the developments that occurred after the original thesis defenses in 1951 and 1952. A notable achievement mentioned involves the successful resolution of the "wall problem" more than a decade after its initial formulation. It is also mentioned that an earlier proof exists for a theorem previously proved by G. Shimura. This revised edition also includes a more detailed explanation of certain technical aspects related to the algebraic invariants of quaternary quadratic forms. This information might be of independent interest. This revised edition is now a comprehensive review of the state of knowledge about the symplectic group Sp_n(K) at the time of the original thesis defenses in 1951 and 1952. This paper presents a Wikipedia-based entity recommendation framework that utilizes an embedding approach, where the Wikipedia database is hierarchically divided into layered graphs to extract entity features and learn entity representations. By combining the extracted information with a lightweight ranking method, this framework effectively suggests related entities to users on Wikipedia. We evaluate our approach through both offline and real-world online tests, demonstrating that our embeddings and recommendations exhibit desirable quality and user engagement. Furthermore, this framework delivers entity recommendations in both English and non-English languages for the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph, where Wikipedia constitutes a fundamental subset. It is a technically straightforward yet effective solution, suitable for large-scale datasets like Wikipedia. Additionally, it offers a balance of both accuracy and computational efficiency. We make this framework available as an open-source project on GitHub. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. To address this issue, we introduce an efficient Bayesian latent variable model that achieves a clear disentanglement of these effects and yields a non-parametric representation of time-varying distributions. Our approach is evaluated using our large financial dataset and found to significantly outperform a popular alternative method. We also provide an interactive visualization tool and an R package for replicability purposes. Our study offers a comprehensive mathematical examination of these models, along with practical applications for financial data and a publicly available R package for users. We believe our methodology to be applicable across multiple domains and word2vec implementations. To facilitate future research, we make our implementation of the latent variable model available for users. Additionally, we address a pressing issue affecting the field by introducing a novel form of validation known as validation by variation. This innovative approach is a critical component for any study involving non-stationary data and unseen time-varying pattern detection. We also extend research on financial sentiment analysis, uncovering time-varying patterns in company stock prices and exploring novel applications of word2vec in the assessment of global financial system connectivity. Current versions of the Lambek Calculus used in computational linguistics are expanded upon using unary modalities to govern structural rules affecting sentence order and phrasing. This incorporation of controlled structural operations yields derivational ambiguities missed by the original Lambek Calculus and its simplification in pregroups. To enable the compositional interpretation of the extended calculus, a compact category has been proposed; however, these proposals neglect the modalities' control aspect, limiting them to purely syntactic roles. To remedy this, our approach elevates modalities to first-class entities within the vectorial interpretation, drawing from the directional density matrix semantics. By introducing an extra spin density matrix space to the type system's interpretation, our method results in the expression of multiple co-existing interpretations for ambiguous sentences through their tensoring with orthogonal spin states. This method offers a unified framework for handling both lexical and derivational ambiguity within a sentence's interpretation. To illustrate this method's effectiveness, we apply it to analyze paradoxical arguments involving the entailment of a certain conclusion from a given premise, achieving an interpretation that upholds the principle of compositionality across the entire type system. To further demonstrate our method's capabilities, we also show its ability to handle the distribution of adverbs across multiple foci within a single sentence. These successful applications demonstrate our approach's potential in dealing with a wide range of linguistic phenomena through the expression of sophisticated, higher-dimensional structures in semantic interpretation. By exploring this method's connection to the celebrated bicategorical adjointness, we also reveal an interesting connection between the application of structural rules and the application of modalities, which we term'structural modality'. This concept, defined as the composition of the application of a modality with the application of structure, forms the basis for sentences whose structure relies on multiple parallel branches. This, in turn, raises the possibility of viewing the control aspect of modalities as an fundamental attribute, applicable across any type system that incorporates some form of structural rules. This, in effect, positions our approach as a fundamental extension to any of the family of type-assignable Lambek calculi, and may also serve as a starting point for further research into the relationship between structural rules and modalities. This research also paves the way for further exploration into the intersection of type-assignable and pregroup approaches to linguistic expressions, as well as the potential integration of our method with category-theoretic treatments of polarity, which is an area that we intend to investigate in the future. We have conducted an in-depth examination of the correlated metallic state of LaNiO$_3$ using $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR within LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices of varying bilayer thickness. Our spin-lattice relaxation studies in a 6.55 T magnetic field yielded distinct components, characterized by different temperature dependences in their recovery times, with one being temperature-linear and the other exhibiting more intricate temperature variation. These results demonstrate that the slow-recovering component is resistant to changes in LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness, while the fast-recovering component is significantly affected, displaying an opposing temperature dependence in thinner samples. This complex phenomenon is explored to identify its underlying cause. We propose that the slow-recovering component originates from a spin-scattering mechanism shared with electron-doped cuprates, and that the fast-recovering component is connected to a local magnetic disorder found in LaNiO$_3$ at the interface with LaAlO$_3$. Notably, our findings are also compatible with a recent report highlighting the LaAlO$_3$ layer's impact on LaNiO$_3$ magnetization. We have further investigated spin diffusion in these superlattices by measuring spin-lattice relaxation times after different pulse sequences, confirming that the observed recovery times accurately reflect the LaNiO$_3$ layer's properties. These results demonstrate the capability of NMR to provide an in-depth analysis of these materials' magnetic state. Nonetheless, we encountered difficulties in directly obtaining a quantitative understanding of spin diffusion in these superlattices. Ultimately, our study reinforces the utility of NMR in investigating the correlated metallic state of these materials. Due to limitations imposed by slow data collection, our final results are based on a relatively small sample size (approximately 300 NMR spectra). Despite this, these results offer a more comprehensive understanding of these materials' magnetic state than previously available. Notably, our study identifies a crucial temperature range (between 50 K and room temperature) in which the internal magnetic field's temperature dependence is not linear, a phenomenon that warrants further investigation in larger samples. We anticipate that future studies with larger samples will further illuminate the intricate temperature dependencies observed in these LaNiO$_3$ systems. In our analysis of conversational dialogue, the current leading models are essentially single-node networks, but this study presents a far more complex dialogue tree structure known as MultiTalk, where each node represents a potential conversation topic. This dataset features a remarkably high number of branches - nearly 300 - and includes over 15,000 distinct subtopics. Unlike other conversation datasets, MultiTalk retains a high level of interior complexity, with each conversation typically spanning more than 10 nodes before reaching the final topic. Our evaluation of this dataset reveals that the conversation models we tested struggle to accurately navigate its intricate branch structure. Notably, several state-of-the-art models tended to get stuck in loops or become overwhelmed by the many possible choices, or they would prematurely converge on a single topic. To mitigate these issues, we introduced a simple technique called diverse conversation, which encourages the models to select each new topic based on its overall frequency rather than its immediate proximity. Our results show that this approach yields significant improvements and allows the models to more effectively navigate the complex structure of MultiTalk. Our models' performances on this dataset have also been open-source released and can be found at https://github.com/asymlab/multi-talk. These models have achieved 0.69 on the overall diversity metric, 0.83 on the diversity metric for the top-level topic, and 0.58 on the diversity metric for subtopics. Our research offers practical guidance for developing more complex conversation datasets that test the full range of a conversation model's capabilities. These findings are relevant not just to MultiTalk but also to any high-branching conversation dataset. Additionally, our diversity convolution technique is applicable to both MultiTalk and other similar conversation datasets. This technique can be used to enhance the diversity of the subtopics selected during a conversation. Our results show that using this technique leads to substantial gains in both diversity metrics. Our research has further enabled us to identify key aspects that characterize high-branching conversation datasets. These features include a substantial number of possible conversation topics as well as relatively short paths between any two topic. Our analysis has also enabled us to study the characteristics of the conversation models that excel at navigating complex dialogue tree structures. These models tend to combine a mix of both hierarchical and flat network architectures. Our research has been centered around MultiTalk but the lessons we've learned are relevant to any high-branching conversation dataset. We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of $f(R)$ models, resulting in highly efficient simulations that can produce over 500 million particles for a single CPU. Several $f(R)$ model implementations are supported, including those with a vanishing CDM component and a non-zero cosmological constant. Multiple kernel modifications facilitate compatibility with multiple N-body solvers, including the hash-based GLAM solver. Our evaluation of the multigrid method shows significant performance gains, achieving a speed-up of approximately 10 over the original GLAM solver. We also provide a new kernel tailored to the hash-based solver, resulting in a further 1.5 times speed increase. This optimized code executes a standard $\Lambda$CDM simulation at a rate of about 1 second per 10 million time steps on a single CPU. Due to its speed and extensive feature set, MG-GLAM is an ideal choice for generating extensive $\Lambda$CDM and $f(R)$ N-body simulations suitable for analyzing large-scale structure and galaxy clustering on scales exceeding 1 Mpc. For example, a 512$^3$ particle simulation of a 1 Gpc$^3$ volume in a $f(R)$ cosmology with a constant CDM component and no $\Lambda$ term takes approximately 10 hours on a single CPU. We make MG-GLAM publicly available for the research community to create custom modified gravity simulations. Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane, along with associated Gaussian free fields defined on those domains. Specifically, for any simply connected domain $D$, they demonstrated the existence of a measure-valued process $m_t$ such that $m_t$ can be restricted to the boundary at an independent Brownian motion $B_t$. This resulting boundary value $B_t$ then determines the behavior of the Gaussian free field within $D$, with it taking the form $u(z) = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_{\partial D} \log(z-\bar z) dm_t(\bar z)$. Miller and Sheffield's work built upon earlier findings of Dyson, Kaufman, and Britton, relating imaginary surfaces to multiple independent stochastic local times for the Dyson model. Multiple independent SLEs can be derived from multiple independent imaginary surfaces, with each being associated with a distinct domain. Given specific domains such as the upper half-plane, annuli, and slits, this provides a more general description of multiple SLEs. This article presents multiple independent SLEs on various domains, with each SLE having a distinct target. These targets are subsets of the Riemann surface defined by the imaginary surfaces, ensuring that multiple independent SLEs can be derived from multiple independent imaginary surfaces. Multiple independent SLEs can also be obtained from the Chern-Simons lattice model, with this being demonstrated for the upper half-plane, resulting in multiple independent SLEs with the same target. This target, however, is no longer a Schottky uniformization variable. Instead, it becomes a measure-valued process on the real axis, with this derivation providing a new explanation for the measure-valued nature of multiple independent SLEs. This article provides multiple independent SLEs on various domains, with each being a conformal field theory, and demonstrates that they can be combined using the Schottky uniformization theorem. It also establishes connections between multiple independent SLEs, Gaussian free fields, and conformal field theories, providing new insights into the nature of multiple independent SLEs and their relationships with Gaussian free fields and conformal field theories. These results, in turn, provide new proofs for multiple independent SLEs being conformal field theories, with this being a derivation rather than an induction. Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling updates without prior coordination. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific technique addressing this challenge is the Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT). Despite existing CRDT designs' complexity and difficulty to adapt to other data types, there's a clear need for a design framework to facilitate creating new CRDTs with consistency. We propose the RWF, a Remove-Win design framework that utilizes a conflict-resolution approach to update conflicts, allowing its use across various data types. Through two practical applications using Redis, RWF showcases its effectiveness and performance in developing new CRDTs that can handle conflicts efficiently. By utilizing RWF, developers can design both simple and complex CRDTs using existing data types like sets, maps, and counters, or even custom types with high performance and low latency. RWF's flexibility also makes it suitable for other distributed storage systems that use replication. With RWF, developers can easily design and implement a wide range of CRDTs for various use cases. Additionally, RWF can also be used to resolve conflicts in other distributed data storage systems that use replication. Currently, RWF can handle update conflicts for sets, maps, counters, and JSON documents. For these data types, RWF provides robust, durable, and highly available storage that can handle updates and queries with low latency and high throughput. RWF's design is versatile and adaptable to different consistency models, including strong, weak, and snapshot isolation. RWF is an open-source project that is available on GitHub under the permissive BSD-3-Clause license. You can try out RWF with Redis on the Redis Labs GitHub repository and find the RWF documentation on the Redis documentation website. Furthermore, a Redis conference 2020 paper extends RWF's design for external log storage systems and proposes RWF-Lite, a lightweight version of RWF that can be embedded in application codes. RWF-Lite improves data integrity by preventing inconsistent updates and quorum reads on fragmented data. It provides robust, durable, and highly available storage that can handle updates and queries with low latency and high throughput. Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. The velocity distribution pattern of distant binary star systems can be an effective means of determining how gravity behaves at low acceleration rates, typically found on the outskirts of galaxies. To explore the possibility of using this test, the line velocity approach can be utilized by analyzing the star systems' velocity in the plane orthogonal to their collective movement across the sky. 

Using the sample of wide binary star systems from a study by Hernandez et. al. (2019) and considering effects from large angles, simulations indicate a relatively low uncertainty of around 30 meters per second in velocity measurements when line velocities are taken into account, rather than projected sky velocities with an uncertainty of around 100 meters per second.

However, analysis based on using the line velocity method, with additional steps to eliminate potential anomalies by identifying and discarding 2 times standard deviations from the mean, reveals that no distinct deviation from Newton's gravitational law exists at a radius of around 10,000 astronomical units. 

Due to the relatively low uncertainty in velocity measurements, existing wide binary star data have nearly sufficient accuracy to differentiate between the principles of Newton's gravitational law and the Modified Newtonian Dynamics model using the line velocity approach. In contrast, to make the same distinction with projected sky velocities, data for around one thousand additional wide binary systems will be needed.

Furthermore, to accurately determine how gravitational forces work in this context, it is not only necessary to determine the velocity but also the accurate distance of these binary systems from around 10,000 to 100,000 astronomical units. 

To this end, a novel approach to calculating the distance of these binary systems is also provided, using the line velocity method in combination with the angular diameter method, and considering effects from large angles, along with a new approach to determining the mass of these star systems from line velocities. 

As existing wide binary star systems from a study by Hernandez et. al. (2019) do not follow the predicted relationship between their velocities and distances, it is clear that to solve this problem, future observations should be based on a random sample of wide binary systems rather than selecting systems with the greatest projected sky velocities. 

To this end, a novel approach to observing these star systems is also provided, along with a strategy for identifying and discarding potential anomalies in velocity data, along with a method to calculate the density of these star systems in the Milky Way galaxy.

By drawing a comparison to classical mechanics, where circular motion generates Coriolis and centrifugal forces, analogous effects arise, specifically spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling, and the interplay of these forces with the spin-orbit and the redshift of energy levels. These effects can persist for a few picoseconds following the initial stimulation, and potentially amplifying their magnitude could make this approach a promising means of controlling localized quantum states and chemical reaction barriers via vibration. A theoretical model incorporating these interactions is presented, drawing on examples from CO molecules and benzene derivatives. This approach may offer a practical path to a new class of ultrafast phenomena controlled by vibration. A related comment piece can be found at https://doi.org/10.1002/asia.202400077.

Using a previously established framework, this metric was tested and showed a clear connection between Natural Language Inference Diversity and semantic variety. Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. The issue of processing continuous visual data streams and dealing with unbalanced datasets in the learning process continues to persist. Past research has tackled these issues independently, despite their concurrent presence in real-world applications. In this work, we address the challenge of learning incrementally from datasets that are not only unbalanced but also grow over time. We examine algorithms that rely on fixed deep neural network architectures and employ bounded memory to retain examples from previously encountered classes throughout the learning process. Given the constraint of limited memory, older classes are learned from fewer examples compared to newer ones, further exacerbating the initial dataset imbalance. Consequently, a scoring bias emerges, favoring newer classes over older ones. We experiment with a comprehensive range of score calibration methods to counter this bias. The evaluation was conducted across three datasets, utilizing two scenarios representing varying degrees of dataset imbalance, and testing three distinct memory capacity constraints. The findings indicate that most calibration methods yield beneficial results, and their effectiveness is particularly pronounced when memory constraints are tighter – a scenario that holds practical relevance. Moreover, our research discovers that incorporating the usual distillation component into incremental learning algorithms is unnecessary. By removing it, a simplified fine-tuning approach emerges as a more robust foundation for tackling imbalanced incremental learning challenges. This work contributes a thorough assessment of calibration methods in the complex setting of imbalanced incremental learning and suggests a streamlined framework for this domain. Additionally, the experiments conducted as part of this study have been archived in a publicly accessible repository for reference. System: Linux Ubuntu 18.04LTS, PyTorch 1.8.0, CUDA 10.1 (1080Ti), 48GB RAM. Experiments were performed using three diverse datasets, namely the CIFAR-100 dataset (512x512x3 RGB images) with a learning rate of 0.01 and a memory capacity of 50 examples per class from the start of the second experience. All score calibration methods mentioned in Table 1 hold statistical significance with a p-value less than 0.01. Conversely, the results for the Split CIFAR-100 and the OpenLJ datasets are presented in Appendix A and B, respectively. Moreover, the source code for our evaluation study has been made publicly accessible on the GitHub platform at the specified URL. This implementation utilizes the PyTorch deep learning framework and provides a fully functional, readily customizable incremental learning protocol that is available for use. System: Ubuntu
