A localized alteration in knot diagrams is referred to as an unknotting operation. It can be demonstrated that any knot diagram can be converted into a trivial unknot through a sequence of unknotting operations, combined with some variations in the diagram configuration, which are referred to as Reidemeister moves. Unknotting operations hold significant value in the field of knot theory; they serve a purpose in analyzing the intricacy of knots and knot-related properties. Moreover, they also have implications in the fields of biology, chemistry, and physics for studying complexly intertwined structures of molecules, substances, and DNA. The purpose of this paper was to introduce a novel type of unknotting operation, which is called the diagonal move, applicable to classical and welded knots. The study shows that the cross-over change, the delta-move, the sharp-move, the gamma-move, the n-gon move, the pass move, and the 4-move can be achieved by applying a sequence of diagonal moves. The study also delves into defining a distance measure that originates from the diagonal move, as well as examining its characteristics. The distance defined by the diagonal move offers an alternative proof for the classification of welded knots, in addition to outperforming the classical knot distance in several cases. The research with the new distance also proves the niticity of torus knots and proves the n-gon move necessary for knots situated on the surface of a sphere. The study's findings on the niticity of links in a real three-dimensional space remain open. The paper concludes with a set of rules that can be applied to remove crossings from a diagram, which is a novel form of braid-like representation of knots and links. The relationship between the new representation, called the diagonal basis, and the original knot diagram is established through a sequence of diagonal moves, thereby proving the existence of a diagonal basis for any knot or link. The study's findings can be applied to welded links, and it also demonstrates that the new basis shares many characteristics with the original knot diagram. The research with the new basis raises additional open questions and potential contributions to the field of knot theory, its applications, and related studies. The study's results can be verified using computer software, such as Jknot. The research with the new basis also provides a theoretical framework for defining a distance measure, which can be applied to knots and links in any spatial dimension. The study's findings can be applied to the study of complexly intertwined structures of molecules, substances, and DNA, and they provide a new perspective

Furthermore, for finite harmonic mappings between tropical curves, the rational function semifield of the first curve can be expressed as a finite set of elements over the pull-back of the rational function semifield of the second curve. This fact demonstrates the significance of our initial discovery within the context of tropical geometry. Additionally, we derive a corollary regarding the finite generation of the semifields associated with subgraphs of a connected graph. This discovery builds on a preceding finding by the second listed author, proving that I(X) integrated over the Gramain 1-cycles generates the Casson invariant, a singular, nontrivial Vassiliev invariant of order two after accounting for scalar multiplication factors. Similarities can be drawn with a part of Mortier's research. Nonetheless, in contrast to but also inspired by his result, we achieve this proof for all long knots without reliance on a specific deformation of knots. Instead, our approach utilizes the Knudsen's modification of Gramain 1-cycles for long knots and integrates it with Fox-Hatcher 1-cycles. As a result, an order three, nontrivial Vassiliev invariant is produced. New research by the KATRIN collaboration provides strong evidence that electron anti-neutrino masses are limited to less than 0.8 eV/c^2. In this study, we analyze how combining this upper limit with an existing minimum mass for neutrinos, around 0.4 eV/c^2 as indicated by stellar stability, may lead to the complete restriction of available parameter space for neutrino masses in the coming years. This research is then expanded to consider sterile neutrinos, establishing a minimum mass for a single such neutrino flavour. Furthermore, we explore the potential for matter-antimatter asymmetry within the neutrino community itself. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings in the context of neutrino extended Standard Model, particularly concerning dark matter problems and the need for additional creation mechanisms. In addition, we mention the importance of distinguishing between active and sterile neutrinos in future high-energy photon and hadron probes of neutrino physics. This work is ultimately a follow-up to our earlier research in the fields of neutrino physics, extended Standard Model, and dark matter. In this paper, we also include a section that explains the underlying mathematics used in the analysis. In the context of neutrino physics, this involves discussing the neutrino density matrix, its relevance to flavour oscillations, as well as the creation and detection of neutrino pairs through two-body processes involving electrons and anti-protons. We demonstrate how the available neutrino mass space is constrained by the recent findings from KATRIN and an existing minimum mass for neutrinos, and discuss the implications of these limitations on the neutrino density matrix. Additionally, we elaborate on the distinction between active and sterile neutrinos, and their respective oscillation behaviours. We also explore the role of neutrino magnetic moments in their production and the associated constraints on such couplings. In the case of neutrino physics, this includes a discussion on the discovery potential of a next-generation dark matter detector, such as the DM-TPC, as well as the importance of distinguishing between active and sterile neutrinos in future electron anti-proton colliders. We conclude by highlighting the significance of further research into neutrino physics, the need to differentiate between active and sterile neutrinos, and the importance of meeting the sensitivity requirements of next-generation dark matter detectors. We also emphasize the value of considering existing limits on neutrino masses, together with any potential constraints that may arise from future research, such as those that could stem from improved accuracy in measuring electron anti-neutrino masses. Consequently, matrix multiplication, the most frequently used matrix operation, can pose performance bottlenecks when applied to large matrices. To mitigate this, the integration of parallel computing techniques, such as CUDA and openMP, has become essential. This study compares sequential and parallel approaches to matrix multiplication, with findings indicating that parallel processing has a profound impact on computational efficiency, particularly with larger matrices. In this context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that enables several entities to train a robust machine learning model jointly, without exchanging sensitive information about their data. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. Given its versatility, vertical FL is deemed particularly suitable for collaborative training by major enterprises. Here we concentrate on FL and delve into possible privacy breaches in actual VFL implementations. Two applicable attacks were created by us - one is called a reverse multiplication attack designed to circumvent logistic regression, while the other, known as a reverse sum attack, targets XGBoost protocols. Our empirical study validates that both attacks are successful, effective, evasive, and straightforward - they do not diverge from the predefined protocol, nor do they lower the model's accuracy; even with data encrypted. Additionally, we found out the stolen information can train a new machine learning classifier which is just as accurate as the one trained using actual data, without knowing beforehand much about the target user. Our analysis highlights potential preventive strategies, while revealing challenges that might give rise to several exciting research opportunities. Finally, due to the widespread adoption of FL in various settings, including critical sectors like healthcare and finance, it is crucial to address these privacy concerns thoroughly. As a result, we make four contributions here - we raise two important research questions; introduce a novel attack on XGBoost; study the overall performance of both attacks on real-world data; and provide both theoretical and practical solutions to prevent these attacks. In the process, we also experiment with cutting-edge encryption methods, offering qualitative and quantitative insights that could benefit the broader FL community. Ultimately, our work underscores the necessity for a more comprehensive exploration of privacy concerns in FL, encompassing both theoretical and practical aspects. As such, we hope our findings will give rise to further research into privacy-preserving FL, an area that holds immense potential but also poses significant challenges that await the next generation of FL researchers. As we conclude, it is essential to emphasize that privacy issues in FL demand immediate attention, given the technology's growing presence in various sectors and its widespread adoption. In fact, it is not uncommon to come across FL deployment guides that recommend ignoring attacks like the ones we introduced, as according to them, such incidents are mere exceptions. However, studies have shown that exceptional cases can actually become the norm

Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. In response, Random Fourier Features were proposed to approximate kernel functions using randomized transformations, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on larger data sets. While widely adopted, this method has significant drawbacks, notably requiring an unnecessarily large number of features, directly proportional to the size of the dataset, in order to achieve satisfactory results comparable to traditional kernel-based methods. In order to circumvent these issues, we introduce an alternative method of kernel approximation that leverages insights specific to the underlying data set, in order to achieve a more efficient and precise approximation. We demonstrate through extensive experimentation that our approach outperforms both RFF and a contemporary, data-agnostic method, achieving comparable results to traditional kernel-based methods on a range of classification and regression tasks. Furthermore, we showcase that our approach yields a practical and efficient solution for handling large data sets. The source code for our method is publicly available online. In particular, we discovered that utilizing features specific to the underlying data set allows for approximations that are multiple orders of magnitude more efficient than RFF, achieving a similar level of accuracy with a tiny fraction of the number of features. In other words, we found that using only 1-16 features per data point is sufficient to achieve a high level of accuracy, in contrast to RFF which requires at least 10,000 features per data point in order to achieve a similar level of accuracy. This significant improvement in efficiency is achieved despite using approximately the same number of computational resources. We believe that this work contributes a novel and effective solution for approximating kernel functions on large data sets, enabling the use of kernel methods in applications with millions of data points. In addition to its general applicability, we also demonstrate that our method is particularly well-suited for handling large datasets in domains such as time series data, text data, and graph data, due to its data-dependent nature which yields a more accurate approximation with a much smaller number of features. This, in turn, allows for more effective reduction of large datasets into lower-dimensional representations, using techniques such as PCA and UMAP. We expect this to further enhance the practical utility of kernel methods in these domains. Reasoning about and sequencing unordered events is a crucial skill to understand real-world procedures, which often require grasping temporal common sense and incorporating various forms of information. Real-world procedures are commonly communicated through a combination of written text and visual aids. The ability to accomplish this task is essential for complex tasks like planning sequential tasks and summarizing instructional content from multiple sources. Although humans can easily understand and sequence unordered multimodal procedural instructions, the same cannot be said about current machine learning models. In our research, we assess the ability of machine learning models to understand and sequence unordered multimodal instructions by compiling datasets from widely-used instructional manuals and gathering extensive human feedback. Our findings show that these models not only perform much worse than humans but also struggle to efficiently use the information provided in both textual and visual forms. In an effort to enhance the performance of machines on this task, we introduce sequential-aware pretraining techniques that make use of the sequential connections present in both written text and visual aids, leading to significant improvements exceeding 5%. When applied to the task of sequencing alone, these techniques result in an impressive 15% increase in accuracy. Our work showcases the substantial challenge that machine learning models still face when reasoning about and sequencing unordered events from multiple sources and highlights the crucial importance that sequential information holds in this context. These insights are valuable not only for machine learning models but also for any technique that aims to enhance their ability to understand real-world procedures from multimodal instructional content. In addition to presenting our findings, we also introduce a new evaluation metric called parallelization, which effectively allocates work between human annotators and reduces the time it takes to prepare datasets of sequential action-event pairs by as much as 50%. This improvement comes without any compromise in data quality as verified by additional human feedback. This technique can be applied to any existing dataset prepared using traditional label schemes that rely on explicit timing information. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is examined in detail. Based on percolation theory, the authors analyze the effects of removing a single node that causes other nodes to disconnect from the main component. Specifically, this paper investigates the number of nodes that become disconnected from the main component as a result of removing one node. By applying this micro-level approach to a random attack on a Cayley tree network, the distribution of the resulting node removal sizes is derived. The findings indicate that this distribution follows a skewed form, characterized by a growing maximum value as the network size increases. Notably, this distribution diverges from the typical geometric form often observed in natural phenomena. Furthermore, this divergence is found to be a broad phenomenon that arises from the specific structure of the network, rather than a characteristic unique to the Cayley tree. In fact, the geometric form can be restored by modifying the network through the addition of loops, a change that affects node removal sizes in a non-intuitive manner. Theoretical calculations are verified through extensive simulations. The results of this study provide insights into the inherent properties of complex networks that give rise to the geometric form of node removal sizes. In turn, this understanding can be utilized to design more effective strategies for attacking these networks. The added loops transform the network from a state where removal sizes follow a geometric distribution to one where they follow a power law distribution, with distinct implications for the spread of diseases or malicious information. Furthermore, this knowledge can be applied to optimize the attack or immunization of these networks by identifying the critical role that loops play in determining removal sizes. The power law distribution observed in these networks raises significant concerns as their vulnerability increases substantially with each additional node. The study extends to a symmetrized form of this weight known as the generalized sextic Freud weight, resulting in a parallel investigation of the associated polynomials' properties. A connection between the semi-classical orthogonal polynomials and a specialized matrix model is established, enabling the derivation of key properties through random matrix theory. This approach is demonstrated through a concrete example with the classical Airy polynomial, where the associated matrix model reveals an interesting relationship between the standard Airy polynomial and a specific tridiagonal matrix ensemble. The general case, however, requires a more complex matrix model consisting of a non-tridiagonal form, leading to an expectation that its corresponding polynomials will exhibit an non-tridiagonal recurrence coefficient matrix. A notable exception is shown to occur under an odd degree condition, resulting in a tridiagonal form for the matrix. The resulting polynomials from this condition are found to be connected to a well-known family of classical polynomials known as the Hermite polynomials. The relationship between the standard Airy polynomial and its underlying matrix model provides an intuitive explanation for its unique zero distribution pattern. The investigation into the polynomials' properties is primarily numerical in nature, due to the absence of a closed-form expression for a critical parameter. The associated recurrence coefficients and zero loci values are presented graphically in a visual format for both the standard Airy polynomial and its higher degree counterparts. The study is further expanded to consider a sub-family of the semi-classical orthogonal polynomials relative to the generalized Airy weight, under an additional constraint which results in an explicit, closed-form expression for the critical parameter. The resulting polynomials are an extension to a well-studied family of classical polynomials known as the Laguerre polynomials, and are demonstrated to possess a central zero location pattern, characterized by an infinite sequence of alternating zeros within the interval [-1, 1]. The generic form of these polynomials allows for a direct, implicit expression of their underlying recurrence coefficients, zeros and asymptotic behavior. The associated theorem provides a formalized proof of this implicit relationship, through a combination of mathematical induction and the properties of a specialized differential operator. The study of these polynomials is an exploration into an unexplored dimension of semi-classical orthogonal polynomials, and is expected to contribute to a broader understanding of the underlying structure shared by classical and semi-classical orthogonal polynomials. A question remains regarding the secondary component of GW190814 - whether it's a neutron star or a black hole of minimal mass. Researchers have introduced an energy density functional, named BigApple, which accurately matches the neutron star's mass of 2.60 solar masses and is in line with GW190814's data. By utilizing BigApple along with four well-established relativistic mean-field forces, a study delves into the characteristics of finite nuclei, nuclear matter, and neutron stars. The predicted properties of finite nuclei and calculated quantities of nuclear matter align well with empirical and experimental values, demonstrating the BigApple parameter set's reliability. Notably, BigApple successfully matches GW190814's data for canonical tidal deformability, while the dimensionless moment of inertia falls within the estimated range based on PSR J0737-3039A's analysis. Interestingly, BigApple indicates that a neutron star can support barotropic modes of oscillation, including f-mode quasiperiodic oscillations with frequencies below 10 Hz. The study also examines the densities and temperatures of neutron star crusts and the quasiperiodic oscillation value, confirming they align with expectations. Furthermore, BigApple demonstrates that a neutron star with a mass similar to GW190814's smaller component can still drive a GW through density fluctuations at high frequencies, thus potentially producing a characteristic signal in gravitational-wave detectors. The study concludes by exploring BigApple's potential for predicting the internal structure of neutron stars in future multi-band observations of quasiperiodic oscillations and tidal interactions in binary neutron star mergers. Researchers suggest that detecting the signature of a neutron star's interior in gravitational waves and quasiperiodic oscillations could serve as a test for general relativity's breakdown and the existence of phase transitions in the strong interaction. Researchers explored the capabilities of the NA62 experiment at CERN to enhance restrictions on a specific parameter in the Standard Model, specifically related to the interaction between a particular lepton and heavy neutral particles. By analyzing the process of $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$, they determined the present limit can be set at $2\times 10^{-6}$ for a particular lepton interaction with masses ranging from 125 to 144 MeV, a region that current production searches lack in depth. Combining existing data with optimized detection tools or improved photon rejection techniques can significantly narrow this limit. For the NA62 full data set, a more stringent limit of $2\times 10^{-8}$ can be achieved at 95% confidence level for a heavy neutral particle mass of 125 MeV. This study also provides a detailed detection strategy which can be applicable to other processes involving long-lived particles like $K^+ \to \pi^0 \mu^+ N$. Additionally, a more precise determination of the $K^+ \to \gamma \gamma$ decay volume, a standard process, can be obtained as a side benefit. This procedure involves using observed events of $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ to calculate the detection efficiency for $K^+ \to \pi^0 \gamma \gamma$, therefore enhancing its already established naively accurate value. This study also includes an update of existing theoretical predictions relating to this process. Naive but accurate numerical simulation tools such as SIMULAKR, NA62 specific version, are capable of handling complex detection processes involving particle identification. These tools are publicly available at https://gitlab.cern/unusualdecays/SIMULAKR.

This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during grid stress. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk-averse decision-making practices. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. Our research provides a framework for addressing this issue and a novel method for assessing storage units' risk and risk tolerance. This allows us to explore storage units' behavior under different levels of risk aversion and provides insights that can be used to design more effective market mechanisms to encourage storage units to participate in local price speculation. This, in turn, can enhance the stability of future low-carbon power grids. This issue is particularly relevant in regions with high shares of solar and wind power, given the increasing presence of energy storage systems in these areas. If left unaddressed, it may impede the development of energy storage technologies and compromise the ability of these systems to stabilize the grid in response to weather-induced fluctuations. This problem will only worsen as energy storage units' market share increases. To better understand storage units' behavior, we developed a novel method that employs a mean-variance approach, combining historical price data and drawing on the Kenen- Rogoff portfolio bubble model. This framework, derived from a stochastic self-scheduling model incorporating real data from the Australian electricity market, includes a logical approach for identifying and excluding anomalous price periods and models storage units' local price speculation activity. This research provides a timely contribution to the debate on the design of energy storage systems' incentives and market mechanisms and could be a valuable reference for researchers studying storage units' behavior in other contexts. Deep neural networks (DNNs) benefit from being trained on optimal subsets of annotated data. Active learning algorithms effectively achieve this by pinpointing data samples that are essential for improving DNN performance. The method is particularly advantageous in large-scale industrial settings where labeling costs are exorbitant. The emergence of self-supervised pretraining underscores the significance of leveraging unlabeled data for enhanced model performance. Integrating active learning with self-supervised pretraining allows the exploitation of vast amounts of unlabeled data in tandem with targeted annotation of crucial samples. 

Our investigation combines active learning and self-supervised pretraining in the context of ImageNet. The evaluation reveals that results on modest, commonly used benchmark datasets do not reflect actual performance. Instead, we find that the best active learning approach is to employ a prototypical network on uncompressed ImageNet data. Notably, our study shows that protocol constraints can hinder active learning effectiveness and highlights the need for unsupervised data augmentation techniques that mitigate shifts in data distributions. 

The investigation continues with the examination of two novel active learning challenges: analyzing uncertain models and accounting for annotation costs. The former is addressed by incorporating a score that gauges model confidence, while the latter is resolved by giving due consideration to the expense associated with annotating specific data samples. 

Our study concludes with the evaluation of active learning methods against two cutting-edge self-supervised pretraining baselines. The evaluation is conducted on the CIFAR-100 dataset and uncovers that active learning algorithms continue to demonstrate superior performance even after employing self-supervised pretraining. The study ultimately highlights the potential for active learning to enhance both supervised and self-supervised pretraining by targeting critical data samples. The potential implications and future research directions in this domain are also discussed. 

The code and models used in this study are publicly available at https://github.com/aleks Appreciate/active-learning-imagenet-scale.

This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively improves both the accuracy and reliability of the model with only a limited increase in training data. The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine structured knowledge for enhanced performance.  Additionally, multiple data augmentation techniques have been discovered to be valuable tools in natural language processing tasks.  Building on prior work incorporating BERT and WordNet knowledge, this study explores various data augmentation techniques in context-gloss pairs to enhance the efficacy of WSD.  Experimental results indicate that both sentence and word-level augmentation strategies are effective in addressing WSD, while the incorporation of hypernyms' definitions from a lexical knowledge base can further improve performance.  A comparative analysis of different context-gloss augmentation techniques is conducted, revealing that the application of back translation to definitions produces the most satisfactory outcomes.  Furthermore, this study investigates the inherent resilience of WSD to noise, introduces a novel evaluation metric named Sense Embedding Distance, and explores the relationship between data size and WSD accuracy.  All experimental code and models have been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zheng-hao-wang/Context-gloss-augmentation-for-WSD. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. This finding paves the way for more complex searches in future proton-nucleus collisions. On the other hand, the ATLAS experiment reported a 4.4-standard-deviation excess in events consisting of an electron or muon, and at least four jets; however, this excess was not statistically significant once the top quark pair contribution was accounted for. Both experiments are now prepared to conduct more intricate searches in future proton-nucleus collisions. A combined analysis of the two experiments resulted in a 6.2-standard-deviation excess, and the resulting cross-sectional measurement was 44.8 ± 6.6 nanobarns. This research focuses on resolving collision avoidance for non-holonomic robots moving at constant speeds in a two-dimensional space, leveraging dynamic vortex potential fields and their gradients to create cooperative behavior between the robots. A variable repulsive force field, sensitive to velocity and position of nearby robots, is introduced to prevent the emergence of local minima, and only activates when a robot approaches a potential collision with other mobile robots or stationary objects. It's demonstrated through kinematic analysis that a cooperating robot can evade non-cooperative robots moving at constant speeds or actively attempting to collide, under conditions specified by potential field parameters, and this cooperative approach is verified through experiments using a mobile robot platform. Additionally, the study finds that its cooperative performance can surpass that of higher-dimensional methods in certain close approach scenarios. Further, it shows that by adjusting the potential field's parameters, a cooperating robot can mitigate the impact of a recurring collision or switch to an avoidance mode in response to dynamic changes in target locations. The research also explores and visualizes potential field landscapes through 3D plotting. It is also shown that its cooperative behavior can be applied to multiple robots through simple extension of the variable repulsive force field method. The study's findings are presented through both simulation and video of actual experiments using a mobile robot platform. It is argued that this method's cooperative and robust performance in complex dynamic scenarios makes it a suitable solution for its target applications requiring non-cooperative robot avoidance, such as cooperative navigation, formation control, and mobile manipulation tasks. The method's potential for handling more complex dynamic scenarios also makes it a suitable solution for its other target applications including autonomous aerial vehicles and spacecraft navigation and control tasks. Recent advancements in wireless communications research have led to increasing interest in the Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology. Comprised of passive reflective components that can modulate the characteristics of incoming waveforms, such as phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization, an IRS offers a means to actively control the characteristics of wireless channels. Given its promising properties, researchers are looking into the potential of incorporating IRS technology into radar systems to optimize target parameter estimation. This paper provides a theoretical basis for implementing IRS technology in radar systems, with a particular focus on scenarios where the line-of-sight (LOS) link between the radar and target is obstructed or weak. We investigate the potential of utilizing IRS technology to create a virtual non-line-of-sight (NLOS) link, enhancing radar performance and target parameter estimation. Through numerical simulations and comparative analyses under both optimized and non-optimized scenarios, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the IRS-provided virtual link in target parameter estimation when the LOS link strength is lower than a relative strength of $~10^{-1}$ in comparison to the NLOS link. Additionally, we explore the optimal reflection coefficients that minimize the mean squared error (MSE) of target parameter estimation and provide a 12-dimensional optimization framework that takes into account both the real and imaginary components of the scattering matrix $\mathbf{S}$, radar waveform $\mathbf{b}$, and IRS reflection coefficients $\mathbf{u}$. A practical implementation of this framework is also discussed, along with the effects of its limitations on target parameter estimation. Finally, we conduct a numerical investigation into the effects of increasing the complexity of this optimization problem, demonstrating the potential performance improvements achievable through further optimization in scenarios where the LOS link strength is lower than a relative strength of $~10^{-3}$. Overall, this research provides a scientific basis for implementing IRS technology in radar systems, with potential applications in target parameter estimation, as well as radar-based communication systems, and may contribute to the development of optimized radar waveforms through the provision of a quantitative framework that considers the characteristics of wireless channels. This research may also be relevant to the development of optimized communication protocols, a problem that is mathematically equivalent to the optimized target parameter estimation problem discussed in this paper. This finding is particularly significant in scenarios where the LOS link strength is lower than a relative strength of $~10^{-3}$. Approximately nine years ago, Azrieli and Shmaya introduced a category of $\lambda$-Lipschitz games where each player's payoff function is influenced by a $\lambda$-Lipschitz rate in response to other players' actions. Their work demonstrated that these types of games have the capacity for achieving $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria under specific $\epsilon$ and $\lambda$ settings. Despite their findings, they left unanswered the question regarding the complexity of obtaining such equilibrium points. Our work contributes a query-efficient conversion from broader classes of games to those defined as Lipschitz games, thereby allowing us to derive a lower-bound restriction for the efficiency of randomized algorithms in finding $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria in $n$-player games with binary actions and specific $\lambda$-Lipschitz properties, with an exponential relationship between the complexity and the ratio of $\frac{n\lambda}{\epsilon}$. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of 'Multi-Lipschitz games' that incorporate distinct Lipschitz rates for each player, followed by a transformation from equilibrium-finding tasks within this broader class to similar tasks within the domain of $\lambda$-Lipschitz games, with implications on the sum of individual $\lambda$-Lipschitz parameters. Finally, we establish a lower-bound restriction indicating that deterministic algorithms experience an exponential increase in complexity in finding $\epsilon$-approximate correlated equilibria in $n$-player games with multiple action options and specific $\lambda$-Lipschitz properties for particularly restrictive $\epsilon$-value settings, thereby advocating the utilization of randomized algorithms in our previous analysis and further contributing to our methodological simplifications over prior work yielding comparable results. Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set. The models are then combined, and the results are averaged to obtain the final scores. We demonstrate that this method yields significantly lower variance compared to standard k-fold CV and facilitates more effective parameter tuning by leveraging implicit ensembles of models. In line with our findings, we recommend utilizing the j-k fold CV method for both parameter tuning and model evaluation to ensure more reliable and robust results. Moreover, we introduce an open-source Python framework called HyperBayesOpt, which provides a flexible framework for optimizing NLP models through Bayesian methods. The framework is designed to handle large-scale experiments, integrates the HyperOpt library for both Bayesian optimization and successively more aggressive variations, and includes a user-friendly interface for easily adjusting parameters such as the number of folds in j-k fold CV. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates significantly, taking on an asymmetric shape as a result of a shift in frequency that is equivalent in magnitude to the natural width of a specific atomic transition in strontium. This effect becomes more pronounced under conditions of high saturation. Our research incorporated momentum transfers resulting from the absorption and emission of photons, as described by a modified version of the optical Bloch equations. To overcome these influences, our findings suggest that using broader light sources or employing counter-propagating light beams may be necessary. Notably, we observed a significant impact on our results when comparing theory and experiment, with the latter showing a greater influence from collisions between atoms. This study supplements our earlier research on WIMP-scattered nuclei, specifically examining how the incident velocity of these particles influences the scattering probability as they interact with target nuclei across various recoil angles and narrow energy ranges. Our simulation reveals that not only do the incident velocity characteristics of halo WIMPs play a crucial role, but so does the angle of the recoil itself, resulting in an irregular correlation of the two in specific energy ranges. Consequently, attempting to infer the 1-dimensional velocity distribution within these ranges directly from the overall WIMP halo velocities may not provide a complete or accurate understanding, which would ultimately distort our calculations of the associated scattering event rates in those particular ranges. Instead, we propose using a 3-dimensional phase-space analysis to accurately quantify the usual event rate patterns in such scenarios. This approach enables us to derive a general formula that integrates the product of the initial and final velocity components relative to the direction of the recoil angle. This formula serves as the standard for evaluating the associated event rates in any given 3-dimensional velocity distributions, which in the case of the standard halo model, equates to approximately 0.42 in terms of the normalized event rates at 90-degree recoil angles. Furthermore, we found that even when considering only scattered nuclei with recoil angles greater than 90 degrees, about 25% of the associated event rates still originate from initial velocities greater than the solar escape velocity, which could have implications for interpreting potential signatures of WIMP scattering in experiments with restricted recoil angle ranges. Our research also highlights the significance of properly accounting for the relationship between the initial and final velocity components in any analytical or theoretical studies related to WIMP-scattered nuclei. We have made our simulation code publicly available to facilitate further investigation into these findings. Additionally, we have introduced a new statistical method for identifying the underlying velocity distribution of WIMPs, which includes a test for determining whether a given velocity distribution is consistent with the observed data, as well as a component that uses a likelihood ratio approach to compare different candidate velocity distributions and thereby determine the most plausible one given the data. This new method can be applied to any theoretical velocity distribution and is highly versatile, capable of handling even complex distributions by integrating an analytical approximation of the scattering cross-section that incorporates the initial and final velocity components. Our study has implications for current and planned direct detection experiments seeking to identify WIMPs, as well as potential signatures of other low-energy particles such as BOSON-stable WIMPs or ALP-scattered nuclei. The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples. This improvement in computational speed doesn't come at the cost of accuracy, as our method produces identical test results to Monte Carlo methods. In light of these findings, we believe that NLP systems researchers should reuse and prefer the exact paired-permutation test over Monte Carlo methods. In addition to sharing our algorithm, we also examine popular structured test statistics widely used in NLP systems and show that all of them can be computed exactly using our framework. This work will give guidance to researchers on selecting suitable test statistics for their tasks and encourage them to incorporate the exact paired-permutation test in their evaluation pipelines. This is also an open-source reproduction of our experiments that other researchers can use as a reference. This work is an extension of our previous research on paired-permutation testing. Graph neural networks have excelled in multiple applications by leveraging relational data. These models combine node features with the graph structure, creating flexible and effective models, but they can be challenging to interpret due to their implicit representation of node interactions and graph connectivity. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called Kedge, which involves explicitly reducing unnecessary graph edges by selectively removing neighboring nodes. By utilizing the Hard Kumaraswamy distribution for edge sparsification, Kedge enables a flexible integration with existing GNN models through gradient-based optimization. Experiments demonstrate that Kedge effectively prunes a substantial proportion of graph edges with minimal accuracy degradation. Notably, Kedge achieved a reduction of over 80% of edges on the PubMed dataset with only a 2% decrease in accuracy, indicating that node features have a more significant impact than graph connectivity. Furthermore, Kedge effectively mitigates the over-smoothing issue prevalent in deep GNNs by maintaining robust task performance even with multiple GNN layers. To facilitate further research, we have made the Kedge code and dataset samples publicly available at https://www.github.com/CompVis-Kedge/kedge. Overall, Kedge offers an appealing solution for interpretable GNNs by striking a balance between incorporating all node features and explicit edge sparsification. Leveraging this approach, we performed comprehensive experiments that highlight its effectiveness in producing more efficient, less complex, and highly interpretable GNN models. Despite only sparsifying the node interaction part of GNNs, Kedge achieved comparable performance to other pruning methods that target both node features and graph structures. As a result, we recommend Kedge for anyone seeking a straightforward way to reduce the complexity of GNNs. To further explore edge sparsification in GNNs, we have also developed an open-source repository along with detailed guidance for utilizing Kedge in various settings at https://www.github.com/CompVis-Kedge/kedge. Effective management of controllable loads relies on the strategic deployment of aggregators that can efficiently convey their flexible capabilities, referred to as aggregate flexibility, to system operators. Current approaches typically involve time-consuming estimates, with minimal focus on real-time coordination between aggregators and operators. This paper proposes a solution to an online optimization problem within a closed-loop system by introducing a real-time feedback mechanism known as maximum entropy feedback (MEF). Analytical properties of MEF are examined, and it is shown that MEF can be approximated through reinforcement learning and utilized as a penalty term in the penalized predictive control (PPC) algorithm, an adaptation of model predictive control (MPC). Key benefits of our approach include (1) reduced communication demands for operators, requiring only MEF information, (2) faster computational processing due to lower variable counts, and (3) lower operational costs, with certain assumptions indicating optimal performance. The proposed PPC is evaluated on an adaptive electric vehicle charging dataset, yielding superior outcomes compared to traditional MPC methods. The code is publicly accessible on GitHub at the specified URL. Scaling and future directions for our approach, centered on reinforcing MEF models, are also outlined. The approach exhibits promising outcomes but involves the use of a relatively expensive actor critic deep reinforcement learning algorithm, which may need further optimization for larger-scale applications. The approach assumes a fixed MEF target, which could be an inefficient representation for certain types of flexibility, such as thermal storage, that can exceed their flexibility target. Instead, a new approach is presented that involves time-varying flexibility targets, derived from historical flexibility data, which can provide a more accurate representation of flexibility capabilities. This approach is referred to as time-varying maximum entropy feedback (TV-MEF). The TV-MEF model exhibits several benefits over standard MEF models, including (1) increased flexibility utilization, (2) reduced operational costs, and (3) lower communication demands between aggregators and system operators. These improvements come at the cost of increased communication demands between the actor and critic networks of the used reinforcement learning algorithm, which could be mitigated by a future optimization of this approach. The proposed TV-MEF framework can provide a more accurate representation of flexibility capabilities for various types of flexible resources, such as thermal and electrical vehicles, which can lead to increased flexibility utilization and reduced operational costs. One of the most intriguing phenomena in astrophysics is the common envelope (CE) phase of binary star evolution, where two stars are enveloped in the shedding material from one of them. This process triggers a shrinking of the orbit as the stars interact with the envelope. Ultimately, it can result in either mergers or further complex interactions, which can involve a mix of compact objects and stars. Certain CE scenarios, particularly those involving white dwarfs, can produce supernovae, while neutron star mergers can result in gamma-ray bursts, and all types of compact object mergers can produce gravitational waves. Predicting the end states of these CEs is challenging due to their diverse origins and the intricate processes involved, which are compounded by the need to consider many systems at once in population synthesis calculations. This difficulty often prompts the use of conservation principles such as angular momentum conservation to simplify complex scenarios, such as in the case of multiple star systems. This method allows for a simpler, more intuitive approach to understanding the evolution of these systems, which can then be compared to more detailed simulations. This particular approach is useful for studying the widest multiple star systems, which are often similar to binary systems but with additional components that can affect their evolution. This paper presents a new formalism, called SCATTER, which provides a detailed simulation of all possible outcomes from the common envelope phase, especially in multiple star systems. This formalism succeeds in producing a comprehensive inventory of all possible end products, which can then be compared to observed populations of binary and multiple star systems. This comparison includes analyzing the secondaries in post-common envelope binaries, multiple star systems that have escaped CE phases, and a sample of 15 narrow multiple star systems which likely underwent CE phases. These findings provide constraints on the parameters of this formalism, particularly regarding the common envelope ejection efficiency of less dense low-mass stars and the behavior of live companions in multiple star systems. These conclusions also shed light on the origin of Type II SNe from post-common envelope secondaries, the rates of compact object mergers, and supernovae from such events. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that multiple star systems provide crucial evidence to support the standard model of common envelope evolution, and it paves the way for further studies on the effects of live companions in these systems. Initially, we consider the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and then compare the predictions with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). Our primary analysis concerns the double Higgs production process in the two EFTs through the dominant subprocess $WW \to HH$. We calculate the cross-section of this subprocess for all polarization channels and relevant effective operators at various energies, and demonstrate how in the HEFT case, the cross-section primarily depends on two leading coefficients at these TeV scales. We then establish the equivalence between the dominant coefficients of the HEFT and SMEFT at the level of the scattering amplitude for this subprocess. We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and hydrogel grains, at various speeds and depths. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood by studying the flow of sediment around the cylinder and estimating the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends. A model was developed that accurately predicts the anisotropy and how it changes in response to differences in speed, the ratio of the cylinder's length to its width, and whether the grains it is moving through have high friction or little friction. This model may be applicable to a wide range of situations where a solid moves through a layer of grains, including the movement of swimming animals through aquatic beds and the flow of wind or water over sandy surfaces. This model also raises questions about the need for further study of how animals move through sediment in water or air. This model was developed through an experiment in which a cylindrical solid with a 20mm diameter and varying lengths was moved through a layer of grains at different speeds and depths. This experiment involved a collaboration of two researchers, though the data was verified by a third. Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas usage times. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows actually exceeds the amount of gas converted into new stars, indicating a limit on how quickly gas can be turned into stars due to outflows. Our findings support the idea that outflows play a critical role in regulating the conversion of gas into stars, highlighting the need for further studies of outflows in galaxies across the universe. Observations of outflows can be used as a diagnostic for star formation rates and gas properties, such as mass and use rate. Our research also suggests that radio continuum observations can be used as a non-expensive indicator of star formation-driven outflows. A supplemental analysis of a sample of galaxies shows that more massive galaxies tend to have stronger outflows, and that there is an overall correlation between outflow strength and galaxy mass. However, when controlling for gas content, this correlation disappears, suggesting that outflows are related to how quickly gas is used up rather than simply being more prevalent in more massive galaxies. Additionally, we found that ultraviolet emission in these galaxies is often offset from the center, indicating that there is a time lag between star formation and the subsequent emission of UV light, and that this lag is consistent with the typical lifetime of a massive star. Furthermore, we observed a linear relationship between this lag and the gas usage time, and that this lag is sufficient for a significant amount of gas to be expelled from the galaxy through starbursts. Our study provides spatially resolved evidence for the regulation of star formation by outflows, and highlights the importance of further studies of outflows in galaxies across the universe, particularly those that are being used up quickly. Our research also offers a new method for detecting and studying outflows in galaxies, and shows that radio continuum observations can be used as a diagnostic for star formation rates and gas properties. Current auto-tuning frameworks for computer systems face challenges due to their large configuration spaces and the difficulties associated with evaluating their performance. Recently, researchers have made progress in this area using probabilistic models in Structured Bayesian Optimization (SBO), a technique that rapidly converges to optimal configurations by exploiting expert-provided contextual information about the system's structure. Despite its effectiveness, the SBO approach has limited adoption due to the complexity involved in building probabilistic models. To address this issue, we introduce BoAnon, an SBO framework that enables the discovery of system structures from logs, allowing for the incorporation of expert knowledge. By combining this learned structure with expert-provided performance models and dependency information, BoAnon generates a probabilistic graph model. This model accelerates the optimization process, allowing BoAnon to identify efficient configurations significantly faster than existing methods. Through evaluation of a hardware architecture search problem, BoAnon demonstrates a notable improvement in energy-latency objectives, achieving a 5-7x factor improvement over the default architecture. The innovative approach of BoAnon, based on its contextual structure learning, paves the way for the successful application of SBO in various computer system optimization scenarios. To facilitate adoption, we release BoAnon's implementation and application notes to guide other researchers and system experts in applying this approach to their own systems of interest. With the framework's rapid configuration evaluation capability, BoAnon has the potential to accelerate the development of efficient computer systems. To further demonstrate this potential, we conduct a case study on the design of high-performance Caches, a critical system that benefits greatly from optimized parameter settings. By applying BoAnon to this problem, we explore different cache design scenarios and show that this approach can efficiently identify efficient cache configurations in a demanding evaluation environment. Ultimately, BoAnon's innovative structure learning approach exemplifies the successful application of SBO in computer system optimization and can serve as a model for the discovery of system structures from logs, accelerating the discovery of high-performance system configurations. To facilitate adoption, we release BoAnon's implementation and application guidelines for researchers and system experts to explore its effectiveness on their systems of interest. With this approach, BoAnon can potentially accelerate the development of efficient computer systems. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. Notably, we observed $v_3$ to be more sensitive than $v_2$ to the presence of an on-average triaxial initial geometry in small-size and mid-central collisions. These findings suggest the interplay between initial anisotropic geometry and flow anisotropy, as well as the dependence of flow anisotropy on transverse particle density and medium viscosity. A more detailed understanding of these correlations is crucial for uncovering the properties of the medium produced in heavy-ion collisions. A comparison with experimental data from RHIC, specifically for mid-central collisions at 200 GeV, further solidifies these findings. A parametric study of the strong scalar field's impact, conducted with a quantum chromodynamics lattice, resulted in a initial geometry that is on-average triaxial in mid-central collisions and contributed to the observed $v_3$ patterns. These discoveries will be valuable for future studies aiming to explore more intricate phenomena and potential indications of collective motion in heavy-ion collisions. Additionally, they highlight the importance of investigating initial conditions and flow patterns simultaneously. Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has surged exponentially with more than 10,000 online datasets now available and formatted according to Linked Data standards, enabling seamless machine readability and interconnectivity.  While such datasets provide numerous opportunities, numerous applications remain hindered due to data of poor quality, significantly affecting tasks such as data integration, search, and interlinking.  Existing quality assessment techniques for Linked Data, although limited, suffer from decreased effectiveness with rising data sizes and become unmanageable for single-machine operations.  To address these challenges, our proposed DistQualityAssessment is an open-source, cluster-enabled implementation designed for comprehensive quality evaluation of large-scale RDF datasets, leveraging the processing capabilities of Apache Spark to distribute quality metrics computation.  This innovative, distributed in-memory approach allows for flexible metric extension via a provided quality assessment pattern and, through seamless integration with the SANSA framework, has been successfully applied in at least three external use cases, showcasing its superiority over existing methodologies.  With its scalable architecture, this project paves the way for wide-scale Linked Data quality assessment, thereby creating a more reliable foundation for applications operating on such data.  Furthermore, this project is an important step towards developing a distributed Linked Data quality dashboard, an innovative tool showcased in this paper's demo section. This dashboard provides an interactive visualization of data quality metrics and allows for configuration via a web interface.  With its innovative approach and extensive evaluation results, this project is an significant contribution to the field of Linked Data quality assessment. When working with data generated by random processes, an appropriate model is often employed for subsequent statistical analysis, but the standard method of maximum likelihood estimation is vulnerable to model imperfections and data contamination. As alternative methods without assumptions about a specific model typically lose efficiency, this paper introduces a robust procedure for estimating parameters in discrete data sets based on a well-known distance measure. Specifically, this method defines and evaluates minimum density power divergence estimators for independent increments and Markov processes, proving its consistency and providing distributional results in the context of dependent stochastic processes, ultimately showing the method's advantages in comparison to traditional maximum likelihood estimation for common processes like Poisson processes, Brownian motion with a drift and autoregressive models. This research is a follow-up to the authors' previous work on robust estimation for censored data and extends relevant results to discrete data sets. As a primary contribution, this paper fills a significant gap in the literature by formally investigating maximum likelihood estimation for continuous stochastic processes and compares the performance of the new method with traditional maximum likelihood estimation. As a practical application, the paper explores and illustrates its use through simulation studies and a real-world example before concluding with potential future research directions. This study presents temperature maps for electrons within one kiloparsec of three high-brightness Seyfert galaxies. The findings from Gemini's GMOS-IFU data, acquired at a spatial resolution of 110-280 parsecs, reveal temperature variations between 8000 to >30000 Kelvin. We discovered temperature ranges in these galaxies are significantly influenced by gas outflows producing shocks, particularly in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348, while photoionization processes fit the results for Mrk 607. The orientation of these shocks in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348 appears to be perpendicular to the axis of ionization, suggesting the potential for shock ionization to be observed more easily when obscured by a dusty torus. This implies that narrow ionization cones can coexist with wider shock patterns. These findings have implications for balancing photoionization and other processes that ionize gas in active galactic nuclei, particularly in situations where the AGN's ultraviolet radiation may not be enough to explain observed emission lines. Mrk 79 and Mrk 348 provide visual evidence of gas outflows previously detected in absorption or through optical recombination lines and support the idea that mass losses due to these outflows can be significant. If multi-ionized gas outflows like the one in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348 are common, they may contribute to the absorption seen in AGN spectra or the shapes of emission lines and have implications for our understanding of AGN feedback. This feedback could be in the form of mass losses due to gas outflows or the excitation of dust through these outflows, further influencing the surrounding interstellar medium. This discovery and its implications for gas outflows in active galactic nuclei make way for new observational and theoretical studies of these processes. As IoT systems shift towards Edge computing and less reliable infrastructure closer to users, the complex environments of IoT pose significant challenges for software developers when testing their applications. Although various testing tools are available for IoT, several issues persist, such as the absence of advanced features for logical dependencies, fault injection, and multi-platform testing. To address these shortcomings, we have developed Frisbee, a framework for the automated testing of IoT applications. By utilizing Kubernetes and virtual testbeds, Frisbee speeds up the testing process by streamlining the setup of distributed virtual environments and enabling complex 'what-if' scenario simulations. The framework's robust architecture also enables multiple testing pathways, including constraint-based searching and the injection of hardware and software faults. With a user-friendly command-line interface and support for popular programming languages, Frisbee has been effectively applied in the development of an IoT speech-based virtual assistant. Compared to traditional approaches, Frisbee accelerates test case creation and execution, reducing overall development time by at least 45%. The framework's versatility and efficiency make it an essential tool for the automated testing of IoT applications. This study concentrates on recent findings from the ATLAS collaboration, encompassing evaluations of rare occurrences like $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays and the determination of CP-violating processes in $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$. These findings contribute significantly to the development of CKM matrix knowledge or set upper limits on new physics appearances. A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. Thorough convergence and stability analyses of the modified iteration are provided, along with numerical examples showcasing its practical effectiveness. This work is a significant contribution to the development of efficient and reliable numerical methods that maintain the fundamental properties of the original PDE solution. Finally, the study is available as an open-source repository, accessible at https://github.com/numericalmathematics/gmres-preserv. Key words: structure-preserving, time-dependent PDEs, implicit time-stepping, Krylov subspace methods, iterative linear solvers. Introduction  In recent years, research on numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations (PDEs) has increasingly focused on preserving the original equation's inherent properties. Such properties, such as conservation, monotonicity, and coercivity, constitute valuable information about the original solution's behaviour, encompassing bounds on the solution's norms and the preservation of specific quantities. Consequently, structure-preserving numerical methods have emerged as the method of choice for solving a broad range of time-dependent PDEs. These methods ensure that the numerical approximations maintain the same properties as the original solution, alongside ensuring high accuracy. While explicit structure-preserving methods are generally feasible for all orders, implicit schemes are limited by the requirement to solve a nonlinear system of equations at each time-step, which is only achievable exactly in small-scale problems. To address this challenge, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and provides a comprehensive convergence analysis for both conservative and dissipative systems.Numerous numerical examples demonstrate the practical effectiveness of the modified iteration. To further showcase its potential, the study also includes a case where the flexible gmres is outperformed by its implicit counterpart.

Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detection, is a crucial capability for autonomous vehicles operating at highway speeds. They need to be able to spot obstacles from afar in order to allow enough time for the vehicle to stop. Unfortunately, the majority of existing evaluation benchmarks, like nuScenes, don't emphasize this challenge because they only assess performance within a certain range. There are a couple of key reasons for this - firstly, annotating distant objects can be difficult because lidar sensors typically only return a limited number of data points at such great distances, with almost 50% of objects more than 50m away from the sensor containing zero data points. Secondly, the commonly used metrics for evaluating three-dimensional detection tasks apply the same tolerance thresholds to near and far objects, which isn't aligned with either human vision or the disparities seen in stereo images. As a result, the task of far-field three-dimensional detection has not been given the attention it deserves. For instance, it has long been believed that high-resolution RGB sensors are key to achieving this level of detection, but a more in-depth analysis shows that lidar-based approaches outperform them. To better assess this challenge, we created a new evaluation protocol and a far-field three-dimensional detection dataset based on the scenes from the nuScenes dataset. We also introduced a simple yet highly effective approach that outperformed existing methods and used it to show that far-field three-dimensional detection is essentially a two-stage process: the first stage involves identifying potential targets and the second stage involves pinpointing their exact location. The code for our method has been made open-source and we're currently running a competition on Codeforces for the best algorithm to solve this problem. The challenge has some unusual constraints - the method must only use the training data provided and any solutions requiring too much computation will be disqualified. We hope that successful approaches to this problem will not only outperform existing methods but also lead to a deeper understanding of far-field three-dimensional detection. The evaluation protocol and dataset we created can also be used to tackle other long-tail three-dimensional detection challenges. The name "Far3Det" represents this challenge and the dataset/evaluation protocol we created to tackle it. The code for the evaluation protocol can be found at https://github.com/AmadeusG/far3det_code and the dataset can be downloaded at https://www.nuscenes.org/en/datasets#far3det. We also released a leaderboards for this challenge which can be found at https://www.nuscenes.org/en

Chemical reactions can be comprehensively understood through a primary analytical tool called the potential energy surface (PES) which maps the relationships between molecular nuclei and their energy levels. Nevertheless, this tool becomes impractically challenging to utilize because identifying a substantial number of ground states across the vast dimensions of PES requires an unreasonably large number of preparations. A recent study suggests utilizing a quantum machine learning algorithm as a more feasible approach. This model utilizes quantum data consisting of different nuclear coordinate-based ground state wavefunctions to prepare the desired states on the PES at will. A classical neural network transforms nuclear molecule coordinates into quantum variational circuit parameters and the fidelity loss function trains it to achieve optimal performance. Notably, this study found that, regardless of the complexity of molecules being studied such as hydrogen chains, water and beryllium hydride, just a small number of samples were enough to achieve high overlap rates with ground states in practice. A theoretical aspect also proves a limitation to these protocols suggesting it would be against the laws of physics if such efficient protocol could apply to regions where the ground state significantly drops in energy as in avoided crossings due to limitations imposed by Grover's lower bound. Also the amount of data that could efficiently be processed by the classical neural network is determined with respect to quantum data requirements from a quantum angle. Overall this study suggests that applications involving quantum chemistry are promising candidates to showcase the capabilities of quantum machine learning in action. The source code for the study's results reproduction is available for reference. A currently ongoing experiment at the University of Maryland aims to implement this algorithm using superconducting qubits. The study concludes by highlighting potential extensions to this research such as incorporating time-dependent situations that call for time-evolved circuits and obtaining experimental evidence for avoided crossings that should pose a limitation on quantum chemistry protocols. Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently apply to novel patient organs without retraining, also enabling robust performance against noisy intraoperative surface inputs during testing. The trained network provides an optimal displacement field to map preoperative volume to the intraoperative surface, demonstrated by multiple experiments showing its applicability and efficiency with real-world data. The developed code is now openly accessible online.
