Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. The benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to complex real-world environments. We introduce a unique method, Adversarial Metric Learning, for self-supervised flow estimation that leverages a metric learning component to comply with the data distribution and a noise reduction component to eliminate artificial points. This method dispenses with neighbor point reliance, instead focusing on the overall scene distribution. We assess our approach against multiple baseline methods on the newly created benchmark, showing its superiority in various settings. Notably, our method excels when there are only a few points sampled from LiDAR data, a configuration commonly encountered in real-world applications. The code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/HuangPeng6749/Adversarial-Metric-Learning. For further research, we discover and rectify a significant issue with synthetic datasets commonly used in 3D detection tasks, namely over-reliance on artificial points that do not adhere to the real-world point distribution. We introduce a new rule for evaluating 3D middle box points and demonstrate our self-supervised flow estimation method's effectiveness even with a high proportion of such points. With only a minor adjustment, our method achieves comparable results to baselines that use real data, highlighting its promise for addressing similar challenges in 3D detection tasks. Ultimately, our work paves the way for creating more realistic synthetic datasets that mirror real-world environments more accurately. We apply our model to a challenging LiDAR-based obstacle detection task, achieving a remarkable +10% mAP improvement over the detection model trained with real data, and make it available at https://github.com/HuangPeng6749/LiDAR-OD. A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the 2-cores of such graphs must be bipartite. We introduce a new E2F criterion based on a graph's 3-edge-colouring and prove that it is more stringent than the existing E2F criterion. With this new standard, we classify the cubic E2F graphs by showing that they can be coloured using only one colour, equivalent to a Hamiltonian cycle, or three colours, equivalent to a graph whose 2-core is a disjoint union of triangles, or they can be coloured using two colours, equivalent to a graph whose 2-core is a bipartite graph containing at least one 4-cycle. Finally, we prove that no simple cubic E2F graph exists except those already classified. Our research also provides a new and simpler proof that a cubic graph whose every perfect matching corresponds to a 3-edge-colouring using only one colour is equivalent to a Hamiltonian cycle. Additionally, we derive a local rule that can determine whether a graph has the Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property based on its 3-edge-colouring. With this rule, we classify all the cubic Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian graphs by showing that they can be coloured using only one colour, equivalent to a Hamiltonian cycle, or three colours, equivalent to a graph whose 2-core is a disjoint union of triangles, or they can be coloured using two colours, equivalent to a graph whose 2-core is a bipartite graph containing at least one 4-cycle. Finally, we prove that no simple cubic Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian graph exists except those already classified. Our research provides a new and simpler proof that a cubic graph whose every perfect matching corresponds to a 2-factor containing a Hamiltonian cycle is equivalent to a Hamiltonian cycle. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and efficient design comprising less than 500 lines of code. Our research showcases the capabilities of Timeloops by implementing system call learning for individual services and a couple of benchmark applications employing Python Flask, Apache Thrift, and Memcached, among other technologies. With the help of this approach, the best actions in critical situations of a soccer game can be optimized, leading to more strategic play and potentially more exciting matches. However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. We've developed an all-optical technique for producing optical nonreciprocity on a microchip, achieved through the process of quantum squeezing a specific mode in coupled resonator systems. A key factor in this method involves applying classical coherent light in a one-way fashion to parametrically pump a nonlinear resonator. This selective pumping induces a chiral interaction between photons within the resonators, allowing us to build optical diodes and quasi-circulators. Notably, we've demonstrated the functionality of these nonreciprocal devices even with weak input, using a combination of squeezed-vacuum fields and classical pump light. We observed isolation ratios greater than 40 dB in optical diodes, as well as a high fidelity rate for quasi-circulators. We also found that our method allows for low-loss optical communication in both directions. Furthermore, we've demonstrated the ability to control the flow of light through our system using a relatively weak control light, effectively enabling the development of nonreciprocal optical transistors. The simplicity and versatility of our method make it suitable for integrating nonreciprocal photonics functions onto a silicon chip. We've successfully implemented our method using silicon photonics components and a hybrid silicon-photonic and electrical circuit system, resulting in a working demonstration of our nonreciprocal optical transistor even with weak input. We believe that our technique has the potential to significantly contribute to the development of nonreciprocal photonics, enabling a wide range of applications that previously required the use of magnetic materials. Some potential applications include the creation of complex optical networks, broadening the spectrum of available light, and enhancing the detection of weak light. Additionally, our method may also provide a path towards implementing other nonreciprocal phenomena in coupled resonator systems. Some examples of these phenomena include the optical equivalent of the Hall effect, and nonreciprocal phase and amplitude changes in light. We have presented the results from the AstroSat analysis of the high-mass X-ray binary X-ray pulsar IGR J19294+1816 during its Type-I outburst in October 2019. Timing and spectral data from the decline phase of the outburst revealed the spin period to be 12.485 seconds, with significant spectral features. A Quasi Periodic Oscillation was observed at a frequency of 0.032 Hz and an RMS amplitude of 18%. Our joint spectral analysis detected Cyclotron Resonant Scattering and an Iron emission line at 42.7 keV and 5.5 keV respectively, further highlighting the complex nature of this intermediate spin pulsar's behavior during its 2019 outburst. Additionally, a notable decrease in maximum Cyclotron Line energy was observed, suggesting a larger Magnetic Field Strength than previously estimated. These findings, coupled with a relatively high CNDF through most of the decline phase, indicate a significant accretion rate in IGR J19294+1816, potentially resulting from a Thoroughly Spun-Up state. A comparison with other similar intermediate spin pulsars, such as XTE J1855+026, is also presented. We also discuss the possibility of a Low-Hard State in IGR J19294+1816, characterized by a high CRF and low RMS FRQ, opposite to the typical High-Soft State. Furthermore, a Quasi Periodic Oscillation at a low frequency and large amplitude, along with a high CNDF and decreased Cyclotron Line energy, have been observed for the first time in this pulsar, making IGR J19294+1816 a more intricate phenomenon in the realm of High-Mass X-ray Binaries. We have also explored the possibility of a mHz QPO originating from a Retrograde Orbiting Disk, and the necessity of incorporating Mass Ratio Variability in its interpretation. given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through numerical analysis, 
we investigate the potential for a phase plate to attain down to 1 Angstrom 
resolution on an uncorrected TEM. By examining various design features 
(fill-factor, pixel pattern, symmetry), we identify how they influence the electron 
probe size and current density. Our proposed designs exhibit probe sizes ($d_{50}$) 
as low as 0.66 Angstrom, indicating that a programmable phase plate with 
electrostatic elements can successfully rectify spherical aberration well beyond the 
1 Angstrom threshold. Given the temporal nature of electron probe size and the 
difficulty of replicating ultra-high resolutions experimentally, our results 
highlight the value of numerical investigations in TEM research. Furthermore, they 
emphasize the need for a deeper understanding of the interplay between the electron 
probe size, current density, and detection system in order to accurately determine 
$d_{50}$ and other performance metrics. Ultimately, they demonstrate the capability 
of a programmable phase plate to provide superior performance in certain scenarios, 
potentially offering a more accessible and cost-effective remedy over the extreme 
high cost of TEM spherical aberration correctors. Our research also provides a 
theoretical framework for optimizing both static and programmable phase plates, 
further paving the way for a novel three-dimensional design with enhanced performance 
capabilities. Nonetheless, there are circumstances under which a programmable

The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on their ability to accurately encode user input to generate relevant and effective responses. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from human or automated sources is insufficient in gauging a model's understanding of dialogue language, prompting the proposal of a set of evaluation tasks to scrutinize the encoder representations used in these models. In experiments, our findings suggest that certain evaluation tasks prove more manageable for certain sophisticated architectures to grasp than others and, interestingly, that RNN-based architectures outperform Transformer models in these evaluation tasks despite underperforming them in standard text generation metrics. Moreover, our study reveals that models can mask key information needed for successful dialogue continuation, as evidenced by the fact that certain evaluation tasks yield better results when the model is not forced to focus solely on the input's surface-level content. This study provides a framework for evaluating encoder representations in generative dialogue models and highlights the difference between their surface-level and intrinsic understanding. This insight can be useful in guiding future research into improving the performance of data-driven dialogue models. In particular, we propose the use of multiple evaluation tasks that assess various aspects of a model's understanding, as a single task may not capture the full capacity of these models. This work also offers a set of practical guidelines that other researchers can adapt to appraise the capabilities of their own dialogue models. Ultimately, this study stresses the importance of delving into the underlying representation of language models to comprehend their ability to anticipate the next utterance in a conversation. This work can serve as a starting point for researchers and practitioners in the dialogue community to engage in a meaningful discussion on the evaluation of models that will soon be used in various practical dialogue settings. This requires significant computing power and, due to rising demand, streaming services now rely on cloud computing to ensure a seamless viewing experience. Cloud providers offer a range of Virtual Machines, each with varying capabilities and prices, which poses the challenge of optimizing cloud utilization for video transcoding. Successful applications of MaskedSpeech in paragraph-to-sentence splitting and speech generation tasks highlight its effectiveness in producing high-quality speech from context. This study provides a detailed examination of the potential inaccuracies in
the output of contextualized language models when analyzing diachronic semantic
shifts in word meanings. We present an enhanced ensemble method that surpasses
earlier contextualized approaches and apply it to investigate the levels of
semantic change in English vocabulary over the course of 5 decades. Our
results show that contextualized methods may inaccurately predict significant
change in words with little to no actual semantic evolution, or whose
status remains unclear. These difficult cases are scrutinized, along with
suggested categorizations, to better understand the challenges faced. We
conclude that pre-trained contextual language models frequently confuse issues
related to word meanings, including shifts in usage, polysemy, and word
similarities, which need to be addressed through the development of more
sophisticated, fine-tuned models that account for the unique characteristics
of diachronic datasets. Furthermore, we highlight the value of employing
ensemble methods involving multiple contextualized models to enhance overall
performance. Our study serves as a call to action for further research to

long-term semantic change. Additionally, we introduce an open-source

between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we utilize extended, high-speed lightsheet and two-photon imaging
techniques in live zebrafish retinas during initial development to gain insights into the underlying mechanisms governing
the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM. Our high-resolution images permit us to accurately map the migration
patterns of multiple densely packed nuclei across the retina. By analyzing these migration tracks, we develop and test
a hypothesis that retinal IKNM is driven by a diffusive process fueled by the accumulation of new nuclei at the upper
retinal surface. Our results demonstrate how the tight packing of nuclei at the upper surface influences their movement
patterns, provide a reliable, quantifiable explanation for the uneven distribution of nuclei across the retina, and may
have implications for random cell fate selection within this system. Our work also highlights the significance of
precise, high-resolution imaging in elucidating the mechanisms underlying this complex cellular phenomenon. Our data
and analysis strategies are openly available for further exploration and reuse. By further opening the black box
surrounding IKNM, our study should offer a useful framework for investigating this process in other developing organs.

van Hove singularity, and that this results in a distinct Lifshitz 
transition distinguished by heightened heat capacity and a nematic susceptibility, 
both consistent with empirical observations.  A material parameter 
adjustment is also achievable by altering lattice compression, 
an experimental influence we've theoretically validated. 
However, this scenario introduces a conflict, as it suggests 
that, although the pseudogap emerges at a high temperature, 
it should still be observable even at absolute zero. 
To resolve this, we propose that the pseudogap is an example 
of a novel type known as an "entangled" van Hove singularity, 
where a strong electron interaction forges an integral relationship 
between two discrete Fermi surface segments, and that this 
results in a broader and more intricate Fermi volume with 
non-trivial topology, responsible for its emergence. 
We further assert that this exceptional van Hove singularity 
arises inevitably from the material's specific Fermi surface topology, 
generated by an exceptional point in the band's Hamiltonian spectrum, 
and propose a strategy for locating this exceptional point 
through a recent theoretical advancement. 
We also predict that, in the broader family of cuprate materials, 
the onset of pseudogap is attainable solely through inducing this 
non-trivial Fermi volume by shifting the two merging Fermi surface 
segments over an adjacent continuum using a strong electron interaction, 
and that this transition is characterized by heightened heat capacity 
and a nematic susceptibility, both consistent with empirical observations.

This paper details a specialized apparatus built for use in Aberdeen Tunnel's laboratory in Hong Kong. The laboratory is uniquely situated to study spallation neutrons produced by cosmic-ray muons with 611 meters of water equivalent in depth. The apparatus consists of six layers of horizontal plastic-scintillator detectors that pinpoint the direction and location of incoming muons. Between these layers, a neutron sensor filled with 650 kilograms of liquid scintillator containing a gadolinium dopant significantly enhances detection efficiency of the produced spallation neutrons. Additionally, we discuss the performance characteristics of this apparatus. Furthermore, we outline research aims for Aberdeen Tunnel's laboratory-based project, including measurements of free neutron flux, validation of geant4 simulations, and investigation of cosmic-ray flux composition. Lastly, we examine potential extensions to the apparatus's capabilities. Specifically, we explore the possibility of retaining event information from multiple-neutron interactions and the corresponding impact on flux measurements. This could result in a substantial reduction in the required detector mass, thereby making it feasible to install the apparatus in deeper laboratory sites. Nonetheless, even with its present design, this apparatus provides substantial scientific value. Originally conceived as a prototype for large underwater detectors, Aberdeen Tunnel's laboratory apparatus now presents an opportunity to test the principles of detector designs suited for next-generation underground detectors in Asia. This includes the 10 kiloton Kamand - a detector that, together with its counterpart in Korea, will significantly enhance global capabilities in the search for neutrino oscillations and other rare processes. Moreover, it is essential to note that although the discovery of neutros and their oscillatory behavior was made possible by combining data from underground locations around the world, there is still a need for further improvement in sensitivity, which Aberdeen Tunnel's laboratory is well-positioned to address through its unique research aims. This includes determining the neutrino oscillation probability by accurately measuring the neutron flux and detecting neutrons produced by cosmic-ray interactions with 1 kilometer of water equivalent in depth, a depth at which systematic uncertainties are minimized. Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were performed for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time path integral for these simulations. Constantly driven cases were simulated using the Nose-Hauke-CarO-Pimienta Hamiltonian, while time-varying driving was simulated by altering the frequency parameter in the NHMC Hamiltonian over imaginary time. Comparisons of simulation results with analytical predictions showed good agreement with an emphasis on visualizing this agreement through plots of the ratio of simulated to theoretical position expectation values. These plots were found to be independent of both oscillator parameters and the size of the discrete time steps. Additionally, limiting cases for the NHMC Hamiltonian were formally identified. For an harmonic oscillator in a thermal equilibrium, the NHMC Hamiltonian is equivalent to the thermal Hamiltonian, and it replicates the behavior of a classical harmonic oscillator when its amplitude is too large for coherent state formation. With a driving force that switches between two different intensities, the simulator was able to replicate the behavior described by an analytical solution derived from the NHMC Hamiltonian. All theoretical expectations were also found to be in line with the rules of quantum mechanics, specifically the conservation of the Wigner function's total probability over phase space. The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this effect in detail, researchers collected archived data and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro, before utilizing a light curve inversion method to match their shapes and rotation characteristics. By modeling the YORP effect and incorporating other relevant parameters into their analysis, scientists were able to detect the YORP acceleration in three asteroids and found that the YORP acceleration in all ten detected cases was positive, accelerating their rotations. Furthermore, incorporating solar precession into their algorithm revealed evidence of this phenomenon in the data obtained for Geographos, which may be a crucial feature that needs further explanation. Additionally, the timing of the solstices and equinoxes were found to have an impact on the light curves of these asteroids, which may be a result of the Yarkovsky effect's diurnal component or another process entirely. By modeling and analyzing this data, researchers were able to refine the orbital and physical characteristics of these asteroids, including their masses, shapes, and spin-vector directions. As a result, it's clear that the Yarkovsky effect has a significant impact on the rotational dynamics of asteroids, which is a crucial area of study for better understanding the evolution and physical characteristics of these small celestial bodies. Furthermore, developing a more comprehensive model that takes into account both the Yarkovsky and YORP effects is essential for accurately predicting the rotational states of these asteroids in the future. Additionally, incorporating solar radiation pressure into their model showed that the Yarkovsky effect's diurnal component has a negligible impact compared to its morning and evening components. The youth are increasingly relying on Instagram as a source of information, with political figures leveraging the platform to disseminate opinions and agendas. We examined online discussions on Instagram in relation to politics from a network perspective, focusing on communities of co-commenters. Our analysis revealed salient co-interactions - instances of user engagement occurring more frequently than chance would suggest - to be crucial in driving online discussions and information dissemination. We based our study on 10 weeks of data surrounding key elections in Brazil and Italy, observing users who commented on posts from politicians and celebrities. We found communities centered on politics to be more active in discussions, with members producing longer comments containing more emojis, hashtags, and negative language compared to communities focusing on other topics. Additionally, we observed a diverse range of topics over time, with some topics receiving fleeting attention while others centered on fundamental issues continued to be actively discussed. Communities involved in politics displayed dynamic characteristics, with some users consistently contributing to discussions and retaining their status as top commenters. A significant proportion of users, classified as core contributors, accounted for a majority of all co-interactions, with some communities experiencing sudden spikes in activity driven by a small group of active users. We based our study on multiple measures of community density, finding that groups involved in politics exhibited higher levels of connectivity and were more likely to maintain active discussion patterns. Lastly, our analysis revealed a trail of footprints left by users as they navigate between communities, with some users exhibiting a diverse range of community affiliations, while others stuck to a single community. Furthermore, we found that users more frequently engage in discussions within communities they have previously interacted with, with a strong preponderance of 'back to the future' effects, indicating that past co-interactions significantly increase a user's likelihood of re-engaging in a community. With these findings in mind, we propose an intuitive model that captures the dynamics of online discussion communities over time, highlighting the pivotal role that co-interactions play in driving active discussion within these communities. This study provides valuable insights for social media influencers, marketers, and platform administrators seeking to effectively manage online discussions and information dissemination across various communities. With the ever-evolving nature of online interactions, it is essential to incorporate temporal networks and a deeper understanding of community dynamics in order to devise such strategies. Furthermore, this study highlights the utility of network metrics in evaluating the success of online discussion campaigns, going beyond basic metrics such as followers, likes, and comments. Precise stellar characteristics are vital for both astrophysics and exoplanetary science, particularly when studying M-dwarfs. Researchers have developed numerous empirical relations that can utilize easily accessible observations to estimate stellar properties. However, these relations are often presented in a non-linear format, which is not suitable for Bayesian modeling. A novel Bayesian approach has been developed to consistently and simultaneously apply multiple empirical calibrations to accurately determine the mass, luminosity, size, and surface temperature of a typical M-dwarf. This new framework incorporates a mass-radius relation for M-dwarfs with a scatter of just 3.1% at fixed mass. The researchers also established the M-dwarf Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Sample (MUSS), and applied their method to obtain consistent stellar parameters for these low-mass stars. The MUSS targets are of interest primarily due to their potential to host exoplanets or serve as benchmarks for stellar activity across different wavelengths. Using the field MUSS stars, a mass range for low-mass stars in the solar neighborhood was defined through a process involving Gaussian Process regression. The resulting data show a distinct feature in the GP derivative, located at approximately 0.337 ± 0.013 to 0.026 M_(? ̇_odot) mass units, which indicates where the M-dwarf sample transitions from being fully convective in its interior to partly convective. No significant variations were found in this feature's location (nor in the M-dwarf mass-range) when incorporating all available data or accounting for potential biases in the sample. This result provides new insights into the internal structure of low-mass stars. Due to the limitations of the available data, especially the UV-based sample, a decision was made to delay any analysis of the stellar parameters for potential exoplanet hosting or to establish activity-rotation relations until a larger and more diverse dataset can be incorporated. Systematic testing of the method, as well as the MUSS data and modeling approaches, is also deferred until a future paper. The new framework and the MUSS data set will enable accurate and consistent stellar parameter determinations for low-mass field stars, contributing positively to future studies of these stars. Furthermore, the recently released TOI-773 multiple system, featuring a planet orbiting one of its components, provides an immediate application of this research. Confining modes at the edge, known as line waves, can propagate on the boundary between two specially designed electromagnetic interfaces that maintain mirror symmetry properties.
Studies have previously analyzed line waves in theory and in practice, revealing their occurrence at both microwave and terahertz frequencies.
It has also been demonstrated that these waves can occur when there's a sudden change from a negative to a positive symmetric resistance and uniform surface reactance present.
Characteristics of line waves include highly confineable mode propagation, polarization dependent on direction, and unique localized field enhancements.
A new study proposes a graphene patch structure, showing that the line waves produced can operate in the optical range.
The design involves a graphene surface integrated with an epsilon near zero substrate, which considers the effects of both dual and uniform reactive impedances.
However, this work specifically focuses on utilizing line waves in dual impedance structures. Moreover, a full wave simulator is utilized to verify the proposed design, producing line waves in a microstructure patch array at 10.5 GHz. The studies demonstrate that line waves can be designed to operate in any desired frequency by adjusting the size of the microstructure patch. Furthermore, the proposed structure offers enhanced local field strength around the edge of the microstructure patch, amounting to an enhancement of approximately 7.5 times the free space value. The theoretical limits of line wave propagation are also investigated, revealing the maximum possible edge mode confinement in a dual impedance structure is twice the value achieved here. The study concludes by highlighting potential applications of line waves in dual impedance structures, specifically highlighting their potential to low cost, compact, and scalable surface plasmon amplifiers. The work also explores the potential of line waves to be steered by dynamically adjusting the impedance boundary, suggesting that this approach offers a simple and effective way to control the propagation of these modes compared to other methods. The study presents a novel approach to achieving this dynamic control, involving an electroactive microstructure patch that allows for the rapid adjustment of line wave properties in response to changes in the surrounding environment. The study concludes by highlighting the potential of line waves in dual impedance structures to provide a solution to the long standing challenge of achieving rapid and efficient amplification of surface plasmons in sub-wavelength dimensions. The study demonstrates that the proposed line wave structure offers a simple and effective way to achieve this rapidly, with potential applications extending beyond amplification, including the sensing of changes in the surrounding environment, the creation of localized field enhancements in sub-wavelength dimensions, and the steering of line waves in real time. A machine learning technique known as reservoir computing generates a model that mimics complex systems and can be trained on significantly smaller amounts of data compared to alternative methods. The latest version of this approach simplifies training by minimizing the need to adjust numerous parameters. In a recent experiment involving a highly complex system with distinct time scales and multiple coexisting patterns of behavior, a reservoir computer of the new design demonstrated several advantages over its traditional counterpart. Specifically, it used a much smaller amount of data for training, a much shorter time to adjust its performance, a smaller number of parameters to adjust, and a much higher level of accuracy in predicting patterns of behavior, even when those patterns change rapidly. In addition to this performance, it was able to predict areas of stability accurately, further confirming the benefits of this new algorithm. These benefits hold particularly important for studying complex biological systems that produce multiple patterns of behavior, such as the electrical signals produced by the memory cells of the hippocampus. In such systems, small changes in their internal or external conditions can lead to large and unpredictable changes in behavior, an phenomenon known as multiple coexistence in dynamical systems. In the case of the memory cells of the hippocampus, multiple patterns of electrical behavior can be seen as different memories stored in the same cellular network. In order to study these systems effectively, scientists need models that can learn from small amounts of data, can handle large amounts of data efficiently, and can handle multiple patterns of behavior simultaneously. In the experiment mentioned earlier, such a model was trained on data from the electrical activity of the memory cells of the hippocampus and was able to predict patterns of attractors, areas of stability, and the switching of patterns of behavior. This model has the ability to learn from any data set representing a combined state of a multi-attractor system, allowing it to predict the identity of the pattern of attractors, the location of the area of stability, and the switching of patterns of behavior in that state. In practical terms, this model can be used to predict the electrical activity of the memory cells of the hippocampus from recordings of the brain's electrical activity, a capability that could be applied to any combined state of a multi-attractor system. Establishing the bias correction involves verifying the local asymptotic normality property and a specific Bahadur-Kiefer representation. We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between programs' inputs and outputs when comparing pairs of programs. The modified Hoare logic, which we call QREHL, allows for the verification of program properties involving probabilities, powers, and angles, by drawing on the principles of Fubini's theorem, the quantum Hoare logic for loops, and the relational composition operator. Through the introduction of expectations, QREHL offers a broader verification framework than the original quantum relational Hoare logic. Additionally, we outline a protocol for the quantified verification of web assembly programs using QREHL. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of a "good set," which serves as the basis for demonstrating the solvability of a category of verifiable web assembly programs compared to solving a specific mathematical problem. Ultimately, our research indicates that many web assembly programs can be easily converted into a simpler form of quantified preconditions, thereby potentially bypassing some limitations of the verification process. Overall, our work presents an enhanced version of the original quantum relational Hoare logic, which we have referred to as the quantum relational Hoare logic of orderless programs, and has also given rise to the concept of a "good set," which may also be applicable to other program verification frameworks. A comprehensive analysis has been conducted to measure the radii of 6097 young star clusters in 31 galaxies from the LEGUS survey. The custom analysis pipeline allowed for a large and contamination-resistant sample, giving us the largest dataset to date of its kind. The study discovered that a vast majority of galaxies exhibit similar radii distribution patterns, with a notable peak at approximately 3 pc. The mass-radius relationship of star clusters in this sample follows a distinct $R_{\mathrm{eff}} \propto M^{0.24}$ pattern. Notably, this relationship applies uniformly to clusters under 1 Gyr old, albeit with a less pronounced slope in cases younger than 10 Myr. Theoretical models suggest that more massive star clusters tend to be nontidally constrained, expanding over time. The study further reveals that a substantial majority of these star clusters in the survey exhibit signs of gravitational binding, especially when viewed at older ages or greater masses. The study's results on the cluster density and surface density show substantial variation, however it seems the dispersion tends to lessen as the age of the cluster increases, where the densest of these youthful star clusters have a typical density of around 100 $M_\odot$ pc$^{-2}$. The study's findings on the projected half-mass radius of the clusters follow a similar trend to the effective radius. A comparison of the survey's data to external galaxies reveals that the typical young cluster radius in normal galaxies is around 2 pc, whereas ultra-bright galaxies tend to have larger standard deviations in this measurement. The study further reveals a positive correlation between the central surface brightness of a galaxy and the average radius of its young star clusters, while an inverse relationship was found between the u-B/V ratio of a galaxy and the average radius of its star clusters. A multivariate analysis indicates that when controlling for central surface brightness, this inverse relationship disappears. The study concludes that a positive correlation exists between the scale length of a galaxy and the average radius of its star clusters. A simple model based on a constant cluster formation efficiency throughout a galaxy successfully replicates this correlation, while a model incorporating factors like tidal dissolution and cluster evolution from gas also fits the data adequately. Nonetheless, more in-depth studies are needed to understand the processes governing the evolution of star clusters in galaxies. A multivariate analysis using a dataset of 16 galaxies from the THINGS survey further reveals that when controlling for dark matter surface density, a positive correlation exists between the dark matter surface density and the average radius of star clusters

We present a novel, direct method for calculating the decay width of hadrons
decaying to two photons, often requiring an indirect estimation via off-shell
form factors. The new method offers an uncomplicated way to study volume effects.
In an example calculation, we apply this approach to $\eta_c\rightarrow 2\gamma$.
Using lattice ensembles with three $N_f=2$ configurations at different lattice
spacings, we derive the final decay width $\Gamma_{\eta_c\gamma\gamma}=6.57(15)_{\textrm{stat}}(8)_{\textrm{syst}}$ keV,
considering systematics in the charm quark mass. This technique can be extended
to additional processes involving leptons and photons in final states. Furthermore,
it may be feasible to extract real parts of form factor poles using this method. 
The proposed method is highly suitable for current lattice infrastructure and can
be used to evaluate ongoing and proposed lattice QCD experiments in the charm and
beauty sectors. The approach has already been incorporated into the lattice QCD
snapshot, but the detailed analysis of the $\eta_c\rightarrow 2\gamma$ decay has been
completed prior to this submission. We express our willingness to provide further

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. For example, a simulation of 16-site, double-layer Hubbard models with negative chemical potential and small interaction energy, which normally suffers from an extreme sign problem, can now be accurately conducted with only 10^6 Monte Carlo steps. Moreover, this model demonstrates a critical temperature of superflow transition at around 0.016 ± 0.002, consistent with theoretical expectations and vastly more precise than previously achieved. With the potential to tackle a broader range of sign problems, this architecture paves the way for Monte Carlo studies of strongly interacting fermions in multiple dimensions. Despite its effectiveness, this model is still short of achieving the same level of precision as the lattice QCD's Hamiltonian Monte Carlo in terms of autocorrelation lengths. Further research into more sophisticated neural network architectures is needed to fully realize its capability. With that in mind, and to facilitate the exploration of additional neural network models, we also make publicly available the source code for our complex-valued affine coupling layer. It is currently being utilized to model the Hubbard model but could be applied to a more comprehensive class of Hamiltonians. The code is written in the PyTorch deep learning framework and can be found at https://github.com/complex-hubbard/neural-sign-problem-solver. Additionally, we have included a detailed discussion of our model's implementation, including the complex-valued affine coupling layer and how we handled issues such as unitary constraint and overwriting of the target vector. The latter problem was mitigated by expanding the target vector to include the imaginary unit, a technique that could also be applied to other types of unitary matrices. The former issue was addressed by incorporating a novel function that combines the hyperbolic tangent and ReLU non-linearity, resulting in an effective restoration of the unitary constraint in each coupling layer. Our approach not only successfully tackled the sign problem but also provided valuable insights into the exploration of neural network applications in quantum many-body physics simulations. By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel method to employ unused task data for selective enhancement of model outputs, incorporating a high-performance retrieval model to facilitate this process.
This method is integrated into a simple augmentation framework that injects diverse, high-quality samples into model training, producing results that outperform existing models and create new benchmarks in areas like natural language inference, by surpassing overall average results by 0.46% on the MultiNLI test set. Moreover, this method proves particularly effective at tackling smaller-scale low-shot learning tasks. The code and models developed as part of this study are now publicly accessible on GitHub. Despite only using unsupervised retrieval methods, this technique sets a new standard for cross-task generalization and has implications for future work on few-shot learning and supervised generalization. Additionally, it highlights the importance of controlling augmentation quality to achieve optimal results. This method can be applied to various models, with potential applications to both single and multiple-model settings. Furthermore, it is worth noting that this technique may also be employed as a starting point for further work on planned experiments involving self-supervised learning and multi-task learning. In regards to experimental results, detailed statistics, including full test set tables and additional metrics, are provided in the appendix. This study itself serves as a initial exploration into cross-task generalization and further research is being conducted on multiple high-priority tasks such as ComGen, Commonsense, and Aristo. In terms of model selection, a key consideration was the substantial size of models like T0 and FLAN, which necessitated the use of select tasks for fine-tuning due to memory constraints. In contrast to continuous models like FLAN, this study also employed discrete models like T0, with both types exhibiting comparable performance. In terms of future work, one potential direction is to explore ways to enhance models like FLAN with multiple tasks using both supervised and unsupervised settings. In terms of methodological contributions, this study introduces a novel method for cross-task generalization and showcases the effectiveness of using unsupervised retrieval methods to enhance models like T0 and FLAN. In terms of results, this study establishes new state-of-the-art performance on various natural language understanding tasks, with results that outperform existing models by a significant margin on the MultiNLI test

This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach ('m-ar-K-FastICA') for feature extraction, combining kernel-based dimensionality reduction with ICA to overcome the limitations of previous methods. For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection. This computational approach enables us to examine the boolean complexes of involutions within a broad family of Coxeter groups, specifically those represented by the arm lengths of their generators. Finally, we introduce an internal decomposition of these boolean complexes, using laminar sets, which complements our previous homotopy-type results and provides a natural, combinatorial framework that can be applied across a wider realm of combinatorial objects. This framework is then applied to provide answers to and a proof of a previously posed question regarding the number of spheres within the boolean complex of involutions of a finite Coxeter group. This solution is a part of a more general theorem that is presented in this paper. This theorem is centered on the boolean complexes of join and meet operations within posets. It proves that for any two elements within a poset, their join and meet operations will result in a poset whose boolean complex has the same type as the original poset's boolean complex, providing a clear, combinatorial proof of this property. This fact was initially observed by Billera, Holmes, and Speyer in the context of their study on the homotopy type of a poset's boolean complex. However, our more general theorem expands this observation to include the realm of laminar sets within a broader family of combinatorial objects, such as forest posets and its extensions, as well as providing a clearer, combinatorial explanation for this behavior. This, in turn, enables us to examine the boolean complexes of a wider family of posets, such as the association schemes and the posets defined by the arm and leg lengths of a Coxeter group's generators. This further leads to a generalization of a previous study on the number of spheres within the boolean complex of a finite Coxeter group to a broader family of combinatorial objects, such as forest posets, as well as a study on the number of spheres within the boolean complex of a finite Coxeter group's antichain. A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE data collection from the Fornax3D survey. By distinguishing nebular emissions from stellar continuum and separating genuine planetary nebulae sources from false positives, a comprehensive database of 1350 distinct planetary nebulae was compiled across 21 galaxies. Each planetary nebula is associated with its specific location, luminosity of a particular spectral line, and velocity along the line of sight. By individually analyzing each galaxy, a reliable method for calculating the distances to galaxies has been applied using comprehensive planetary nebulae frequency distributions while also accounting for detection biases, and the resulting estimates of the distance to the Fornax cluster were calculated as 19.86 megaparsecs with an associated margin of error. Additionally, a significant agreement was observed between these new measurements and previously estimated distances using surface brightness fluctuations. This comprehensive database of planetary nebulae, along with previously obtained data on stellar population properties and the morphological structure of galaxies, is now available for further analysis. It is also proposed that future wide-field observations of planetary nebulae within the Fornax cluster be conducted using wide-field surveys from space-based telescopes.

Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. These analyses involve complex computations on significant datasets, necessitating high-performance data processing systems that can balance efficiency and simplicity. To address the limitations of existing data processing solutions, we present \emph{LifeStream}, a robust stream processing engine specifically designed to handle physiological data efficiently. LifeStream optimizes performance while providing intuitive temporal query language support, thus striking a balance between ease of programming and computational speed. Furthermore, LifeStream exhibits superior performance, outperforming other leading stream processing engines and hand-tuned numerical libraries by up to $7.5\times$ and $3.2\times$ respectively, on realistic datasets and workload simulations. To facilitate seamless integration with existing data analysis frameworks, LifeStream provides advanced low-level optimization techniques, including a novel hybrid approach that combines dynamic operator reordering and data blocking to accelerate execution. The engine's performance benefits originate from its straightforward, low-overhead design that minimizes overhead, allowing for higher-level optimization opportunities that enhance performance by a total of up to $2.4\times$. LifeStream's novel architecture also provides a unique low-level infrastructure that enables third-party developer support, encompassing both system and application-level extensions. The LifeStream system, along with its detailed architecture and code, is made available for public use. Additionally, the paper introduces a novel dynamic reordering algorithm, a novel data blocking strategy, and a comprehensive suite of physiological data-driven workloads that are available for download. Moreover, the paper provides an in-depth evaluation of LifeStream's scalable architecture, showcasing that it is capable of handling up to $10\times$ larger datasets and up to $5\times$ more complex queries on real-world data. Moreover, the paper presents an in-depth case study of LifeStream, where it is applied to analyze real chronic heart failure datasets in collaboration with Stanford's Division of Cardiovascular Medicine. The analysis conducted using LifeStream discovers several significant insights, such as identifying patients with the highest risk of mortality and the factors that contribute to their mortality. Moreover, the paper introduces an automated application of LifeStream that is used to continuously monitor the failure rates of heart transplants across the United States. The paper's evaluation and case studies provide concrete evidence of LifeStream's capacity to efficiently analyze large-scale physiological data, paving the way for scalable and real-time analytics in the healthcare industry. A stabilizable boundary feedback controller is designed for the Navier-Stokes equations using a linear control scheme with an oblique boundary orientation. The control system consists of the Navier-Stokes equations coupled with a boundary feedback operator, and its stability is ensured through a spectral approach inspired by the boundary feedback resolvent estimate. A specific choice of control gain is identified to achieve boundary stabilization and a related stability estimate is derived. Furthermore, the constructed boundary feedback controller is directly applicable to the linearized and full Navier-Stokes equations. For the linearized equations, a boundary stabilization result is obtained under which the solution's norm is bounded by a term involving the square of the $H^1$ norm of the input. For the full Navier-Stokes equations, a global stabilization result is derived, indicating that any perturbed solution converges to the original solution due to the boundary feedback controller. A numerical study confirms the theoretical stability results. The designed boundary feedback controller is oriented at an oblique angle to the wall, providing an alternative to the traditional tangent-oriented control. This construction leverages the entire boundary orientation to enhance the control's efficacy, particularly for the rotating flow application. One significant issue in Imitation Learning (IL) is that obtaining perfect optimal demonstrations from a teacher is a challenging task due to the complexities involved, especially in robotics. Providing quality feedback is further constrained by the need to supply demonstrations for multiple state actions at once. To overcome these difficulties, researchers propose an alternative where the teacher can provide corrective feedback in the form of preferences or rewards instead of demonstrations. However, existing algorithms are designed to work with specific types of noisy feedback, limiting their application across various teachers and tasks. To tackle this problem, we suggest a different approach, one where we model a variety of feedback types as different loss functions. Using this approach, we can leverage any online learning algorithm to minimize the combined losses and learn from a diversity of weakly correlated feedback. Our proposed method can handle different forms of feedback by treating the teacher's cost function as latent. By applying a general corrective feedback meta-algorithm that unifies prior work, we can achieve similar regret bounds regardless of the type of feedback. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by successfully learning to perform a complex household navigation task on a robotic platform using a variety of noisy feedback. This research provides a unified framework for addressing common challenges in online learning from various forms of weakly correlated feedback and can be applied to a range of tasks that involve complex robotic demonstrations. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for $K$ symbol delays, the trellis structure and relevant branch and cumulative metrics are derived, resulting in an optimized criterion for $K$. This criterion is based on the minimum Euclidean distance between differential signals, ultimately facilitating the selection of ideal delay periods for popular CPM formats through simulated error rates verification. A significant error rate increase is observed when switching from optimal to suboptimal delay periods, ranging from 10 to 30 dB across various CPM formats and differential detection delays. Notably, certain CPM formats can tolerate increased delays without substantial error rate increases, providing valuable implications for their implementation. In conclusion, introducing delays into conventional differential detection can accommodate up to $K=5$ symbol delays for most CPM formats, offering a practical strategy to combat channel phase fluctuations at the receiver end. In such cases, the resulting system performance approaches that of coherent detection, without the need for receiver complexity adaptation. Furthermore, this study provides a foundation for further investigation into more advanced detection techniques. In particular, it paves the way for research into optimum differential detection, which is presented in the companion paper. In that study, the derivation of an optimal differential detection method is presented, along with a more general delay optimization formula that can be applied across a broader range of signals. In contrast to conventional techniques, optimum differential detection can accommodate any delay period, achieving a significant performance gain of up to 20 dB for $K=5$ in some cases. In addition, it offers a greater insight into the effect of increased delays on system performance, showing that error rate increases result from the generation of additional cyclical CPM signal components, rather than receiver end issues, as initially suspected. This understanding provides a ground for further investigation into more complex signals, such as CPM signals with variable pulse and/or symbol duration. Lastly, this study demonstrates that high-level digital signal processing, such as error detection and correction, can tolerate increased cyclic signal components, as long as the overall system is properly synchronized, leading to the conclusion that CPM is an robust modulation technique suitable for a wide range of wireless communication channels

Furthermore, it examines the influence of birth velocities and neutron star sizes on the generation of such systems, along with any potential electromagnetic counterparts associated with them. Current deep learning techniques used for removing rain from images have achieved notable success in processing artificially created rainy images.  Nonetheless, their effectiveness drastically drops when confronted with genuine rainy conditions, primarily because they often employ highly simplified models of rain which contrast with the complex real rain scenarios.  This study posits that rain simulation and elimination are mutually interconnected and hence need to be inextricably linked.  To accomplish this, a joint approach to learning real rain simulation and elimination within an integrated disentangled image transformation framework is proposed.  A proposed model consists of two main components: a disentangled image transformation network that learns to dissect the disentangled components of an input image, namely its original content and rain effects; and a direct image transformation network that directly generates rain-filtered images from these components.  A joint loss function that incorporates a disentanglement loss, along with both adversarial and cycle consistency losses, is used to train the model.  A complementary loss is also used to train the disentangled image transformation network.  The proposed approach is applied to both artificial and real rain scenarios with the former involving easily controllable amounts of rain, whereas the latter involves more uncontrolled conditions.  The model's effectiveness is evaluated by conducting a disentanglement test, along with a qualitative as well as a quantitative assessment.  The results show that the proposed approach outperforms other competing techniques.  The model's code is made publicly available at this link https://github.com/ghr2016/closingtherain. Evaluating a person's risk of drug abuse is crucial, and online self-report surveys have proven effective for gathering relevant data. The five-factor model (FFM) of personality, consisting of extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, neuroticism, and openness, has been extensively examined in relation to substance abuse. Previous studies have often used shortened versions of personality assessments which may have implications for the accuracy of results due to potential information loss. In this study, a comprehensive and unreduced version of the Big Five personality traits was used to explore its association with drug consumption risk, assessed through the RAND36, in a randomly selected group of 1000 people from the general population. The data was collected through a self-report survey via the web. The results showed strong correlations between the FFM personality traits and the perception of drug consumption risk, with the highest correlations found for the neuroticism and conscientiousness factors. The influence of personality traits on risk perception varied across different drugs, with personality factors accounting for up to 15% of the variance in risk perception. The findings highlight the significance of considering the full range of personality traits when evaluating drug consumption risk and suggest that risk communication strategies may benefit from taking personality factors into account. However, the results also indicate that personality traits alone may not suffice in fully capturing an individual's risk perception of drug consumption. Therefore, researchers should explore additional factors that contribute to risk perception, such as descriptive, injunctive, and absolute risk information, in addition to personality traits. In fact, recent studies have shown that personality traits and risk estimates have significant interaction effects on risk perception, with the influence of these estimates being influenced by the type of drug consideration. In light of these findings, it would be beneficial to include a drug consideration feature in future studies, along with instructions on how to respond to risk estimates, in order to further delve into the complex relationship between personality traits, risk estimates, and drug consumption risk perception. In light of these advancements, it would be interesting to see if the relationships discovered in this study are also evident in individuals who use drugs for recreational purposes, as opposed to those who have never used drugs. Additionally, exploring potential differences in the association between personality traits and risk perception among those with different levels of drug experience may provide valuable insights. Furthermore, investigating potential variations in the association between personality traits and risk perception for different types of drugs could also be an interesting direction for further study. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.  We make available a comprehensive web-based tool that enables anyone to explore these reasoning rules.  This dataset and our associated research lay important groundwork for exploring the rules that govern how people think about the world and how these rules can be captured through machine learning techniques. Portfolio optimization is a critical application in Finance, yet its computational intricacies compel financial institutions to resort to simplified methods that require considerable time. By leveraging the Lagrange multiplier method, the mean-variance portfolio optimization issue can be formulated into a set of linear equations and potentially take advantage of the accelerated performance offered by the HHL quantum algorithm. Nevertheless, certain HHL components are not well-suited for operation on Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware. This research introduces NISQ-HHL, the first hybrid rendition of HHL that is capable of supporting end-to-end execution of compact-scale portfolio-optimization tasks on NISQ devices. NISQ-HHL enhances the hybrid version's stability and efficiency by integrating error-prone data transformation procedures, and is equipped with an optimized execution protocol that minimizes the required number of extended HHL iterations. Our study incorporates a portfolio size constraint, derived from a real-world investment scenario, and employs the Port-Hubard algorithm for accountability. Furthermore, we evaluate NISQ-HHL's performance using the full-scale finance benchmark developed by MCsim, and employ actual financial data from the 2021 US equity market. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the learning of both the ASR and text encoders using a multi-modal learning method. The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 offered initial insight into its composition, yet a detailed analysis with current spectroscopic methods has been lacking, especially concerning its atmospheric features, which display unusual properties and contradict earlier estimates of the dwarf's mass and orbit, requiring further examination due to their implications for intermediate population object formation processes. With a distance of tens of astronomical units from its host star, GJ 229B exists near the boundary between the planetary and stellar domains, offering an opportunity for its atmospheric analysis to shed light on formation mechanisms. Broadbent and Lord introduced the concept of unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects:

  - Flexibility in Usage: We've identified a significant drawback in the previous unclonable encryption constructions by Broadbent and Lord, as they either only guarantee single-use security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. Our research presents two novel constructions for both public-key and private-key settings that maintain security even after repeated use and are founded on minimal assumptions.

  - Understanding Cloning Capacity: We've investigated the one-time secure construction proposed by Broadbent and Lord, specifically aiming to determine if achieving a nearly optimal $0.5^n$ success probability for cloning is attainable. Our findings generalize the construction based on various forms of monogamy of entanglement and present attacks against specific schemes with cloning probabilities reaching as high as $0.75^n$.

  - Applications to Copy Protection: We've discovered that strong forms of unclonable encryption can lead to enhanced security, specifically copy-protection for unlearnable functions. Our research paves the way for potential new constructions meeting these requirements, thereby expanding the realm of copy-protection methods. Additionally, we introduce the concept of unclonable encryption for a specific function, leading to a new form of software protection known as unclonable software, which guarantees that, even with access to the program's source code, an adversary cannot create two different outputs from the same input. We provide a concrete construction for this type of unclonable encryption based on quantum assumptions. Our findings also demonstrate that wide classes of learning parities in multiple dimensions are susceptible to unclonable encryption, providing a practical application for this concept. Lastly, we explore the interplay between unclonable encryption and leakage, highlighting potential future research directions. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. To validate these findings, a 3 GeV energy recovery linac currently under construction in Korea will serve as a practical demonstration example. By fine-tuning its filling pattern, this project aims to delay beam breakup above its designed current level, allowing for ultimate utilization of this facility in both particle and photon applications. The constructed test stand for this linac, located at the University of Hawaii, has facilitated the development of a practical beam-RF modeling approach that considers actual construction tolerances and errors, providing more reliable predictions for threshold current and beam breakup frequency. This approach has been incorporated into detailed design for the University of Hawaii Test Facility (UH-TF), a next-generation energy recovery linear collider with a sophisticated recirculation system. To tackle this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) which addresses multiple challenges in imitation learning, including nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP can learn from multiple demonstrations, adapt skills to various target points, avoid obstacles, and meet complex linear and nonlinear constraints. With nonlinear hard constraints addressed, we expect EKMP to enhance the learning of complex robot skills that consider various constraints and obstacles. Analyzing crustal deformation in Central and West Africa enabled researchers to reconstruct the pre-break-up history of the conjugate West African-Brazilian margins.  Their model indicates that shifts in extension direction and speed significantly influenced the development of the Pre-salt sag basin and the S~ao Paulo High.  An initial, low-velocity E-W extension phase occurred between South America and Africa until about 126 million years ago.  Following this, rift activity increased and an NE-SW directed extension phase began between 126 and 126 million years ago and around 126 Ma. An intermediate phase of 126.57 Ma and Base Aptian featured strain localization, weakening of the lithosphere and increased velocities, with extension direction rotating towards NE-SW.  Breakup occurred around 113 Ma and then between South America and Africa. Additionally, they depend on the movement of partons in the transverse direction, related to parton spin alignment, which is rooted in the interactions represented by corresponding correlators. Our proposed functions can be accessed through semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering processes, and they lead to asymmetries that are sensitive to the internal structure of hadrons and are not limited by Boer-Mulders function's constraints. Our approach introduces two specific functions: one related to the alignment of partons and accounting for partons' intrinsic motion, and the other related to the alignment of hadrons and their collective motion. Both functions can be tested using a semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering process with an unpolarized incident electron. Our research also yields a specific experimentally accessible target, the spin-aligned moving in the positive z-direction, that can be used to test our proposed functions in a DISS process. This target demonstrates the characteristics of parton motion and spin alignment simultaneously. Our research paves the way for deeper understanding of hadron structure and the possibility of testing quark and hadron spin alignments in a single experiment. This approach introduces an new approach to study hadron spin alignments and uncover the quark's spin-dependent distribution inside hadrons. Our research also indicates that the detection of the charge-asymmetric cross-section can specifically test the target's spin-aligned hadrons for the first time. Additionally, our research shows that the proposed DISS process with an unpolarized incident electron and an unpolarized detected electron can directly probe the rest-frame properties of hadrons. Our study also points out that the proposed experiment can be carried out using a current electron accelerator and a existing detector system with a high luminosity and a high degree of precision, which can result in a precise test of the hadron structure in the next decade. The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. This finding is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations. Through this approach, we demonstrate that the natural state of proteins contains valuable information about their folding history and that topological models can be employed to analyze this information. This work also paves the way for the exploration of folding processes in other complex biological molecules. By applying this approach to proteins with higher-order knots, we discovered that the folding landscape becomes increasingly complex as the knot complexity increases. This study offers a glimpse into the intricate relationship between protein structure, sequence, and their historical folding processes, an aspect that holds key to understanding various diseases caused by misfolded proteins. Additionally, we find that proteins with trefoil knots exhibit unique biophysical properties such as enhanced thermal stability and the ability to interact with other proteins more efficiently, which could be exploited in developing new biomedical therapies. Moreover, our analysis reveals that some proteins with shallow trefoil knots are more prone to being cleaved by specific proteases, which could be beneficial in identifying specific protein cleavage sites that are associated with particular diseases. This knowledge can be utilized to design novel cleavage-specific probes, which in turn, could be employed to diagnose and treat these diseases more effectively. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that the natural state of proteins with trefoil knots can exist in two different conformations, which can be cleaved by different proteases. This knowledge can be applied to identify specific protein cleavage sites that are associated with particular diseases, which can be diagnosed and treated using novel cleavage-specific probes. This study also sheds light on the unique biophysical and chemical properties of proteins with trefoil knots, some of which can be cleaved by specific proteases more efficiently, which can be beneficial for developing new biomedical therapies
