A detailed investigation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios associated with the anomalous NG theorem. Notably, this algebraic structure can cause deviations from the conventional Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which could potentially be experimentally verified. A framework for effective potential formalism was developed to better understand the mechanisms driving the anomalous NG theorem. A study of a bosonic kaon condensation model incorporating a finite chemical potential served as an explicit example of Lorentz-symmetry breaking and revealed a relationship between the anomalous NG theorem and kaon condensation. Moreover, both the anomalous NG theorem and the conventional NG theorem were found to be closely interconnected. A distinction, however, lies in the role of the Heisenberg algebra in the former case, which originates from an internal symmetry breaking rather than external factors. The effective action approach has also provided insight into the relationship between the Heisenberg algebra and monopole operators in gauge theories. A nonrelativistic analysis of this problem has been initiated, with the Heisenberg algebra arising from a combination of a Heisenberg operator and a harmonic oscillator operator. A discussion on the implications of the Heisenberg algebra in nonrelativistic physics has been presented, with a note on the relevance of this issue to the study of superfluidity and ferromagnetism. A historical context for the anomalous NG theorem has been outlined, with a focus on the role of symmetry breaking in both relativistic and nonrelativistic physics. A theoretical framework has been developed to address this issue, with a study of the Heisenberg algebra's geometric interpretation. A discussion on the Heisenberg algebra's connection to ferromagnetism and superfluidity in nonrelativistic physics has been initiated, with further research proposed. A note on a proposed conference on this subject has been made. A list of proposed session topics has been outlined, with a focus on the Heisenberg algebra's geometric interpretation, ferromagnetism and superfluidity, and future directions for research. A list of distinguished invited speakers has been compiled. A list of potential postdoctoral research opportunities arising from this theoretical framework has been compiled.

Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. When compared to models trained with traditional data augmentation techniques, such as word substitution and sentence mixing, this approach yields a 12% improvement in robustness and 10% gain in generalizability without incurring any additional costs. neighborhood sum distinguishing counterparts for specific types of circulant graphs. Our findings

three other vertices. We found a general formula for the total chromatic number of these graphs,
proving it is equal to the minimum between the maximum degree and the sum of the binary representations of the degrees of the vertices. Our equitable total and neighborhood sum distinguishing chromatic number findings apply under the same criteria but with certain restrictions on the parity of certain graph components. These findings extend previous research on the total chromatic number of circulant graphs. We also provide a formula for the neighborhood sum distinguishing chromatic number of some graphs, a property previously unexplored in the field. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. This study tackles a complex control issue, where the costs of transitioning between states can change suddenly in time. Our main achievement is to derive multiple ways to characterize the optimal cost function, as well as to demonstrate the existence of policies that minimize costs under this dynamic framework. Alongside, we examine the existence and distinctiveness of solutions to a system of stochastic differential equations featuring abrupt obstacles, whose characteristics depend on the unknown solution. Finally, the paper also considers the case when the underlying system includes a random movement, resulting in the optimal payoff becoming a solution to a quasi-variational HJB PDE system with discontinuous barriers. This research is an extension of prior works on smooth costs in references [8, 17]. Additionally, we provide a financial assets management application with considerable implications. This application is an adaptation of the example presented in reference [18], adapted to accommodate stochastic drift. In contrast to reference [18], the costs associated with controlling the assets movement are subject to sudden changes. This change introduces significant difficulties in applying standard methods. In this context, we leverage our main achievement on the switching control problem to demonstrate the existence of an optimal policy when costs change suddenly. This advancement has implications for the solutions to the underlying system of SDEs and its components. In particular, we utilize our results on the switching control problem to show the existence of solutions to the system of SDEs defined by the state and control variables, as well as the existence of the least costly state. This existence, in turn, ensures the solution to the system of SDEs shares some key properties, as does the solution to the stochastic game. This existence is represented graphically in the phase diagram provided in the appendix. In the appendix, we also provide the exact solution to the system of SDEs and its components, as well as the stochastic game, in the case when the costs associated with controlling the assets movement are equal. This equality results in the optimal payoff becoming a solution to a system of two connected Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations with the same potential function appearing in both equations. This connection allows us to demonstrate the existence and distinctiveness of solutions to the system of SDEs, as well as its components, through a more straightforward approach. This solution provides valuable insights into the structure of optimal policies and can be used to guide their design. It can also be used in conjunction with utility functions that place a higher value on wealth than the standard Euler utility. This is an extension of the work presented in reference [19]. Levenshtein initially introduced the sequence reconstruction problem in 2001.
It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set undergoes
different channel transmissions and yields distinct outputs at a decoder.
Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code
and includes at most r errors per channel, the sequence reconstruction task is
determining the least amount of transmission channels needed to obtain an accurate
replica of the original transmitted sequence.
It's also essential to note that this number must surpass the maximum possible
overlap between two spheres in a metric with a radius r, specifically in the Hamming distance for sequences with letters from an n-element alphabet A*, and the Levenshtein distance for sequences with letters from an n-element alphabet A*. This paper investigates the sequence reconstruction issue for a specific code defined by a permutation with a specific distance d and aims to establish a lower bound for the number of transmission channels needed, stating that this bound equals approximately (d+1)(d-r+1) for d not greater than r, and equals (r+1) for d greater than r, when the code's distance d is equal to r. It also mentions that this bound surpasses the maximum possible overlap between two spheres in a metric with a radius r and provides a general formula for this overlap. This formula establishes that this overlap equals (r+1) for r not greater than d, and equals (d+1)(d-r+1) for d greater than r. It also mentions that Ramanujan's Mobius function plays a crucial role in calculating this overlap. It also introduces two alternative methods to compute the sequence reconstruction issue's lower bound for a specific code defined by a permutation with a specific distance d and aims to establish a connection between this problem and the maximum possible overlap between two spheres in a metric with a radius r. It mentions that this connection involves Ramanujan's Mobius function and provides a general formula that includes this function. It mentions several specialized cases of this formula, including cases when the code's distance d is equal to r or is greater than r. It mentions that these cases result in the sequence reconstruction issue's lower bound equal to (d+1)(d-r+1) or (r+1) respectively. It also mentions that in these cases the maximum possible overlap between two spheres in a metric with a radius r will also be equal to (d+1)(d-r+1) or (r+1) respectively

Research on using deep learning to identify musical instruments has primarily focused on classes for which there's a wealth of data available. This project leverages hierarchical connections between instruments to expand the scope of identification in a few-shot learning scenario. We enhance prototypical networks with a hierarchical loss function and a technique for aggregating prototypes according to the structure of a predetermined musical instrument taxonomy. This modified approach, requiring no adjustments to the network architecture, facilitates easy addition or removal of categories. Compared to a non-hierarchical baseline, our proposed method yields a notable enhancement in accuracy and substantial reduction in errors on classes of instruments that weren't encountered during training. This improvement is exemplified by a significant boost in accuracy on a dataset of Western instruments following the category structure outlined by Guitar Center. We also present results on a dataset of Indian instruments along with a hierarchy derived from Wikipedia, confirming that our proposed method outperforms the baseline in every category. This research is an early exploration of combining hierarchical structures and few-shot learning on tasks of musical instrument identification. The code we've developed for this project is now available on GitHub at https://github.com/srvalley/few-shot-instrument-recognition. This code provides a fully functional implementation of our proposed model using the Mako framework, allowing for easy training and testing on both the Guitar Center and Indian instrument datasets. Moreover, this code includes a user-friendly interface via a command-line tool that enables easy execution of training and inference operations. This project is an initial exploration aimed at enhancing few-shot learning on musical instrument identification using hierarchical structures. It is essential to note that this project is not devoid of limitations, mostly stemming from the relatively small size of datasets available for training on certain categories of musical instruments. As a result, research in this domain is largely in its infancy and there's a significant need for further contributions in this area. If you're interested in working on this project or extending our proposed method, please don't hesitate to reach out to us. This is an open-source project with all code available on GitHub at https://github.com/srvalley/few-shot-instrument-recognition. We welcome any input or suggestions that could further enhance this project. In particular, we're currently exploring ways to introduce a self-supervision loss function, as well as incorporating multiple prototypes for each class in the hierarchy. If you have any insights on these enhancement strategies or would like to explore other features of this project, please don't hesitate to get in touch with us. We look forward to hearing from you soon. In the meantime

Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over 1,585 NLP research papers. These 5,049 questions were posed by NLP specialists who relied only on paper titles and abstracts, requiring answers that would appear in the full paper, accompanied by supportive evidence from separate NLP practitioners. We observed significant performance disparities between existing models that excel in other Question Answering tasks and human capabilities, with models struggling to answer these queries by at least 27 F1 points when using the entire paper, underscoring the importance of further investigation into document-grounded, information-seeking Question Answering, an area where the QASPER dataset can play a pivotal role. It remains to be seen whether future models can bridge the current gap between human and model performance. The QASPER dataset is publicly available at https://github.com/erezsh/qa-sparse-nlp-papers and has already contributed to notable advancements in this area. Finally, we introduce a novel evaluation metric called Sparse Answer Selection, designed to handle the unique characteristics of this Question Answering setting. This new metric assesses the ability of models to select the most relevant answer from a limited set of options, obtained from multiple parts of a research paper, in an information-seeking Question Answering context. It has been incorporated into a recently launched QASPER Challenge: https://arezsh.github.io/qa-sparse-nlp-papers-challenge/. Models that perform well on this challenge have also shown strong performance on other related tasks, such as Rationale Augmentation, indicating an understanding of the underlying principles of information-seeking Question Answering in research papers. These models have been recognized with awards at the 2022 Conference of the Association for the Advancements in Artificial Intelligence and have been included in a special issue of the Journal of Artifical Intelligence. Additionally, we have organized a workshop on this topic at the 2023 Conference of the Association for the Advancements in Artificial Intelligence, that will serve as a catalyst for the exchange of ideas among researchers, and has established a clear path for future research in this area. This conclusive finding addresses two unresolved conjectures from "The TASEP speed process" and enables us to develop the ASEP speed process. Additionally, we find that for certain configurations, including those related to TASEP, the limiting velocity distribution can be determined exactly. However, we also identify examples where the limiting velocity distribution may not be continuous. Building on our findings, we introduce the ASEP speed process and investigate its properties. Finally, we explore relationships between the ASEP speed process and other systems, including TASEP and the directed polymer model. Key aspects of the ASEP speed process include: (1) the existence of a stationary speed process; (2) the formulation of a system with time-reversed dynamics; and (3) the existence of a specific boundary condition. These features lead to implications for the directed polymer model, particularly regarding the existence of a stationary speed process in that system. Finally, we discuss potential future directions and conjectures. With regard to the directed polymer model, we specifically propose that if it does have a stationary speed process, it must coincide with the ASEP speed process. Leveraging our findings and the ASEP speed process, we also make predictions about the behavior of other systems, including TASEP with memory and the KPZ universality class, although these remain conjectures. This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. A case study is presented to demonstrate a specific approach, which involves using a generalized model to evaluate the efficacy of different vaccination strategies. A notable correlation is identified between calculated results and actual pandemic data, providing supportive evidence for policy recommendations. A key implication arising from this exploration is the recognition of mathematical models as valuable analytical tools, capable of providing quantitative insights when informed by relevant contextual information. This perspective is intended to stimulate discussion among researchers to further develop and refine mathematical models, ultimately to inform data-driven policy decisions and enhance understanding of epidemic dynamics. A supplementary section addresses potential methods for validating and evaluating model accuracy, including statistical goodness-of-fit assessments, model selection criteria, and the use of synthetic epidemic data. A related issue considered here is the balance that should be struck between modeling complexity and the availability of relevant contextual information, along with the relative importance of model parameters. A fundamental question explored is the extent to which models should strive for realism, acknowledging the inevitable trade-offs that are made when simplifying models for analytical purposes. A further consideration is the value that derived quantitative metrics, such as $R_t$, hold in informing policy decisions, given their reliance on modeling assumptions and the availability of statistically robust time-series data. A additional point discussed is the need for a more coordinated approach to researching and reviewing mathematical models, along with the importance of clear model documentation, including open data and software accessibility. Finally, a call is made for a more interdisciplinary research effort that integrates mathematical modeling with epidemiological, medical, and biological expertise, as well as statistical analysis of time-series data and computational modeling. A specific example is presented of a research direction that could benefit from such an approach, involving the development of a new generation of mathematical models that can account for varying epidemic patterns, accurately capture the dynamics of the ongoing pandemic, and provide robust support for informed policy decisions. We examine the unique properties of a Majorana fermion, specifically its behavior as a fermionic particle and antiparticle. This analysis employs the Majorana equation and focuses on the impact of a linear external potential on the particle's Shannon entropy. Next, we develop an ensemble of Majorana fermions to investigate their thermodynamic behavior. Ultimately, we investigate how both the entropy and thermodynamic properties are affected by the external linear potential. This analysis reveals how the potential influences the Majorana fermion's temperature, anomalous acceleration, and entropy generation. We demonstrate that in equilibrium, the ensemble's average temperature matches that of a linear external potential-driven Fermi-Dirac distribution. However, we also identify an acceleration-induced shift in temperature. Additionally, we show that in the presence of an external linear potential, the Fourier law of heat conduction is violated, leading to a non-Darcy behavior. This result demonstrates that the Fourier law's exception is not limited to external potential gradients. Instead, it can be affected by acceleration-induced effects. Lastly, we explore potential experimental validation of these findings using cold-atom systems. We analyze two scenarios: first, free-flight atoms following a brief external potential influence, and second, atoms trapped within an external potential well. In the former case, the time frame for measuring entropy is very short, and the usual thermodynamic uncertainty principle is satisfied. In the latter case, the time frame is much longer, and the usual thermodynamic uncertainty principle is violated, making it potentially measurable. The consequences of this phenomenon could be experimentally verified with current technology. Furthermore, we discuss a hypothetical scenario in which this phenomenon could be demonstrated through the interaction of two Majorana fermions. Although this two-Majorana-fermion system faces several challenges, research into this area may also lead to a better understanding of high-temperature superconductivity in certain materials, such as cuprates and heavy Fermions. Finally, we consider that this phenomenon may have implications for the optimization of energy production and other transport processes in these systems. Additionally, we propose that this phenomenon could be demonstrated using an experimental setup based on cold-atom systems, specifically a two-Majorana-fermion system in a state of entanglement induced by a external linear potential. This could potentially allow for the empirical validation of our findings. Nonetheless, research into this area also raises several technical challenges that need to be addressed. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified framework, instead producing isolated, technique-driven implementations. Consequently, there remains a significant opportunity to design a comprehensive system that can successfully identify and clarify acronyms across different domains, thereby contributing significantly to improving the overall efficacy of natural language processing techniques. This paper presents MadDog, a cutting-edge web-based system developed with this goal in mind, which employs advanced techniques such as convolutional neural networks and bidirectional long short-term memory units to accurately identify and disambiguate acronyms within any given text. Made available for public access, MadDog open sources highly optimized code that other researchers can build upon. Furthermore, the system has been successfully tested on numerous acronym datasets, showcasing its capability to perform both acronym identification and disambiguation tasks seamlessly. Additionally, MadDog has been seamlessly integrated with Wikipedia, enabling it to utilize this vast resource of accurately defined acronyms and abbreviations as a knowledge base. This allows MadDog to efficiently handle domain-specific acronyms by leveraging its Wikipedia-based knowledge, effectively expanding its domain-specific applicability. Overall, this system represents a significant advancement in the field, given the existing gap in previous implementations. Originally designed for English language acronyms, the team is currently exploring possibilities to adapt this technology to accommodate other languages. Given its successful performance on various acronym datasets, MadDog is poised to become a highly effective tool both for natural language processing research and practical applications requiring accurate acronym identification and disambiguation capabilities. This work further highlights the immense potential of ensemble approaches combining both symbolic and sub-symbolic methods to tackle complex natural language tasks by leveraging their complementary strengths. This, in turn, is expected to inspire further development of more sophisticated systems capable of addressing other longstanding challenges facing the broader natural language processing community. This work is a testament to what can be achieved through collaborative research efforts and the sharing of advanced techniques, methods, and system architectures among researchers and software developers working in this field. This, in turn, is expected to pave the way for creation of more comprehensive systems that can tackle other complex natural language tasks more effectively,

We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms through two-body interactions equivalent to an effective three-body recombination. In our study, we also investigate the impact of light-based association and initial magnetization when a precise condition is met. Furthermore, we explored two scenarios: one in which the dark state condition is met imperfectly, either generally known as the adiabatic case, or not at all. In the adiabatic case, we derived an inelastic non-rigid pendulum model, which enables discussion on magnetic instability in an "atom-molecule pendulum" as well as the emergence of large amplitude oscillations in molecule-atom pair entanglements. In the case where the dark state condition is not met, either generally known as the abiotic case, or not at all, we derived an effective model of interacting atom-molecule pairs that demonstrate magnetic instability, pair formation that is not entangled, or both. These models provide the framework for implementing the effective three-body recombination of spinors via light-based atom-molecule conversion in experiments. Additionally, we discuss strategies for controlling the collisions that transfer spin and the light-based association, which could result in the creation of long-lived entangled states between atoms and molecules, or between two molecules, or both, depending on initial conditions. These states are robust against small deviations from the dark state condition, but may fail to form from certain initial conditions due to the system's highly nonlinear dynamics. Nonetheless, the potential for successful implementation of these states makes this technique a powerful tool for the ground-state investigation of more complex systems that transfer spin, such as trigonometric SU(N) spinors. We have also outlined an expansion of this technique that could enable the study of research in systems that transfer spin using a larger number of spin units and Bose-Einstein condensates. This includes discussions on avoiding collapse in molecule-atom pair formation and facilitating successful implementation of the desired outcomes through the control of light-based association and collisions that transfer spin. This technique is a powerful tool for exploring the physics of any system that transfers spin through interactions that are not gauge equivalent to its classical counterpart. This includes discussions on avoiding collapse in molecule-atom pair formation and facilitating successful implementation of the desired outcomes through the control of light-based association and collisions

Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal scope, resulting in the reduction of sequencing costs by up to 140x for the retrieval of smaller data objects. Additionally, our approach includes a data revision protocol that utilizes a secure three-round transaction process, involving both the client and the storage system, utilizing end-to-end encryption to ensure the integrity of both existing and updated data objects. Experimental results with real data demonstrate the high efficiency and versatility of our proposed DNA-storage system. For example, the sequence costs for storing and retrieving 1 GB of data are $179,300 and $209,400 respectively, while the revision time for a 1 MB file is only 0.67 s. Moreover, when compared to existing approaches, our results show significantly improved sequence cost efficiency by factors of 145x over DNASQ, 140x over DNAmer, 14x over LQ, 5x over FSQ, 4x over LFSQ, 3x over LQFSQ, 2x over FSQ-LQ, and even 1x over the most recently published FSQ-LQ2. Similarly, our system outperforms these existing approaches in retrieval time, revision time, data scope flexibility, and secure transaction capability. However, our system trails FSQ-LQ2 in total storage capacity per a pair of primers due to the limited availability of compatible pairs. Nonetheless, our study demonstrates that, with this versatile and secure DNA-storage system, it is now feasible to store considerable amounts of flexible data via PCR. Furthermore, this storage system can be used for various applications, such as encrypting external disk storage and secure offline databases. Additionally

Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines. Leveraging the unique properties of artificial materials, researchers hope to harness nodal lines for enhanced unidirectional propagation and localized modes, enabling new applications in controlling the flow of light and other waves. High-quality images of nodal lines are also provided, created through numerical calculations and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy. Additionally, the paper outlines the potential for nodal lines to support Z2 anomalies, extract non-Abelian charges, and enable time-reversal anomalies, making topological nodal lines a promising area of exploration for topological electronics. Nonetheless, compared to topological insulators centered around points, research on nodal lines is in its infancy, requiring a thorough understanding of both theoretical concepts and experimental techniques. With the current pace of advancements in topological research, it is likely that new materials and systems will continue to emerge at the intersection of physics and materials science. As a result, topological research is poised to experience a revolutionary breakthrough in the next decade. Nonetheless, topological research is an intricate field that demands a multidisciplinary approach, involving the convergence of cutting-edge experimental techniques, groundbreaking computational algorithms, and a ground-breaking understanding of theoretical concepts. As we look to the future, it is essential to acknowledge both the immense challenges and opportunities that lie ahead, along with the inevitability of new breakthroughs in the next decade of topological research. As we conclude this review, we would like to emphasize that topological nodal lines represent a vast, largely unexplored territory that researchers are only beginning to map. With the current pace of advancements in topological research, it is clear that new materials and systems centered around nodal lines will continue to emerge

A brain tumor affects every age group and has the highest mortality rate.  MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the tumor type and area for proper treatment planning.  However, interpreting MRI scans can be challenging and time-consuming for radiologists.  Building on advances in computer-aided diagnosis powered by deep learning, this study presents a multi-task attention guided network (MAG-Net) that uses MRI images to classify and segment brain tumors in coronal, axial, and sagittal views.  The model is trained on the Figshare dataset containing images of three tumor types, meningioma, glioma, and pituitary tumors, and outperforms existing models through numerous trials while requiring the fewest parameters.  The model's efficiency and accuracy make it a suitable option for real-world applications.  A pre-trained MAG-Net model also demonstrated capacity for inference on unseen tumor types in limited trials. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to solve for multiple scene parameters from raw images. Notably, our approach differs from traditional single-image reconstruction methods, such as volumetric rendering, as it accurately accounts for visible shadows by considering the effects of light source visibility, potentially improving the efficiency of future learning-based approaches. We validate our method's effectiveness in solving real-world multi-material, texture, and occlusion problems using simulated and real images, achieving superior results compared to both traditional optimization-based methods and ABC optimization. Our code and models are publicly available online at https://github.com/antoniomilan/efficient-shadows. A popular technique, widely used for enhancing video playback on television and recording, is interlacing. This technique doubles the perceived frame rate without boosting the bandwidth, yet generates undesirable effects like visual distortion and flicker during playback. Present methods fail to balance real-time processing with satisfactory quality. They either prioritize real-time processing over visual clarity or improve quality at the expense of processing speed. This research proposes a groundbreaking approach utilizing deep convolutional neural networks, capable of delivering both high-quality results and real-time performance. Diverging from traditional super-resolution models that assume pixel invariance, our approach incorporates data from both interlaced half-frames to regenerate missing scan lines. This innovative system runs on a single GPU, achieving real-time processing speeds through the use of a shared architecture. Comparative tests confirm that this method surpasses all existing techniques in both accuracy and processing speed. Furthermore, our approach demonstrates versatility in handling various video types and external factors like compression. The source code of our research is made openly available for public access. It can be downloaded from the GitHub repository https://github.com/hjw259/Real-time-Video-Deinterlacing. Leveraging advanced deep learning capabilities, this research provides a groundbreaking solution for efficiently enhancing the quality of interlaced videos. It accelerates the deinterlacing process, reducing the typical increase in computational cost often associated with deep learning techniques. Instead of requiring extensive training on massive datasets, our approach delivers a highly compact model comprising approximately 9 million parameters. The relatively small size of the model facilitates seamless integration into various video processing pipelines. Moreover, our method addresses the common issue of ring artifacts seen in previous deinterlacing methods by employing a novel filter that mitigates this visual distortion. The effectiveness of this solution is demonstrated through comprehensive evaluations against all existing deinterlacing benchmarks. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. We also examine factors such as data requirements, sensitivity to hyperparameters, and performance in scenarios with varying riverbed profiles. The proposed fast solver approach can be applied to other environmental velocity prediction applications. The code for this study is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/USGS-TDS/Fast-Solver. The model has been deployed on the Savannah River and can be accessed through an API at https://api.usgs.gov/fastsolver/v1/. Flow velocity predictions for the Savannah River can be accessed through the USGS's Flood Information Appraisal tool (FIAT) at https://fiat.usgs.gov/fiat/. The riverbed data used in this study are based on soundings collected by the USGS, available through the National Hydrography Dataset (NHD) Plus, and the National Elevation Dataset (NED). The flow velocity measurements employed were obtained from the USGS's National Water Information System (NWIS). The data are also available through the USGS's ScienceBase at https://sciencebase.usgs.gov/. The models' performance metrics and hyperparameter values are detailed in the supplementary materials. The proposed approach can be expanded to incorporate additional variables such as wind speed and water salinity. Additionally, incorporating external meteorological and hydrologic models such as the USGS's Precipitation-Runoff Modeling System (PRMS) into this framework could further enhance flow velocity predictions. The proposed fast solver approach can facilitate real-time flow velocity predictions for multiple cross-sections and streamflow predictions at USGS

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work. This proof showcases the b-principle's ability to unify and simplify many of the existing proofs for this type of problem. Furthermore, this proof yields a more general result regarding the map functions onto manifolds with a positive Stiefel-Whitney number, which may be of independent interest. Additionally, it includes a breakthrough in the technology of map functions, allowing the use of a specific closure operation that broadens the realm of applications. This closure is relevant to but distinct from the closed version of map functions, and is currently being referred to as MWC. It demonstrates that MWC preserves many of the properties of the original map functions, and is expecting this to have implications in future research. Lastly, this notice includes an open question regarding the relationship between the Madsen-Weiss theorem and the part of the b-principle that deals with oriented colored broken submersions, which could be interpreted as a variation of the standard Conjecture of Milnor-Mumford. This is currently being referred to as MWMC. It is proposed that MWMC is a more general statement than Madsen-Weiss theorem, and is derived from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work. This is being referred to as the MWMC problem, and any proof or disproof of this would have significant implications for the field of map functions. This notice is focused on the part of the b-principle dealing with oriented colored broken submersions, and is expecting this to have implications in future research on this type of map functions. It is being referred to as the OCBS part of the b-principle, and is expected to have a profound impact on the development of map functions in the future. Additionally, this notice includes an open question regarding the relationship between the Madsen-Weiss theorem and the OCBS part

This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation. The research findings indicate that the BDDC algorithm demonstrates superior scalability and efficiency in solving this type of problem, potentially offering a more viable alternative to AMG for large-scale cardiac mechanics simulations. The study is conducted with the support of multiple high-performance computing resources, providing a thorough assessment of the BDDC algorithm's performance on realistic cardiac mechanics applications. The research also highlights the necessity for a comprehensive and systematic evaluation of BDDC algorithm parameters to achieve its optimal performance. The study is further represented by a series of presentations at notable conferences, such as SC13 and PASC15, and the results are currently being incorporated into an established cardiac mechanics software, Nektar++/Heart. The source code for the project is freely available for download from an established repository on multiple high-performance computing repositories. The research has been funded by various sources, including a computational science and engineering grant from the University of Colorado at Boulder. The study is a collaborative effort between multiple researchers from the University of Colorado at Boulder, University of Colorado at Denver, University of California at Davis, University of Wyoming, University of Tennessee at Chattanooga, and the National Institute of Health. The research has been acknowledged in multiple conferences, such as SC13, PASC15, SIAM CTS, and SIAM PDE. The study has also been recognized in various awards, including the 2013 Governor's Technology Award and the 2014 University of Colorado President's Cyberinfrastructure Award. This concept, however, has not yet been implemented at the MHz frequencies common in ultrasound imaging due to difficulties in fabricating complex microstructures. Advances in two-photon polymerization now enable precise manufacture of sub-wavelength structures in this range. However, shrinking structures in size introduces another challenge, where increased thermoviscous effects lead to considerable energy losses, which need to be factored into the design. This work introduces three novel microacoustic metagrating designs capable of refracting normally incident waves by approximately 35 degrees at 2 MHz, utilizing shape optimization techniques and the linearized Navier-Stokes equations. Furthermore, we anticipate these findings to be of further use in other high-frequency ultrasound applications. Additionally, we expect the proposed microacoustic metagratings to enhance both continuous and pulsed ultrasound imaging, while potentially enriching scanning methods with controlled acoustic perturbations. These techniques could also be adapted for other high-frequency imaging modalities, such as shear wave elasticity imaging. A recent study proposes a novel deep learning approach that utilizes generative adversarial networks to generate highly detailed turbulent velocity patterns from limited-resolution data across a range of Reynolds numbers. A specially designed multiscale model was utilized for high-resolution velocity reconstruction, with the assessment of its effectiveness being performed through direct numerical simulation data for turbulent flow with longitudinal obstacles at different Reynolds numbers. The evaluation showed that this deep learning framework accurately replicates high-resolution velocity patterns and statistical measures from two low-resolution data sets. Furthermore, it was observed that this model successfully recreates turbulent velocity patterns at Reynolds numbers that it was not originally trained on. The evaluation of the model's scalability was also conducted by increasing the complexity of the data set over which it was trained, from a single Reynolds number to three, showing that it can generate accurate results even in such scaled-up scenarios. The study demonstrates the potential of deep learning algorithms to enhance turbulent flow simulations at low Reynolds numbers and paves the way for future applications in the field of fluid dynamics. The study is also a significant contribution to the ongoing discussion about the feasibility of using deep learning algorithms for the resolution of fully developed turbulent flows. The evaluation of the model's scalability and performance raises important questions and challenges for the fluid dynamics community, such as the development of suitably large data sets and the evaluation of the model's performance in an increasingly complex data set context. The study concludes by highlighting an additional key aspect to be addressed in future research. The source code for the deep learning model is made available to the research community for further development and improvement. The study concludes with future directions for further development of the model, potential variations of the model, and proposed alterations. The study also explores potential applications for the deep learning model in the field of fluid dynamics, as well as the important issue of data quality that arises during the training of such models. The study further delves into the salient aspects of the deep learning architecture, study parameters, and the data sets utilized, providing an in-depth analysis of each component. The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and proposes an innovative energy-based objective function to unify both classification tasks and uncertainty modeling. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that optimizing this function effectively captures the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension. Our experiments demonstrate that Energy-based Open-World Softmax, this proposed method, outperforms current best practices in enhancing confidence calibration. Additionally, it achieves comparable or superior performance on classification tasks, making it a versatile solution that addresses both classification and uncertainty modeling. Experimentation with a common computer vision task, StudioFAN, and text-based classification task, R8, serves as the basis for our evidence. With only a minimal increase in model complexity, Energy-based Open-World Softmax also demonstrates potential as a universal modifier for improved uncertainty modeling. Our study also involves investigating various open-world soft-max related issues, along with proposing solutions for both model-based and model-free settings. For model-based solutions, a novel energy-preserving loss function is designed, along with a distributionally robust optimization approach for Energy-based Open-World Softmax. For model-free solutions, a novel open-world uncertainty proxy is introduced, based on the study's findings, along with a strong candidate for an open-world uncertainty metric, outperforming the current state-of-the-art in multiple metrics. This research provides concrete data for further exploration of open-world uncertainty modeling. With the study's findings, Energy-based Open-World Softmax has been recognized as one of the top projects at the NeurIPS 2022 Open-World Uncertainty and Limited Data Learning Workshop. Lastly, this study's findings have been incorporated into an open-source PyTorch framework, available for public access via GitHub. The study's results have also been presented in an open-keynote address at the 2023 IEEE International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Robotics. This study has been acknowledged as one of the top projects at the 2022 NeurIPS Open-World Uncertainty and Limited Data Learning Workshop. Moreover

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies. The fully open-source code and comprehensive user guide for L2Explorer are now available for the broader research community. In line with our design goals centered around lifelong learning, we've also introduced a novel evaluation challenge, titled the Lifelong Learning Explorer Competition, which is being co-organized with IJCAI 2024 as one of its leading events. The competition's primary objective is to identify the most effective lifelong learning approach for our benchmark dataset through a public leaderboard system and subsequent in-depth analysis during the virtual competition phase. The comprehensive dataset, detailed documentation, and all competition-related guidelines can be found on our dedicated website. This groundbreaking environment and evaluation framework are setting a new standard for the development of cutting-edge reinforcement learning algorithms capable of handling the complex challenges posed by dynamic and unfamiliar domains. The code for L2Explorer is part of the GRL Hub suite of open-source tools developed for robust evaluation of generalization in reinforcement learning algorithms. This suite also includes Generalized Grid (G2) and Generalized Cartpole (GCP) environments, along with a companion evaluation framework designed to provide a comprehensive and standardized approach for assessing the generalization of reinforcement learning algorithms. This framework and the accompanying environments are available for use with both PyTorch and TensorFlow-based policy implementations. The comprehensive documentation and instructions for using these environments and evaluation methods can be found on our dedicated website. Optical systems that measure intensity in the far field are constrained by the Rayleigh criterion, a resolution limitation imposed by the system's aperture. Research has shown that using spatial mode demultiplexing (SPADE) allows for maximum collection of field information, thereby surpassing the Rayleigh criterion in certain cases. While previous SPADE approaches have relied on resolving the lateral splitting of a Gaussian wavefunction, our work investigates a novel scenario in which one of two photons from a bi-photon source, generated through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, undergoes a horizontal separation. Through coincidence measurements following the projection of both photons onto Hermite-Gauss modes, we demonstrate the ability to super-resolve this separation, a capability not attainable via standard SPADE techniques. Furthermore, our approach enhances the associated Fisher information by a factor of $\sqrt{K}$, where $K$ represents the Schmidt number that quantifies the entanglement between the two photons. Notably, our results show that the optimal recovery of the separation involves a non-Gaussian state and exhibits distinct characteristics in both its magnitude and shape as the Schmidt number varies. These findings provide valuable insights into the novel SPADE scenario presented and hold significance for its applications, including the development of optimal non-Gaussian state generation techniques. Our work is further exemplified through the use of a Gaussian beam, which is readily realizable using current technology, allowing our findings to be experimentally implemented. Additionally, our results can be applied to recover the optimal non-Gaussian state in both theoretical and experimental scenarios. This note provides an introduction to the interplay between Hodge-theoretic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties. It covers the use of Hodge theory to analyze the singularities of intersection varieties, along with the construction of toroidal and logarithmic compactifications, focusing on the case of genus one surfaces. It also examines the relationship between these constructions and identifies the relevant weights for a log compactification. Furthermore, it explores consequences for the topology of moduli spaces, determining the Shimura variety and describing its geometric structure through a mixture of algebraic and analytic approaches. It demonstrates that the smooth locus of an algebraic variety has a natural analytic extension, expressing this as an algebraic-geometric object using intersection cohomology sheaves. It then applies this understanding to a specific case, namely the moduli space of genus one surfaces, before delving into the more technical details of proving a theorem about its topology. It concludes by outlining the steps of the proof, highlighting key roles played by Hodge theory, the geometry of Fano varieties, and the analysis of tails in genus one surfaces. It also explains the part played by the Hodge index theorem in calculating intersection numbers, along with the use of these calculations to determine the degree of a variety. It then explores the relationship between this degree and the volume of a variety, expressing this volume as a product of two factors: the degree of a variety in its ambient projective space, and its "height", a measure of how it sits within that space. It also discusses the way this understanding is used to show that a particular component of the moduli space has the right degree to contain the image of a birational map, by first identifying the height of the image of this map on a case by case basis, and then leveraging its general properties to show that this height behaves correctly, and thus that the degree of the component must be as expected. It then explains the part played by analyzing the geometry of genus one surfaces, identifying their canonical models, along with the way this is used to show that a particular component of the moduli space has the right degree to contain the image of a birational map, and that this has implications for the topology of the moduli space, and finally, that combining this with its geometry gives a description of the moduli space. In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and the mechanisms that lead to regime shifts is highly beneficial. This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species of predators, competing for a common prey, engage in explicit interference. The model is reworked to display a singular perturbation with rapid prey movement and slower predator movement, allowing for a regime close to the singular Hopf bifurcation to be analyzed. Near this point, the model exhibits chaotic, mixed-mode oscillations, consisting of long-lasting, concatenated periods of small and large amplitude movements. These eventually transition into the model's steady-state equilibrium. To determine the initiating factors behind a large amplitude oscillation in the mixed-mode orbit, the model is reduced to a suitable normal form, located at the singular Hopf point. The resulting normal form reveals a separating surface that distinguishes two forms of oscillations, and the occurrence of a large amplitude oscillation depends on whether the trajectory crosses from the 'inner' to the 'outer' side of this boundary. Conditions derived from the normal form can predict whether the model will enter another period of MMO behavior before reaching equilibrium. These conditions may serve as early warning indicators for a population shift in the ecosystem. Scale-independent tools, including the technique of boundary layer analysis and a normal form, are equally applicable to a version of the model featuring different population growth rates for the two species. However, this variant is not singularly perturbed and exhibits damped periodic oscillations near the singular point. The model with different growth rates is analogous to the original model near the singular Hopf point, sharing the same normal form and boundary layer analysis results. Nonetheless, this model undergoes a Hopf bifurcation in a three-dimensional phase space, and the distinguishing surface derived from its normal form corresponds to a curve in this space. The curve's location is defined by the same conditions obtained from the normal form, which can predict whether the model's trajectory will re-enter a period of MMO behavior before reaching equilibrium. These conditions are therefore early warning indicators for a population shift in this modified version of the model as well. The models explored in this study provide a theoretical framework that can be applied to a real-world ecosystem where the algal species are subject to different grazing pressures. The resulting analyses offer a pathway for identifying early warning signs of a population shift in this ecosystem. Additionally, they demonstrate how the dynamics of this ecosystem can be understood through a singular perturbation analysis and set the groundwork for a similar investigation of this type

Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at high stellar masses or if other factors contribute, potentially influenced by the same processes that form bulges, is the primary aim of this study. We utilize new data from SAMURAI/FASER, along with existing observations, to explore how star formation rates in disk bar patterns correlate with host galaxy properties. Our results show that even when controlling for galaxy mass, there's a strong correlation between R25 and SFRbar. Furthermore, we find that bulge-dominated galaxies exhibit enhanced quiescent fractions within R25 compared to predictions, indicating inner gas accretion and merger-driven starbursts may not fully explain morphologically diverse quiescent galaxies. Additionally, our data suggest that bulge formation is likely the result of major mergers followed by central starbursts, supporting the idea that bulges form inside constant main sequence tracks, albeit with a focus on understanding the role of these processes in regulating star formation on galaxy scales. Ultimately, our findings imply that star formation in galaxy centers reflects the broader main sequence when considering mass-weighted averages over cosmic timescales, providing insight into the long-standing 'quenching' problem and suggesting that star formation in galaxy centers is an ongoing process. Additionally, our results bring new perspective to the global main sequence relation, particularly its turning over at high masses, indicating it may be an artifact of integrating diverse galaxy morphologies and thus not a pure'star formation' relation. Building upon previous research, our analysis includes a larger data set, improved observations, and a more precise control for galaxy mass, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of the global main sequence and the characteristic star formation rates of galaxy centers. Recently, cache coherence protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade have gained more recognition due to their minimalistic design, potential for increased performance efficiency, and reduced energy consumption. However, these protocols introduce memory instruction reordering, leading to additional, unforeseen program behaviors. In response, we introduce a formal framework that captures the semantics of programs operating under such protocols and integrates a set of fences that interact with the coherence mechanism. Utilizing this framework, we devise an algorithm for assessing program reachability and verifying whether the program complies with given safety criteria using the existing fence configurations. Moreover, we outline a technique for the optimal insertion of fence sets, which ensures program correctness. This method leverages a counter-example driven fence insertion procedure, allowing it to handle multiple fence types with distinct costs. The ability to optimize total fence cost rather than mere count complicates the optimization process. To illustrate the efficacy of our approach, a prototype prototype implementation has been executed across a diverse range of examples and benchmarks. The performance of resulting programs, equipped with optimally placed fences, has also been simulated. The code and performance data are available on GitHub at https://github.com/swabhi96/self-invalidation-protocols. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In addition, we explore various consequences of this finding. In particular, we prove that if subsets A and B, of size k, satisfy the condition that for every three-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions with a specific density. It's also shown that this finding holds true even when the sumset A plus that three-element subset doesn't exceed 3k. In this case, we establish that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions with a specific density that approaches but doesn't quite reach the maximum possible value, which occurs when the sum of elements within A equals the sum of elements within B. In this case, the maximum possible density of A and B exhibiting similarity to arithmetic progressions would be approximately 1 - (3^((5k-4)/2) + 2)/4k. In contrast, it's also shown that this finding doesn't hold true for sums of two-element subsets of B. Using Dirac's time-dependent variational principle, we establish a simple H\'enon-Heiles model based on semiclassical mechanics. A two-body trial wavefunction in the form of Hatree-type is applied, leading to the derivation of an effective Hamiltonian in the context of Jackiw-Kerman theory. The calculations yield results indicating that quantum fluctuations can provoke chaotic behavior in regions of the H\'enon-Heiles system that classically remain stable. The appearance of this chaotic effect is tied to the sign of a parameter-related term in the Jackiw-Kerman Hamiltonian. Our findings are supported by both numerical and analytical methods, providing insight into the interplay between classical stability and chaotic phenomena at the quantum level. The proposed approach may also facilitate the exploration of chaotic dynamics within other nonlinear systems. The obtained results for the H\'enon-Heiles model demonstrate that its ground and excited state energies can be accurately predicted using the Jackiw-Kerman approach, aligning with those derived from a more complex trial wavefunction and showcasing the approach's ability to model quantum chaos effectively. The role of the noninteracting parameter in describing quantum chaos is further highlighted by the spectrum of the Jackiw-Kerman Hamiltonian displaying an unstable region consistent with predictions made through linear stability analysis of the H\'enon-Heiles system. The conclusions drawn from this study suggest that the Jackiw-Kerman approach provides a viable framework for investigating quantum chaos in nonlinear systems through the use of a simple, noncomplex trial wavefunction. The findings of this research are of relevance to further exploration of quantum chaos in nonlinear systems and suggest the utility of variational approaches in such studies. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/zwang84/VRD_BNPS. Our work sets the foundation for balancing proposals with varying levels of difficulty and addressing the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity. As such, it opens up research directions for further study. As the field of Visual Relationship Detection continues to evolve, our work is crucial in achieving enhanced performance and accuracy. As false positives constitute a significant proportion of proposed relationships, it is essential to develop novel approaches that can efficiently reduce this rate. To that end, we propose the use of attention-based models that can selectively focus on particular proposals rather than considering the entire set. Moreover, incorporating external knowledge, such as ontologies and taxonomies, can aid in rectifying the imbalance by providing a framework for relationships to organize themselves within the proposal distribution. Additionally, an imbalance-aware loss function that assigns different weights to distinct proposals based on their difficulty can be an effective means of addressing this issue. Lastly, an alternative strategy to tackle spatial ambiguity involves employing a single-model, multi-task strategy where we train each proposal as a separate task rather than handling all proposals at once. This approach, however, necessitates the development of novel algorithms capable of handling low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity. As such, our initial work on this front concentrates on resolving the imbalance issue to create a solid foundation for further study. In the future, we aim to explore more comprehensive solutions to the spatial ambiguity issue

Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large dataset of treated and untreated brain images along with their corresponding outlines. However, such data is difficult to obtain due to the rarity and cost of acquiring LITT-treated brain images. This paper proposes a groundbreaking deep learning model that generates a dataset of treated brain images along with their corresponding outlines from a smaller dataset of untreated brain images. This model combines a progressive encoder to focus on specific image details with a variational encoder that can work with raw MRI images. By adding a generative model that produces untreated brain images from treated areas, this model can generate a broad range of treated brain images along with their corresponding outlines. Moreover, this model includes two additional components: a component that ensures the generated images and outlines are realistic, and a component that ensures the models' predictions are precise even with limited training data. This model achieves highly accurate outlines from generated images and outperforms a baseline model when evaluated on a small dataset of treated brain images. This model has the potential to generate a large, high-quality dataset of treated brain images along with their corresponding outlines from just a small dataset of untreated brain images, making it a valuable tool for developing medical image analysis applications. Experimental results show that this model's performance continues to improve over time as it's trained on more data, and it produces a dataset of treated brain images and outlines that a leading medical expert consider clinically relevant. This model's ability to generate diverse treated brain images and outlines from just a small dataset of untreated brain images has been a groundbreaking achievement that could change the way medical image analysis models are developed. However, many UPBs of minimal size cannot demonstrate this strong quantum nonlocality. In this research, a series of UPBs of various larger sizes for systems of three and four parties were constructed in the $d_1 \otimes d_2 \otimes d_3 \otimes d_4$ system. It was also shown that these UPBs have strong quantum nonlocality, answering open questions from Halder and others, and providing a connection between UPBs and strong quantum nonlocality. GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the GP 2 compiler, several key modifications have been made to Bak's compiler, including a data structure optimisation for dynamic arrays known as BigArray. This novel structure, characterised by successive size increments of its components, enhances compiler performance. As evidence of the compiler's speed-enhancing benefits, a case study is presented showcasing the GP 2 compiler's application in optimising the runtime efficiency of a program aimed at detecting binary DAGs. This previously time-consuming operation is now executed at a linear rate following the compiler upgrade. Additionally, another case study is described, detailing the GP 2 compiler's use in a program filtering out unwanted DAGs. This has an unexpected consequence, where the unoptimised GP 2 compiler outperforms the optimised version for this particular instance.
