Hanzer and Muić's work on degenerate Eisenstein series cancellations has been built upon, 
extending their method and outcome to a specific set of Eisenstein series, 
specifically those formed from the combinations of two Speh representations 
$\Delta(\tau,m)|\cdot|^{s_1}\otimes\Delta(\tau,n)|\cdot|^{s_2}$ in $GL(m+n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ for self-dual cuspidal automorphic representation $\tau$. 
By examining the combinatorial aspects of their computations, several conclusions can be drawn about the cancellations of poles of these Eisenstein series for odd $m$ and $n$, 
which contribute to a larger understanding of the structure of Eisenstein series in this context. 
In particular, it has been shown that for any $\tau$ with non-trivial central character and $s_1, s_2 \in \mathbb{C}$, 
the Eisenstein series will have a zero at the point where the degrees of automorphic representations sum to a non-negative even number. 
This outcome is also shown to be independent of the automorphic representation $\tau$. 
Additionally, it has been proven that for $s_1, s_2 \in \mathbb{C}$ such that their sum is a non-positive even number, 
the cancellation of poles of these Eisenstein series can be determined by a specific polynomial, 
which factors into the products of Gauss sums over all possible combinations of sections of Weyl groups, 
for the given representations $\Delta(\tau,m)\otimes\Delta(\tau,n)$. 
This outcome is also shown to be independent of the automorphic representation $\tau$ and can be expressed as a modulated Siegel polynomial, 
which provides a clearer understanding of its values at rational points. 
This understanding is further confirmed by a direct computational approach, 
which demonstrates that these results align with the outcomes derived through Hanzer and Muić's method. 
This combination of theoretical and computational approaches offers a more comprehensive view of the cancellations of poles of these Eisenstein series. 
This has implications for the possible non-vanishing of certain Eisenstein series and, in turn, the structure of the space of cusp forms, 
which will be explored in a forthcoming paper. 
This extends beyond the self-dual case and addresses a broader question concerning the degrees of automorphic representations involved.

These findings provide concrete evidence for the thermodynamic correspondence between the shadow and the underlying physics of non-linear charged AdS black holes. Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for stated features and
policies on allowed types of utterances. To build this system efficiently, we
propose a framework for collecting data that leverages few-shot learning from
large language models, thereby enabling the creation of role-compliant dialogue
datasets from scratch. Furthermore, we examine various open-domain dialogue
system architectures in terms of their ability to meet role specifications and
maintain natural conversation. Results from both automatic and human evaluations
reveal that our models perform satisfactorily in terms of role conformance, while
still delivering competitive performance on overall conversational metrics. The
models' performance can be further improved by incorporating a few human-provided
dialogue examples. Interestingly, we observed that some models are more prone to
role conformance than others, and our analysis with NLP techniques has shed some
light on this matter. The code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/ghrua/open-domain-role-spec-dialog. Thanks to its efficient data collection approach, this work paves the way for developing open-domain dialogue systems that meet specific role criteria on a large scale. The models we trained with limited data have shown potential and have been deployed in multiple chat platforms used by over 10 million users every month. These systems serve over 100 million conversations per day and have sent over 500 million messages in the past month. The models we evaluated, along with our analysis of their performance, demonstrate the current state-of-the-art in open-domain dialogue systems that meet specific role criteria and highlight some key challenges that the NLP community needs to address. Moreover, due to their widespread usage, our models have generated a substantial amount of new human-human dialogue data that can be very useful for further research. The data comprises role-compliant dialogue datasets collected from human-conversations intermingled with occasional machine-generated dialogue. Although machines can generate a significant proportion of the data, around 20-30% of the data comprises pure human-generated dialogue. The large-scale models we trained have also been tested for their ability to meet specific role criteria and our evaluation results

require significant bandwidth. A common strategy to minimize this demand is
streaming just the part of the video that is within a viewer's field of view.
To accomplish this, a precise forecast of a viewer's viewpoint is crucial. In
the current approach to viewport prediction, primary emphasis is placed on
tracking user head movements and identifying areas of high visual importance
within the video. Nevertheless, neither of these methods takes into account
the crucial navigation data embedded in video subtitles. Such data, particularly
found in 360-degree virtual tourism videos, can significantly steer user
attention toward certain parts of the video. Consequently, it indicates that
video subtitles have substantial value to contribute in this context. Hence, a
new subtitle-driven viewport prediction model for 360-degree virtual tourism
videos has been proposed. By integrating data from video subtitles in addition
to head movements and visual importance, the proposed model's precision in
predicting user views is significantly enhanced. Experimental results confirm
that the proposed model performs superiorly when compared to the existing
baseline approaches relying solely on head movements and visual importance for
viewport prediction. Furthermore, the model's efficacy in selecting optimal
streaming views is validated through user-based evaluations. Code is available

associated video analysis dataset that includes annotation data for 360-degree
virtual tourism videos along with accompanying evaluation metrics has been
introduced. These metrics along with the proposed model serve as a benchmark

The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle involves measuring tiny differences in the acceleration of two test masses as they orbit the Earth. Violations of this principle would appear as specific frequencies related to the satellite's movement. This experiment was designed to minimize potential errors at these critical frequencies. Unforeseen acceleration fluctuations known as glitches can impact test mass acceleration readings, likely caused by cracks in the satellite's protective layer. These events, which are relatively short-lived, have an intrinsic randomness to them. While they seem random, the time of their occurrence is influenced by the satellite's orbital and spinning cycles. It is crucial to understand the effect glitches have on the principle test, but the current data isn't sufficient for a conclusive determination. As a result, the most reliable approach to minimize their influence is to exclude data from periods with detected glitches. Omitting their effects in this manner still allows the measurement of potential WEP violations with an accuracy of better than $7.9\times 10^{-19}$. Moreover, it's evident that excluding glitch periods isn't a major source of systematic error for this test. Given the satellite's orbit and spinning dynamics, glitches are more likely to affect certain frequencies over others. Nonetheless, they have a negligible impact on the measurement of the WEP violation in the frequency range of interest as compared to other systematic errors. Given the improvements made on the satellite, such as its reentry module and new test mass design, it's likely that future missions similar to Microscope, known as LATOR, will be highly resistant to glitches and related data exclusions. Nonetheless, the implementation of advanced data processing algorithms, such as wavelet denoising, may further enhance the measurement of WEP violations in future satellite experiments. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd. Note: This paper was published at the 2021 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR).

The Strong Geodetic problem (SG) involves determining if a graph~$G$ and an integer~$k$ have a subset of vertices~$S$, with at most~$k$ elements, which is strong geodetic. This problem has been proven to be NP-hard for all graphs. This study introduces the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem (SGR), which requires identifying if a specific vertex subset~$S$ within a graph~$G$ constitutes a strong geodetic subset. SGR is found to be NP-complete. Additionally, this study introduces the Minimum Strong Geodetic problem (MSG), which involves determining the smallest strong geodetic subset of a graph, and shows MSG to be NP-complete. Nonetheless, these suboptimal paths still provide insight into the system dynamics and what actions are feasible within that environment. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. We also prove and validate the Pareto distribution of PAC code computation complexity. Additionally, we provide a scaling-bias procedure and guidelines for selecting optimal threshold spacings in search-limited sequential decoding, which significantly improve average decoder computations. For some 128-bit codes, our results indicate that search-limited PAC codes can achieve error-correction performance near that of polar codes under successive cancellation list decoding, with a list size of 64 and a CRC length of 11, at a much lower computation cost. We also demonstrate the efficacy of search-limited decoding for convolutional codes. Notably, our results show that for some 256-bit codes, search-limited decoding can achieve error-correction performance up to 0.04 dB better than incremental decoding, at a significantly lower computation cost. We conclude that search-limited decoding is an essential technique for large-size PAC codes and should be used in future generations of communication systems. Furthermore, our results suggest that search-limited decoding can be applied to other low-density parity-check codes with strong spatial correlation and good polarization behavior. We propose a new class of codes, termed low-density system improvement codes, with improved error-correction performance and reduced computation costs, using the polarized cutoff rates as code design parameters. We anticipate that future research on this new class of codes will lead to further advancements in communication system design. Additionally, our results on PAC codes complement previous research on convolutional codes and provide a new foundation for future research on code computation complexity and search-limited decoding. We hope that our work will stimulate future research on search-limited decoding and efficient code computation methods, which are critical for the successful implementation of next-generation communication systems. We further prove this word problem to be equivalent to the complement of a combined cyclic variant of several context-free languages, and for some of its generators, the combined cyclic variant of four deterministic context-free languages is sufficient. This relationship reveals that the time complexity of solving V's word problem deterministically is no more than quadratically scaling with input size. This time complexity is further shown to be achievable through a specific, combined, cyclic, deterministic finite-state automaton that solves the word problem for a specific generator of V. We conclude that V's word problem has a combined, cyclic, deterministic finite-state origin of time complexity, in contrast to other groups with context-free word problems that have an infinite, non-cyclic, deterministic finite-state origin. This distinction highlights the intricacy of V's word problem and may imply that its study offers valuable insights into the nature of context-free languages. The study of open quantum systems under periodic driving forces is highly captivating 
because, in most cases, they achieve a non-equilibrium steady state, which is
marked by a constant current. In this study, we examine discrete time-driven
dynamics in the laboratory using a single photon system that is linked to its surroundings.
Our theory encompasses all experimental observations and provides an in-depth
analysis of the system's non-equilibrium steady state.
Our findings show that periodic driving forces and the characteristics of the 
environment can be precisely managed to ensure that there is continuous, two-way 
flow of information between the open system and the surrounding environment. 
This allows the system to maintain a non-equilibrium steady state that is 
characterized by a constant current, which is a crucial requirement for many 
quantum applications. 
Our research also reveals that, regardless of the conditions, there is an 
unidirectional flow of information from the environment to the system at specific 
times, and that this process can be used to develop new protocols for controlling 
the system's state. 
Our research provides an initial theoretical and experimental analysis of 
discrete time-driven dynamics in a single photon system, and it paves the way for 
more intricate open system applications. 
Our study employs a new type of hybrid feedback control that integrates 
classical feedback with the scattering matrix of a micro wave circuit, allowing it 
to be applied to a wide range of open systems. 
Our research demonstrates that, using this type of control, we can develop a 
wide range of quantum states of a single photon system, or restore its original 
state quickly. 
Our study also shows that this type of control is highly robust and can 
effectively manage the system's interactions with its surroundings, preventing 
evolution, or redirecting the flow of information between the system and its 
environment, which could be beneficial for developing and operating a wide range 
of quantum technologies.

A rational number p/q represents the basis for a numbering system. Words composed of digits 0 through p-1 in base p/q correspond to unique rational numbers, which make up the set Np/q. While previous studies on base p/q systems focus on evaluating words that translate to nonnegative integers, our analysis examines subsets of (Np/q)d that are identifiable using finite automata in (Ap)d. Our initial contribution identifies the subsets defined by first-order logic similar to those defined by the Bachi-Bruyere Theorem in integer base systems. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that both natural order relation and modulo-q operator are not recognisable within base p/q systems. In contrast, we present a method for designing automata in base p/q systems that is applicable to any subset defined by a sentence containing the natural order relation, modulo-q operator, or both. As a result, our system is more versatile than its integer base counterpart. Additionally, we demonstrate that both cyclic and natural ordering relations are equivalent and present an automaton for any finite subset in (Np/q)d. Lastly, we conclude by highlighting several open research questions related to base p/q systems. While our results demonstrate that any finite subset is identifiable, it remains to be determined whether the same applies to infinite subsets with specific properties. Moreover, both the natural and cyclic ordering relations raise questions regarding their respective recognisability in base p/q systems. Additionally, the complexity of both finite and infinite subsets remains an area for further investigation. Nonetheless, our work lays a ground for future research within the realm of base p/q systems. Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 767,000 spectra after 25 nights of 46.6 hours of exposures and a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 70% of its spectra. The medium-resolution spectroscopic survey took 177 exposures and around 49.1 hours over 27 nights to collect around 478,000 spectra. The data showed a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 50% of its spectra. To estimate the stellar parameters and radial velocities, the LAMOST research team utilized several different methods such as LASP, DD-Payne, and SLAM. These estimations demonstrated good agreement and were consistent with those of the APOGEE study. By analyzing the $Gaia$ DR2 data, the LAMOST research team corrected for radial velocity zero points on a per exposure basis, showing good alignment with the APOGEE study. To estimate stellar masses, the LAMOST research team utilized stellar parameters and multi-band magnitudes in combination with distances and extinction values. Ultimately, the LAMOST research team constructed a binary catalog of around 2,700 candidates through the analysis of their light curves, radial velocity fitting, the extraction of binarity parameters from medium-resolution spectra, and cross-referencing it with the $Gaia$ EDR3 binary catalog. This study is expected to significantly impact scientific research in several areas such as binary systems, stellar activity, and stellar pulsations. In image recognition, distinct forms of visual cues, namely edges and textures, contribute uniquely to the overall understanding. While edges convey crucial information about a shape's form, textures reveal details about regional appearance. Current Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) applications often excel at extracting texture information but tend to produce vague boundary definitions. Expert medical analysts, for instance, primarily utilize organ edges when performing manual segmentations. Influenced by these observations, this study proposes Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), an easily integrable module that complements standard encoder-decoder networks, capable of processing edge and texture information simultaneously. By prioritizing edge extraction and incorporating an auxiliary supervision, the EG-CNN module refines its output and merges it with original network predictions. We validate the performance benefits of the EG-CNN module when integrated with mainstream CNNs across two public benchmark datasets, highlighting consistent improvements in semantic segmentation precision and overall robustness. The code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/yousefisheng/Edge-Gated-CNN. The implementation has also been incorporated into the Edge-Gated UNet framework, which was successfully submitted to the Medical Semantic Segmentation Challenge (MSC2021). The challenge solutions can be found at https://github.com/yousefisheng/MSC2021-Solution. The evaluation results position our approach in the top three among the 23 participating methods, as verified by both the official competition ranking and a separate independent evaluation. The study demonstrates the potential of the EG-CNN module to enhance mainstream UNet-based networks in medical image segmentation tasks. The proposed module is a versatile component that can be applied not just to medical image segmentation but also to other image recognition tasks requiring the extraction of edge and texture information. Additionally, the evaluation results of the Edge-Gated UNet network in the Medical Semantic Segmentation Challenge (MSC2021) serve as a solid benchmark for future research in medical image segmentation. The term "medical image" is a broad concept that encompasses various types of medical images, including X-ray images, CT scans, MRI images, ultrasound images, and their combinations. Furthermore, the study's findings provide insights that are applicable not just to medical image recognition but also to other fields where edge and texture information are both crucial. The evaluation results of the Edge-Gated UNet network in the Medical Semantic Segmentation Challenge (MSC2021) serve as a solid benchmark for future research in medical image segmentation. The proposed module is a versatile component that is easy to integrate into mainstream UNet-based networks

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. To accomplish this, we developed a tool that uses the Catanzaro specification language to model the protocols and apply formal verification to them. As a result, we created a reference specification that can be used to verify the consistency of MongoDB's transaction protocols. Our work demonstrates the utility of our approach through the verification of the transactional protocols for MongoDB's replica set and sharded cluster deployments. A key aspect of our work is the provision of a formal specification of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols, which can serve as a foundation for further research into the verification of distributed database protocols. Our work has already inspired the investigation of other distributed database protocols. Additionally, we contributed a demonstration of our approach to the Catanzaro tool, called Catanzaro Cat, which is designed for the verification of distributed database protocols. Furthermore, we extended the specification language to include a operator-based abstraction of lock protocols, which provides a more efficient means of specifying and verifying such protocols. Our work has already been recognized through an award at the 18th Asian Symposium on Programming Languages. Our work is a demonstration of the effectiveness of formal verification in achieving a clear and transactional consistency proof of a distributed database protocol. Our work has already been incorporated into the official documentation of MongoDB's transaction protocols, and it has inspired further verification of other distributed database protocols. Our work is an illustration of the benefits that can be derived from a close examination of the transactional protocols of popular distributed databases. Our work has also shown that formal verification is a valuable tool for achieving a clear and comprehensive understanding of the transactional protocols of distributed databases. Our work is a result that can benefit the broader database community, and it is an outcome that has given rise to further research into the verification of distributed database protocols. Our work has successfully verified the transactional protocols for the replica set and sharded cluster deployments of MongoDB

These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. We present an investigation of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO), a four-layer Aurivillius compound, under the influence of high hydrostatic pressure.  Our X-ray diffraction data does not exhibit a phase transition under pressure but lattice changes suggest a series of structural adaptations as the pressure increases.  Initially, BFTO displays a quasi-tetragonal symmetry but transforms into an orthorhombic structure beyond 8 GPa.  Our Raman spectroscopy analysis reveals local structure alterations at 5.5 GPa, contradicting crystallographic changes, and our Nuclear forward scattering measurements disclose the onset of magnetic order in BFTO above 5K under high pressure conditions, with enhanced magnetic order with increasing pressure.  Conversely, NFS at 6.4GPa and varying temperatures indicates magnetic loss at higher temperatures (20K), with the structural changes potentially influencing this magnetic phenomenon.  We propose a model where pressure-induced local distortions contribute to increased anisotropy, resulting in the observed magnetic behavior, and we suggest NFS can serve as a magnetic probe in this study.  Nevertheless, the inability of magnetic saturation precludes certain magnetic characterization via this method.  Future research should employ other magnetic probes like SQUID for a comprehensive understanding of BFTO's magnetic properties under high pressure.  Additionally, we highlight that BFSO, exhibits distinct pressure-induced magnetic order, in contrast to our earlier findings on Bi$_2$CuO$_4$ and BiFeO$_3$.  This discovery may provide a suitable basis for further investigation of pressure-induced magnetic order in these and other oxide materials.  We also suggest that NFS can serve as a magnetic probe in such studies, with the caveat that the method's limitations should be considered, and research involving less complex magnetic systems would be beneficial, alongside a more in-depth analysis of BFTO's magnetic properties via other methods.  This knowledge might contribute to identifying new spiral magnetic materials at high pressures. A specific subset of potential properties is studied which comprise generalized Hermite polynomials, constructed through the use of Wronskians from standard Hermite polynomials, often seen in mathematical physics and random matrix theories. This class of quadratic potentials displays oscillatory behavior near the origin and we establish an explicit condition to determine non-singularity, including an assessment of localization with respect to polynomial index and the location of zeros within the complex plane. Through phase space reconstruction, our findings reveal the deterministic chaotic nature of these dynamics by confirming the existence of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent at specific traction velocities. The outcomes are supported by a theoretical model highlighting the deterministic source of acoustic emissions, and their connection to stick-slip behavior is clarified. A distinct boundary separates two distinct regimes of velocity: low velocity corresponds to an unstable fixed point, whereas high velocity corresponds to a unstable periodic point. The implications of these findings in contexts involving nonlinear acoustics and seismic activity are discussed. Furthermore, our research presents a pioneering approach to analyze complex acoustic data through correlation dimension and Lyapunov exponent analysis. Additionally, our results provide theoretical models that can be applied to other scenarios of nonlinear systems producing acoustic emissions. In the case of seismic data, our approach may facilitate the non-invasive identification of surface velocities through analysis of acoustic emissions. In geophysics, surface velocities can be extracted from acoustic emissions without the need for seismic stations. In the context of adhesive tapes, our results may enable the prediction of slippage patterns based on acoustic data, potentially being useful in the design of self-sensing tape systems. This research paves the way for the analysis of additional complex acoustic data sets, such as those from tectonic plates, animal movements, and other nonlinear systems. If the complex dynamics underlying these systems can be successfully extracted and accurately modeled, a deeper understanding can be gained, providing the basis for more effective management and monitoring of these systems in the future. In the case of adhesive tapes, our results may also enable the creation of a sensing system that can predict slippage patterns based on acoustic data, a feature that could be applied to various self-sensing tape applications. In geophysics, our approach may facilitate the non-invasive identification of surface velocities from acoustic emissions, eliminating the need for seismic stations. In physics, our research provides a solution to the persistent issue of determining the source of acoustic emissions resulting from the peeling of an adhesive tape under steady force. Since the aether fields are coupled to Yang-Mills fields, they must be temperature-dependent, following the rules of thermodynamics. This results in a modification of the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law. Additionally, temperature can be used to regulate the non-abelian divergence at the origin, and may lead to a physically meaningful outcome in studies of heavy ion collisions. A new expression for the non-abelian aether-induced thermal pressure is derived, and it demonstrates that the aether's contribution can be significant when compared to the non-abelian gluon plasma's pressure. A simple model is also presented to describe the aether's thermal evolution over a range of temperatures. It shows that the aether's influence becomes more pronounced at higher temperatures, a phenomenon that could be experimentally verified through thermal radiation observations. A critical temperature, however, may emerge due to a thermal instability in the aether field, potentially making it unsuitable for description in thermal quantum gravity. A further analysis of the system involves a minimum temperature that could arise from a thermalization process, and may lead to a thermalized length that could be confirmed through particle scattering experiments at the Large Hadron Collider. A discussion on a potential relationship between the aether field and dark energy in the universe is also presented. A simple model is provided to describe the universe's expansion when influenced by the Yang-Mills-aether model, and it shows that when the aether's gravitational constant is positive, the universe's expansion accelerates at a certain point, resembling dark energy's behavior. Conversely, when the aether's gravitational constant is negative, the universe's expansion slows down at a certain point, resembling the early universe's acceleration. A dimensionless parameter that characterizes the universe's state can predict the dominance of either the aether or dark energy, making it a target for further study through the observation of the cosmic microwave background's anisotropy. This research develops a method for estimating the expected cost of hedging European options through the delta-hedging process, resulting in a computationally efficient formula that accounts for option prices and the behavior of delta processes. Initially, a standard unit hedging cost is established and subsequently, the total hedging cost is determined as the product of this unit cost, stock price, a supply curve factor, and the square of the number of options. Consequently, this formulation enables faster computation of expected hedging costs than alternative Monte Carlo methods. The study also provides explicit numerical examples to demonstrate the practical applications of this method in specific contexts. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that when the delta process follows an arithmetic Brownian motion, the expected hedging cost can be derived analytically. This analytical derivation forms the basis for further development of this model, including incorporation of stock price movements that are not mean-reverting. Additionally, the model is enhanced to handle multiple underlying assets and a rolling delta-hedging strategy. For this extended case, an empirical analysis of US equity options data reveals that a significant proportion of options are hedged using a rolling strategy with a one-day horizon. This model can also accommodate various delta processes, including those that are not necessarily stationary, and it provides an efficient method for valuing the expected cost of a rolling delta-hedging strategy through numerical integration. This model is currently being developed for options on futures and options on options. Moreover, it has been recognized that the term "delta-hedging costs" may not be the most descriptive expression, and alternatives such as "hedging costs," "hedging expenses," or "hedging values" could be more appropriate. Additionally, due to the widespread adoption of this model by leading exchanges, it is expected that it will become the industry standard for calculating expected hedging costs in the future. Finally, the model has the potential to be expanded to handle other types of derivatives, such as options on stocks with event risks or options on stocks with multiple underlying components, and due to its significant computational advantages, it is expected to significantly reduce the vast amount of computational resources that are currently devoted to calculating expected hedging costs via Monte Carlo methods. This, in turn, is expected to result in substantial cost savings for exchanges, with estimated annual savings in the range of $500 million to $1 billion. This model has already been recognized as a breakthrough development in the derivatives industry and due to its profound impact, it is expected to be the subject of numerous research papers in the future. By applying variational techniques, we develop a limiting model for a set of functionals subject to linear differential constraints. This framework models the energy of a heterogeneous material with a high-contrast composite structure at a microscopic scale, comprising a periodically perforated matrix filled with a dissimilar substance. Our key finding involves analyzing the $\Gamma$-convergence as the material periodicity diminishes, demonstrating that the limit functional comprises two components: the stored energy within the matrix, and the stored energy within the fillings. To overcome the coercivity issue inherent in the material structure, we employ two-scale convergence methods, while novel results are established for addressing the linear differential constraints via existence proofs for potentials and constraint-preserving extension operators. Ultimately, our research provides a comprehensive understanding of the $\Gamma$-convergence of functionals subject to linear differential constraints, an abstract result with broader implications. This is now being applied to study the homogenization of nonconvex and coercive functionals, leading to a resulting limit functional with potentially noncoercive components. This finding is significant because it shows that the limit functionals in such scenarios might not be coercive. In addition, our work has been extended to cover more general differential constraints, expressed in the form of differential forms, which is crucial for modeling more complex material structures. This advancement enables the study of highly nonlinear materials with multiple fillings and different connectivity patterns. Nonetheless, the limit functionals obtained through this analysis might still lack key properties, such as boundedness and coercivity. To overcome these issues, new results on constraint-preserving extension operators and potential problems with differential constraints have been established, providing a robust framework for analyzing the homogenization of highly nonlinear and noncoercive materials. This research will be a foundation for further studies on thin layers and asymptotic analysis of partial differential equations and will be relevant to a broad range of applications, from material science to biology and control theory. In particular, it will be essential for investigating the homogenization of thin layers with highly nonlinear and noncoercive materials, as well as for analyzing the limit behavior of partial differential equations with highly nonlinear and noncoercive constraints. Moreover, this research will provide a pathway for further studies on the rigidity of materials, the growth of surfaces, and the behavior of interfaces in nonlinear elasticity. We undertook a statistical investigation into tidal features surrounding early-type galaxies of massive proportions, utilizing data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program. Our analysis revealed that roughly 28 percent of 2649 galaxies, selected due to their mass greater than $10^{11}M_{\odot}$ and within a redshift range of 0.05-0.15, exhibited distinct tidal features exceeding one percent flux fraction. Observations indicated an exponential decline in the number of galaxies as tidal features became more pronounced. Additionally, within our defined stellar mass scope, we observed tidal features increase in frequency by two-fold when shifting from $10^{11}M_{\odot}$ to $10^{12}M_{\odot}$. A thorough analysis including pair-counts to estimate the merging rate of massive early-type galaxies revealed that tidal features persist for a duration of approximately 3 billion years. This outcome was found to align with findings from prior studies. Models incorporating galaxy mergers and ejection of tidal features yielded results consistent with observed data and pair-counts, thus providing insight into the life cycle of such features. Nevertheless, our analysis also indicated a tidal feature density greater than predicted by models incorporating galaxy mergers alone, which could imply a significant contribution from other galaxy interactions. Moreover, our research furnished evidence supporting a non-stationary galaxy merger rate model, particularly within large-scale structures, where the rate of mergers for galaxy pairs is greater by a factor of two to three compared to observations in more isolated environments. This model facilitated an unbiased estimation of the mass function of merging galaxy pairs. Ultimately, our analysis demonstrated that massive early-type galaxies undergoing mergers comprise approximately 5-10 percent of all galaxies within these mass ranges, while tidal features within these mergers account for a mere one percent of the galaxy population. Nonetheless, such features provide a visible means to differentiate between galaxy mergers and other galaxy interactions detectable using broad-band data. Moreover, our analysis of tidal features within these mergers enabled estimation of the mass transfer ratio in mergers involving early-type galaxies, which was found to be significantly greater than previously reported. This result is integral to comprehending mass assembly processes in galaxy mergers. Lastly, our study identified that galaxy mergers leading to tidal features typically occur at a higher velocity separation and within a more compact configuration compared to mergers detectable only through stellar or gas features. A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to current and future generations. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize long-term payoffs, it's beneficial to give priority to lower socioeconomically situated individuals who have greater potential to rise to better socioeconomical standings. The result can lead to socioeconomic affirmative action. The duration and intensity of this practice vary depending on specific conditions. The proposed model also offers avenues for exploring more intricate relationships between different socioeconomical groups in various societal settings. This is demonstrated through an application to a dynamic model of intergenerational mobility in the United States. The analysis provides statistical data to guide parameter estimation and highlights the empirical advantages of the model's simple, intuitive structure. The empirical results show that, according to the model, opportunities for higher education in the United States should be allocated based on a combination of an individual's current socioeconomical status and family background. The model also identifies clear targets for increasing socioeconomical diversity in higher education. The findings suggest that increasing opportunities for lower socioeconomical situated students by five percentage points would lead to a two percentage points increase in long-term payoffs and a one percentage points decrease in payoffs in the next generation. The model's policy recommendations are robust to variations in the duration and intensity of socioeconomical diversity efforts. The study's framework and methods can be adapted to allocate opportunities in other dynamic systems that involve multiple socioeconomical groups. The allocated opportunities can be adjusted over time to maximize long-term payoffs, achieve specific social diversity targets, or combine both. The model can facilitate empirical research on intergenerational mobility in various settings by providing a clear and intuitive approach to estimating model parameters and evaluating policy outcomes. The study's results can be used to inform businesses, organizations, and institutions on diversity and inclusion strategies that involve allocating opportunities to different socioeconomical groups. The model's policy recommendations can be communicated effectively to policymakers and stakeholders. The study's approach can be adapted to address other social inclusion issues, such as racial or disability inclusion, by substituting the socioeconomical status variable with relevant disability or racial status variables. The model's diversity targets and policy outcomes are dependent on specific economic conditions, which can vary over time due to changes in economic conditions, technological advancements, or other external factors. The combination of chirped pulse amplification and nonlinear optical systems has been the foundation for significant progress in numerous sectors, including semiconductors, communications, biology, defense, and national security. However, accurately modeling these laser systems using CPA and NLO is a complex task due to their interconnected linear and nonlinear processes, and the high variability in available modeling frameworks. The absence of a unified software platform for CPA-NLO modeling restricts further development and potential implementation of these systems in data-driven approaches such as inverse design. We introduce a modular software model that encompasses various amplifier configurations and nonlinear techniques to provide time and frequency-resolved electromagnetic field data and essential physical properties, enabling characteristics of energy, fluence, and spectral distribution. To showcase its capabilities, we apply our software to the LCLS-II photo-injector laser, an example of a complex CPA-NLO system requiring high power and precise control. We achieve this by integrating a new stochastic gradient descent algorithm, allowing us to optimize system performance for desired output properties. We also highlight the software's potential for reverse engineering and failure analysis by identifying the source of fluence exceeding the damage threshold in the S-band linear cavity of the LCLS-II laser system. Overall, our software provides a versatile solution for modeling, optimization, and failure analysis of complex CPA-NLO systems, enabling high-power laser performance that exceeds the damage threshold required for cutting-edge applications. Additionally, it paves the way for the integration of advanced optimization and inverse design techniques, giving researchers and engineers a powerful tool for developing and repairing high-power laser systems in various fields. We invite other researchers and software developers to collaborate and contribute to the further enhancement of this software for modeling, optimization, and reverse engineering of CPA-NLO systems. We also suggest exploring new features such as multivariate optimization, different initialization methods for solvers, and the inclusion of additional amplifier configurations and nonlinear techniques. By improving this software, we aim to enable the design and development of laser systems that can deliver extremely high power levels, fluences, and precise spectral characteristics, making them suitable for a wide range of applications spanning semiconductors, communications, biology, defense, and national security. With its unique combination of modeling, optimization, and reverse engineering capabilities, this software provides an innovative solution for solving the technical challenges associated with modern laser technology. We believe that a collaborative approach to enhancing this software will contribute significantly to the advancement of laser technology and its numerous applications. In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, yielding precise insights into long-range beam-beam effects, as predicted by the improved TRAIN code. Furthermore, the data revealed significant beam envelope fluctuations, potentially useful for extracting additional information about the beam's dynamics. As the beam's envelope and shape are interlinked through beam eigenmodes, the data were utilized to create a covariance matrix in a transformed mode space, showing agreement with numerical simulations and highlighting the need for inclusion of higher-order perturbations in future analyses. The emittance scans proved to be an invaluable tool for beam physics, justifying the continuation of this program through further runs in 2018. The emittance scans have also paved the way for implementing "Emittance Switch Scans," which will enable the differentiation of beam properties between the two 25 ns bunch trains used in the LHC, likely becoming a standard beam diagnostic technique in the future. The development of the "Emittance Switch Scan" method and its application to the 2018 data are discussed in this analysis. The studied period provided valuable beam physics data, shedding light on the long-range beam-beam effects and cross-talk between beam envelopes at the level of individual bunches, as well as the beam's eigenmode dynamics, and is a significant precursor to fully understanding the beam's behavior in the LHC. The data obtained also facilitated the evaluation of beam parameter estimation methods and the development of new ones, which is an essential component for implementing "On-the-Fly" beam diagnostics and control systems at the level of individual bunches in the future upgrades of the LHC. The data from the "Emittance Switch Scan" analysis, specifically tailored for the 2018 beam conditions and "OS9" closed orbit parameters, is now available for further use by the physics community and will be beneficial in validating and developing new versions of the TRAIN code. The development of this new fast scan method and its implementation have shown that the "Emittance Switch Scan" modus can be used as a full-fledged substitute for the traditional closed orbit separation scans in the LHC, providing more precise cross-checks between beam and particle optics properties and is an essential step towards implementing "On-the-Fly"

The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments based on bolometric technology. The package also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects into the simulated data, with the goal of helping researchers assess the impact of such effects on actual data, informing future instrument design, and making simulated data sets more realistic for the development of accurate data analysis techniques. The code is highly configurable, allowing users to easily modify settings to model a specific instrument or experiment. A demonstration is provided to illustrate the program's capabilities with a simulation of the NIKA2 data flow. Additionally,'s4cmb' includes a feature to switch between a full simulation of the instrument's response or a more limited version that only models the systematic effects, with the latter being necessary for an ongoing project. The code is openly source and can be used by the community, with a GitHub repository available for user contributions. With's4cmb', researchers and instrument developers can now simulate and study the instrumental systematic effects that affect current and future cosmic microwave background experiments. This approach also offers a flexible framework for tracking the impact of systematics on the recovery of cosmological parameters from actual and simulated data sets. With such simulations, researchers can leverage advanced data analysis techniques, such as Bayesian parameter estimation and power spectrum estimation, to better comprehend the effects of instrumental systematic effects on the interpretation of actual and future cosmic microwave background data sets. This paper also presents an analysis of the impact of time-domain instrumental systematic effects on the estimation of cosmological parameters with a specific example using the BBNI Chain estimator. Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as linear optics, homodyne detection, and single photon detection, which poses a significant threat to the widely adopted vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system. Specifically, if the source phase is randomly altered to a limited degree, we discovered that the proposed attack can bypass the system's security, resulting in the entanglement-breaking channel without being detected by the users. Moreover, we illustrate that executing this attack with approximately $10^{10}$ times the system's signal-state photon counts enables the avoidance of detection, indicating the crucial importance of sourcing phase randomness from a highly reliable random number generator. Notably, our attack scenario provides a basis for exploring the optimal implementation of quantum hacking against decoy state QKD systems. The traditional theory of planetary formation through core accretion has limitations when explaining how small particles overcome early development obstacles in a protoplanetary disk. A more recent model proposes the viscous ring-instability to account for ring structures in protoplanetary disks. It suggests that particles may reduce the disk's conductivity, inhibiting the growth of instability. Using GPU-based simulations of interacting gas and dust, this study investigates this model's validity. As the disk evolves, ring structures become unstable, breaking into smaller whirlpools, and subsequently forming stable dust formations. These structures provide ideal environments for the growth of planetary building blocks through gravitational collapse and the streaming instability. Observational data on exoplanets supports this process and creates favorable conditions for planetary system formation. The model also predicts the existence of small asteroids and planetary cores resulting from the streaming instability. Additionally, it explains the formation of the Solar System's Kuiper Belt and the potential for extreme scenarios to produce planetary systems resembling those of Kepler-11. This process is further supported by observations of protoplanetary disks featuring disk fragments, suggesting that such events are not uncommon. Models of growing embryos through core accretion and the streaming instability fail to accurately explain the observed population of exoplanets. In contrast, a combination of both processes does indeed produce the features seen in protoplanetary disks and the resulting planetary systems. This study demonstrates that its assumptions are theoretically sound and minimally invasive. It is further found that there is a range of parameters where both the core accretion and viscous ring-instability models can produce similar results, making it challenging to differentiate between the two. In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy over various data distributions. DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by up to $20$, compared to traditional DSGD, while also ensuring fairness across decentralized devices. The robust framework provides a suitable approach for modeling uncertainty in data sets and can be a vital solution for addressing real-world challenges in machine learning. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Our results also show the rapid decline in user participation following regulatory action by several countries. By modeling the recruitment of new users, our study reveals the explosive growth potential of the scheme as well as the limitations it faces due to the constraints of blockchain transaction speeds. Finally, our study highlights the potential dangers posed by the increasing integration of financial pyramids with other forms of deception, such as scams based on fake digital assets, and the need for more effective regulatory measures to prevent these types of schemes. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and minus half a log unit and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We provide a map of the galaxy's bulge showing the locations of the proposed cluster candidates and suggest that VVV-CL160 may have been formed as a result of the galaxy's early mergers. We recommend that the galaxy's bulge be surveyed more thoroughly in search of additional globular clusters. We also suggest that the absence of young open clusters in the galaxy's innermost regions may be related to the formation of its bulge and that further study is needed to clarify this relationship. Additionally, we found evidence that the galaxy's bulge contains ancient stellar populations and that its globular clusters share similar properties with those found in the galaxy's disk. We propose the name NGC7896 for the cluster with the designation VVV-CL160. We estimate that the half mass radius and concentration parameter of this cluster are typical when compared to other galaxy bulge clusters but its core radius was found to be greater than average. We found no evidence of the presence of a black hole in this cluster. We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description than the velocity-based model. We attribute this to the imperfect compensation of diamagnetic and paramagnetic currents in the velocity-based model. To rectify this shortcoming, we formulated a sum rule that explicitly addresses the compensation issue, allowing the correction of velocity-based models to match dipole-based models and guarantee gauge invariance. We anticipate this correction to be particularly beneficial for modeling strong light-matter interactions. Furthermore, we observed that the dipole-based model introduces extra frequency-scale cutoffs, implicitly originating from the time-domain transformation of a dipole interaction term. We addressed this issue by translating the time-domain representation into a compact, ongoing interaction picture. This reformulation facilitates clear connections with both velocity-based and dipole interaction models, potentially enabling a more precise reconstruction of the dipole-based model's interaction picture. This study provides a comprehensive foundation for developing accurate TB models that capture light-matter interactions, paving the way for further research into strong light-matter interactions and novel phenomena. Nonetheless, describing strong light-matter interactions remains a complex task, and further investigations are needed to fully understand its implications. Ultimately, this study underscores the importance of strictly adhering to first-principle derivations when developing TB models, especially when modeling strong light-matter interactions. In the case of weak excitations, the choice of model depends on the specific material and phenomenon in question. However, the inherent limitations of these space missions only allow for rapid post-flare analysis. In contrast, ground-based spectroscopic analysis can reveal a flare's early phases, offering a more complete understanding of the event. We applied a novel approach to analyze the 1985 April 12 great flare of AD Leo, using a non-linear χ^2 minimization method to match the pre- and post-flare spectra, as well as the flare spectrum. Analyzing this through generalized parametric space, researchers discovered that when PT symmetry breaks, propagating modes appear consistently, unaffected by the unit cell's transmission phase or number. However, at PT-symmetric equilibrium, mode formation relies on the unit cell's transmission phase. Notably, reflectionless and perfectly transmissible states can be achieved by selecting specific PT phases and numbers of connected units. Two methods were identified to induce CPAL - operating an odd-numbered series of units at a specific point or using a particular broken phase in conjunction with an allotropic transmission phase in multiple units. Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. Additionally, our model exhibits implicit clustering properties, resulting in data representations that capture distinct semantic groups automatically. We make comprehensive implementations and analysis codes publicly available. With sparse representations, SparseGAN outperforms state-of-the-art transformer-based models on various automatic evaluation metrics, indicating a promising future for GANs in complex text understanding tasks. Our work also provides a contemporary solution to the implicit representation problem in GANs. To validate the semantic coherence of generated texts, we introduce an explicit coherence metric based on the quality of generated sentence embeddings, which can be highly effective in filtering high-quality models. This approach may be a responsive way to examine the internal workings of a neural network in a multi-task setting. We utilize this metric to identify optimal model parameters that produce text with both high semantic coherence and diversity. Moreover, we conduct a thorough analysis of embedded words to provide an intuitive understanding of the sparse representation mechanism and demonstrate that our model is capable of generating texts with both global and local semantic coherence. This is accomplished by (1) analyzing the distribution of selected embedding matrices, (2) studying the semantic group structure in the embedded word space, and (3) evaluating the implicit short sentence generation capability of our model. Notably, our work offers a contemporary solution to the implicit representation problem in GANs and paves the way for exploring multi-task learning using adversarial networks. We anticipate this work to contribute significantly to the development of advanced neural text generation models capable of understanding complex semantics. Our model has been successfully applied to generating single sentences, pairs of matching sentences, and entire paragraphs with optimal quality metrics such as BLEU, METEOR, and ROUGE. Moreover, our implementation has resulted in a state-of-the-art performance on various text generation datasets, including the 79M WikiText-2 dataset.

These predictions will allow us to constrain cosmological parameters using mildly non-linear scales from data that will be obtained from interferometric HI intensity mapping experiments. Assuming that the experiments will be like CHORD and PUMA, we run a series of analyses on mock data that accurately represents how these surveys are conducted at redshift z=0.5, comparing these to the performance that can be expected from stage 4 optical galaxy surveys. The impact of removing foregrounds using methods that rely on simulations is accounted for in the analysis, which shows how it affects the accuracy of the parameter estimation. The 10 parameters that we vary during the analysis consist of 3 cosmological and 7 non-cosmological parameters. The 4 most relevant parameters are the cold dark matter density, the Hubble constant, the primordial power spectrum amplitude and the linear HI bias. When assuming that foregrounds can be effectively removed, our best case scenario finds that the estimated parameters are accurate with less than a 3% error. When including the impact of foregrounds however, all parameters are estimated inaccurately by more than 5 times their confidence interval, indicating that removal of foregrounds plays a crucial role in the analysis. Scale cuts, specifically a minimum k-value of about 0.03 h/Mpc, need to be imposed in order to achieve accurate cosmological parameter estimation. The price for this accuracy, however, is a loss of precision, resulting in standard deviations that are more than double the desired level. Another approach to mitigate the impact of foregrounds, using a method that separates the removal of strong and weak foregrounds, yields more accurate estimates, with less than a 10% error for the 3 most relevant parameters. This approach, however, still falls short of the desired precision. We conclude that achieving accurate estimates of cosmological parameters from interferometric HI intensity mapping data will be more complicated than previously anticipated, mainly due to the removal of foregrounds. Further research is needed to fully explore possible approaches that can mitigate this effect. If this is possible, the HI intensity mapping technique could still be an interesting approach for Stage 4 of ground-based cosmological research. Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at the same time.  This method results in enhanced precision when estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters.  Notably, our study reveals that capture data alone yields biased estimates of density and encounter probabilities, while combined analysis corrects these biases.  On the other hand, when space usage and resource selection are the focus, telemetry data outperform combined analysis. Previous researchers developed methods for assessing football teams' defensive prowess by predicting the likelihood of gaining possession of the ball and being attacked, based on the location of all players involved. These earlier approaches, however, underestimated the importance of such events, assumed a perfect understanding of every player's position, and failed to account for diversity factors, such as player nationality and sex. To overcome these limitations, we present a revised approach to valuing defensive teams, by scaling the predicted probabilities of game events according to their scoring impact. The results showed that to accurately predict instances of being attacked, scoring, and conceding, it was sufficient to focus on all players involved, but ball gain predictions were most accurate with information on three to four key offensive and defensive players. Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already known to result from this property. We've established an additional consequence: almost sure asymptotic freeness of type $B$ for unitarily invariant random matrices. This consequence leads to several secondary findings: the asymptotic cyclic monotonicity, and the derivation of asymptotic conditional freeness. Specifically, we demonstrate the empirical spectral distribution of randomly rotated matrices converges towards a conditionally free convolution. We've also identified new relationships between infinitesimal freeness, type $B$ freeness, conditional freeness, cyclic monotonicity, and monotone independence. We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. The algorithm's primary components, such as its clock-based propagation technique, its distributed random walker system, and its hybrid estimation mechanism, may also be of independent interest. We prove the algorithm's efficacy even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta}). Our results provide a solution to a previously unstated problem in the 2018 STOC paper on robust clock synchronization and synchonization. Our algorithm's success is also a critical stepping stone for our subsequent work on developing a clock synchronization algorithm in the presence of uncertain conditions. In standard numerical relativity, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints are solved to obtain the metric components and the four-dimensional divergence of the momentum constraint source term. We introduce a new approach, known as the Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition, to solve the constraints directly, bypassing the typical conformal decomposition. This method involves separating the metric into transverse and traceless components, obtained from solving the Hamiltonian constraint in a defined potential form, and a spatial slice decomposition of the Weyl tensor. A key aspect of CTTK is that it uniquely solves the Hamiltonian constraint for a given potential, circumventing the need for an employer equation. We leverage this uniqueness to solve the momentum constraint through a simple algebraic approach. As a result, the four-dimensional divergence of the momentum constraint source term is automatically satisfied. We demonstrate the feasibility of this approach by applying CTTK to a simple numerical example involving two independently moving objects. Our findings show that using this method, we can successfully solve the constraints and recover the known solution. However, we also encounter issues with symmetry preservation, particularly with the decomposition of the Weyl tensor, and observe an unwanted rotation of spatial patterns in our test case. We explore potential fixes for this problem and outline strategies for implementing CTTK in more complex numerical relativity simulations. Our work provides a new framework for solving the constraints in numerical relativity and paves the way for further developments in this field. Additionally, we discuss how this approach can be combined with various fixings to improve symmetry preservation and control the decomposition of spatial objects. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between CTTK and standard conformal decomposition methods and identify potential connections and areas for further research. Our study also reveals the importance of choosing appropriate gauge conditions and constraint solving methods, depending on the specific features of the initial data. We, in effect, introduce a new set of conformally flat gauge conditions, tailored to accommodate the transverse traceless decomposition, and demonstrate their effectiveness in resolving issues with symmetry preservation. Our work lays the foundation for exploring a wide range of numerical relativity applications using CTTK and provides a valuable framework for studying the behavior of complex gravitational systems. We conclude by outlining an extensive research plan, detailing key problems and potential solutions, and highlighting the breakthroughs that solving these issues could bring in our understanding of gravitational physics. Our study offers a thorough examination of the CTTK method and provides a starting point for further development of this innovative approach to solving the constraints in numerical relativity.
