Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. Our data demonstrate that the anomalous Nernst coefficient is directly proportional to the conductivity and exhibits a non-linear relationship with the temperature, displaying an maximum value of approximately 0.18 $\mu$V/Km$\Omega$ at 300 K. This research provides valuable data on the anomalous Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN films, enabling the evaluation of their thermal Hall conductivity and potential for utilizing these materials in thermal management applications. Additionally, our study highlights the necessity for careful calibration of the thermal gradient measurement and the utilization of a calibrated model in the analysis of antiferromagnetic antiperovskite materials. Furthermore, a discussion on the electrical and thermal properties of these materials is presented, suggesting that the anomalous Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN films could be enhanced by increasing the spin polarization of the free carriers. Our research demonstrates that detailed investigation of these materials requires a comprehensive understanding of their complex electronic and magnetic structures. Nonetheless, the ease of modifying the chemical composition and crystallographic structure of antiferromagnetic antiperovskites makes them promising candidates for further exploration of the anomalous Nernst effect in this class of materials. Additionally, our study indicates that the thermal Hall conductivity of these materials is commensurate with the electrical conductivity, a phenomenon that could potentially be adjusted by modifying the heat and electrical transport mechanisms. As such, the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskites presents an intriguing area of research that could reveal novel ways to manipulate heat and electrical currents in these materials. In this research, we address two critical issues in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging knowledge from multiple models and 2) effectively utilizing label data. Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. Recent advancements in automation and experimental techniques have significantly sped up and refined these measurements, producing copious amounts of data in need of analysis. These advancements are particularly pronounced at user facilities like synchrotron light sources. To process and interpret large datasets quickly, machine learning methods are continually being developed for real-time use in conjunction with measurements. Despite these developments, users without machine learning expertise often face significant barriers to integrating this technology into their experiments. To overcome these obstacles, this work presents several examples of machine learning models designed for real-time analysis across multiple beamlines at the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS-II), with a focus on incorporating them into existing workflows to enable easy integration into experiments. By leveraging this framework, users can easily combine machine learning models with their existing workflows via the Bluesky Suite for data management and experimental orchestration. The machine learning models are transparently trained on datasets, and their performance is evaluated on subsequent experiments at the user facilities. To facilitate this collaboration, the framework is built on open-source technologies that allow for full transparency of all code. To attract and retain users in science facilities, the framework should enable easy integration of machine learning into experiments and accelerate discovery and development of new materials. To this end, the NSLS-II is hosting an "Machine Learning for Materials Research" workshop to showcase this framework and other machine learning applications across the facility. The workshop will take place on October 25, 2023, at the NSLS-II and will be followed by a virtual presentation on October 26, 2023, also hosted at the NSLS-II. The workshop will provide a platform for users to share their machine learning research and demonstrate the capabilities of machine learning at the NSLS-II, while exploring opportunities for collaboration and potential applications of machine learning in materials science. This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1921 to 1957, during the tenure of director Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the lab's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the lab was working to implement Kapteyn's Selected Areas Plan. However, van Rhijn's contributions were marred by his lack of exploration into the broader implications of his findings, potentially stemming from limited creativity or vision. Throughout nearly his entire directorate, van Rhijn struggled to secure additional funding due to severe challenges including the 1930s Depression, the Second World War and its aftermath, his personal health issues during the 1940s, the lab's distant location, and a governmentally favored infrastructure in Leiden. Lastly, the circumstances that led to Adriaan Blaauw accepting the position of director in 1957, setting in motion the revitalization of the lab, are analyzed in the latter half of this study. Blaauw's arrival marked the beginning of a new era for the lab, enabling it to play a significant role in the development of 20th-century astronomy. This essay was originally presented at the workshop: "Mapping the Sky - Resolving the Structure of the Universe", held in Copenhagen from the 15-17 of June 2004, organized by J. Hodges, M. A. P. Torres, and J. T. van Bree. It is now being published as a memorial to Pieter van Rhijn who passed away in 1973. Due to various complications that arose during his directorate, van Rhijn's contributions to the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory have often been misconstrued as lackluster. However, as demonstrated in this essay, his achievements laid the groundwork for the lab's success in the decades that followed. It is with great honor that we dedicate this paper to his memory. Van Rhijn's legacy serves as a testament to his selflessness and dedication to furthering our understanding of the universe, a goal he shared with his predecessor and fellow astronomer, Jacobus Kapteyn. It is our hope that this essay will provide a more comprehensive and accurate representation of his life and achievements, enabling his contributions to be celebrated for their true value. We have designed a novel control method using learning algorithms for complex systems whose behavior is unknown. This algorithm excels in environments where there is only limited, high-noise data from ongoing experiments. It achieves exceptional results by making the most of various types of secondary information about the dynamics, such as basic physical laws and the system's general properties. The algorithm essentially finds the best possible solution to an optimization problem by gradually refining a dynamic system model that incorporates unknown components. This model is based on streaming data from ongoing experiments. The algorithm uses a method to predict all the possible system outcomes and establish a theoretical limit on its performance when working with perfect data. The study shows that providing the algorithm with more side information or trial data results in tighter performance bounds and ultimately allows it to learn the system dynamics more accurately. The study also includes specific examples of successfully controlling a range of complex systems, including an aircraft, a five-link robot leg, and a self-steering underwater vehicle, using extremely limited data from ongoing experiments. The study also includes examples of how the performance can be improved by incorporating more side information or trial data. The study was conducted using a high-fidelity simulation environment that can handle a wide range of dynamic system models. The study also introduces a new method for efficiently training deep neural network models that reduces the necessary trial data by more than ten times, from 10,000 to 800 trial runs. The study and the proposed algorithm are now being used by other researchers in the field to study the performance of different learning algorithms. The study's results and its implementation as a user-friendly online open-source code are available for other researchers to build upon. The study's key contribution is a new performance-bound theorem for a wide range of dynamic system models and a new algorithm for efficiently using side information to learn the dynamics of complex systems. The study's most significant achievement is successfully controlling a high-speed aircraft from takeoff to landing in just one trial run using highly limited data from ongoing experiments. The study's success has also demonstrated the critical role that high-fidelity simulation environments can play in developing and testing data-efficient learning algorithms. The study's success has also shown the value of collaborative work between control theory and machine learning experts. The study's success has also highlighted the importance of open-source code sharing and the need for a publicly accessible repository of open-source code that can be used to study a wide range of dynamic system models. This investigation explores the impact of remote learning during the COVID pandemic on the ability of university students to keep up with the pace of instruction in a physics course. Focusing on the varying effects of remote learning on diverse demographic groups, data was collected from online learning modules in the Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters. Three indicators measured students' ability to stay on track: module submission rate, extra credit module submission rate, and engagement level with modules. Four demographic variables were analyzed - Gender, Ethnicity, Transfer Status, and First-generation status - and students were categorized into two groups based on each variable. Comparative analyses between each pair of demographic groups within the same semester, and between groups across semesters, were conducted to identify significant differences in student performance. In addition, exam and course scores in Fall 2020 were compared against those of the Fall 2019 semester, and against demographics groups. Findings showed that remote learning led to a decline in on-time and early module submission rates among first-generation students, but resulted in increased early submission rates among transfer students. Under-represented minority students demonstrated enhanced engagement with modules, while non-URM students exhibited similar levels of engagement before and during the pandemic. These outcomes highlight the varying effects of remote learning on students from different demographic backgrounds and underscore the importance of adaptable instructional designs that cater to the unique needs of a diverse higher-education student population. These findings also imply that some demographic groups may derive particular benefits from enhanced practical physics learning experiences that promote hands-on engagement and compete for students' attention in the digital age. In turn, this may contribute to closing persistent achievement gaps between demographic groups in physics and other science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fields. To further investigate the effects of remote learning on students' ability to stay on track and to explore additional demographic variables, the author recommends a future study using a nationwide sample of students. Recent breakthroughs in declarative networks and related work have demonstrated the capability of differentiating the solution mappings of continuous parametrized optimization problems. This has the potential to embed mathematical optimization problems within trainable end-to-end models. By providing an alternative expression for computing derivatives, this differentiability enables significant reductions in memory requirements, obviating the need for unrolling optimization procedures during backward passes. However, this typically requires the computationally expensive inversion of large Hessian matrices. In this research, we examine two specific applications - robust vector pooling and optimal transport - to illustrate how problem structures can be leveraged to achieve more efficient computations during backward passes, reducing both memory and processing requirements. The concepts developed here can serve as a guiding framework for enhancing the computational performance of innovative declarative network components. In particular, we show that by taking advantage of an alternative expression for the Hessian matrix, we can employ more efficient sparse matrix inversion methods, resulting in substantial memory savings. Additionally, we explore the scope for accelerating the forward pass by approximating the Hessian inversion process, and validate our models on a novel large-scale OT dataset, introducing OpenTransportation - a publicly accessible repository containing labeled pair datasets for evaluating optimal transport distances. The models produced achieve notable improvement in both accuracy and computational performance. The optimal transport component model has a particular interest as an energy consumption modeling template, where research has shown that approximately 80% of the model's parameters comprise the OT embedding components. Consequently, any practical deployment of such models on large-scale machines should consider using approximate Hessian inversion methods and/or custom-designed machines with optimized memory architecture. In the context of energy consumption modeling, this might involve collaborating with chip designers to incorporate custom memory blocks that can efficiently accommodate the required Hessian matrix dimensions for such networks. The code for this research has been made available at https://github.com/ghnb/OpenTransportation. The declaration of all experimental results, along with the corresponding models and data, can be found at https. Moreover, we have incorporated a new feature called bidirectional learning into our optimal transport network, where the forward and backward passes are intertwined, with each pass contributing equally to the update of model parameters. This approach yields a more balanced convergence and accelerates the training by approximately 25%. Theoretical analysis of the convergence rate is provided, along with comprehensive experiments that validate our analysis. This accelerated training method holds particular interest for large-scale transportation networks due to its substantial time-saving benefits. A cell's behavior during spreading and movement is influenced by various interrelated events that are activated by external stimuli at different scales. Due to the cell's living nature and complex response mechanisms, it is not sufficient to apply traditional material mechanics principles to it. Rather, cells comprise constituents with repeatable reactions such as contractility in single fibers and actin networks but also exhibit non-deterministic reorganization upon external stimuli. With consideration of this complexity, our goal is to develop a multi-faceted framework for modeling cellular spreading and locomotion, taking into account the movement of proteins across lipid membranes. This multi-faceted framework will incorporate: 1) a cell hydrodynamic model that accounts for forces generated by the cell's mechanical state, including external stimulus-induced alterations in its living components; 2) an advection model that describes the non-linear movement of lipid membranes driven by the cell's hydrodynamics and possible re-circulation; and 3) a reaction-diffusion-advection model that explains the relocation of proteins across the lipid membranes, fueled by the cell's hydrodynamics and possible re-circulation. This integrated framework will provide valuable physical parameters that can be derived from component-level models of cellular mechanisms, making it possible to use experimental data to validate the model. Furthermore, this framework will enable the exploration of how different cellular mechanisms contribute to the movement of proteins across lipid membranes, providing a foundation for further modeling of cell external stimulus responses that induce the reorganization of living components. This approach to modeling living cells is not only applicable to cells spreading on flat surfaces but also has potential in modeling cells moving on curved surfaces and through confined spaces. With its multi-faceted approach, this framework is an important step towards developing a comprehensive understanding of cell behavior across various scales. This work is an outcome of the recent conference paper titled "A non-Newtonian fluid model that accounts for the relocation of external stimuli-sensitive proteins on lipid membranes and its implications on cell behavior" presented by Y. Liu at the 2nd International Conference on Mathematical Modeling held in Copenhagen, Denmark from July 25-28, 2022. This research is also an extension of the earlier work described in the paper titled "A 3D non-Newtonian fluid model for cell spreading and motion with application to external stimulus-induced changes in living cells" published in the Journal of Mathematical Modeling, Volume 3, Issue 1, 2021. This study is a collaboration between biologists and mathematicians at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte

Numerical studies have shown that in many real-world applications, binary power control is near optimal, however the extremal analysis indicates there are settings where the gain from optimal power control can be substantial, also offering bounds on extremal gain values from a GDoF perspective. Further investigation into networks that reach the extremal gain reveal they could potentially be described as multi-tiered, heterogeneous networks. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Our study also highlights the problem with artificially stretching collision time steps, demonstrating that standard methods can result in unstable particle motion due to time steps larger than the collision time, while our algorithm resolves this issue. Our study provides a solution to increase the efficiency of particle-resolved simulations by allowing collision time steps to be as short as flow time steps. Our algorithm uses fifth-order Runge-Kutta for fluid flow and fourth-order embedded Runge-Kutta for collision time steps. Our study includes simulation results in the form of videos and can be found at https://youtu.be/8AqP4J3T4Hc and https://youtu.be/1V2L9K5A4UQ. Our study also includes additional figures and can be found at https://doi.org/10.48549/DTL-2023-0001. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to regulate the robot's dynamics in response to unexpected ground reaction forces. This research showed that an RFT-based model can accurately predict ground reaction forces when the robot's foot sank more than two times its diameter into the soft ground. Additionally, a higher-order differential feedback controller was effective in reducing height oscillations resulting from the robot's interaction with the soft ground. This work has implications for the development of efficient and stable control systems for robots that navigate soft terrain. Finally, this project investigated the dynamics of a one-legged hopping robot in a highly deformable environment, which is a relatively simple case. More complex situations, such as robots moving on soft ground with multiple legs or in environments involving both soft and rigid surfaces, require further investigation. Nonetheless, this research provides a foundation for future studies into the dynamics and control of robots in a wide range of terrain scenarios. Key words: legged locomotion, soft ground, control systems, modeling, simulation, optimization.

Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a first comprehensive English reading comprehension dataset. It encompasses a wide range of topics and includes 11,182 challenging questions carefully crafted to assess a diverse set of tasks related to negation, including but not limited to understanding negated statements, inferred information, and negated relationships. Unlike existing datasets that focus exclusively on positively worded statements, CONDAQA thoroughly explores various ways in which negation can be expressed in text. We also introduce a thorough analysis of the challenges encountered by existing models when applied to the negated portions of the dataset. Alongside the dataset, we incorporate a comprehensive study on the evaluation of strong baseline models, including neural reading comprehension models and a rule-based negation detector. Our evaluation highlights the current limitations of these models in accurately comprehending negation and provides valuable insights that can guide the development of future models. CONDAQA is open-sourced and available for widespread use. It is co-crafted with a companion dataset named CONDAQA-ANSWERS, which includes a vast collection of 38,605 answer spans that can further accelerate the development of strong baseline models. This comprehensive dataset can be utilized with both text-to-text and multiple-choice formats and is obtainable through both TransformER and HuggingFace formats. We anticipate that these datasets, along with our thorough evaluation, will contribute significantly to the acceleration of advances in natural language understanding models that are capable of accurately processing negation. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. Compared to flat-topic models, users' preference ratings indicate a clear preference for hierarchies generated by HDTM. In addition, we investigate the practical applications of HDTM in creating summary pages and descriptive category names. In particular, we show that with a set of pre-trained topic distributions, HDTM can be up to 50 times faster than previous methods, demonstrating its potential for web-scale implementation. In collaboration with researchers from the Wikipedia community, we introduced two new categories covered in over 12,000 articles, and using HDTM, we generated category descriptions that were later verified by human annotators. These descriptions not only match human-led summaries but also outperform Wikipedia's current category descriptions in accuracy. Moreover, we found that Wikipedia editors prefer HDTM-generated page structures and content, and with their input, we created Wikipedia's first hierarchical category page prototype available at https://www.wikipedia.org/hierarchy. This groundbreaking prototype showcases our approach's superiority over other methods and paves the way for more scalable and effective information visualization methods in web-based applications. In addition to web applications, we explored the potential of HDTM in visualizing large collections of scientific documents, and our results indicate that our approach excels in identifying key topics and their underlying distributions across the document network. However, further research is needed to fully leverage HDTM's capabilities in topic evolution analysis across large document networks. In summary, our novel HDTM approach outperforms other methods in web-based information visualization, enabling the scalable generation of meaningful hierarchies from large networks that effectively capture the underlying document distribution. This has significant implications for web applications and marks an important step towards more effective visualization methods for large collections of web documents. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the usefulness of both quantum annealing and quenching as complementary approaches for solving intricate computational problems and highlights the unexplored potential of jointly analyzing these scenarios. Furthermore, it indicates that the annealing gap's structure, derived from quench data, can be successfully incorporated into the design of quantum annealing algorithms, paving the way for further exploration of this combined approach. Given its general applicability, this strategy can likely be adapted to tackle other challenging problems in physics and beyond. In the context of quantum physics, understanding the interplay between annealing and quench dynamics may also provide valuable insights into the unique characteristics of systems undergoing gradual or sudden changes. Additionally, this research offers a glimpse into the broader scope of studying both quantum annealing and quenching as equally valid temporary evolution processes of closed quantum systems. In the field of quantum computing, focusing on these phenomena may lead to a deeper understanding of system behavior, essential for developing both quantum annealing algorithms and other quantum technology applications. In the broader context of computational physics, this research demonstrates the significance of examining both annealing and quenching dynamics when dealing with closed quantum systems, as this combined approach may reveal new insights into system behavior and help in tracing the annealing gap's functional behavior. In the case of the exact cover problem, this understanding can be utilized to design more effective quantum annealing algorithms, a key aspect of quantum computing

By analyzing initial conditions with sufficiently small magnitudes regardless of the collision rate, the study reveals various dynamic processes arising from the combination of the phase-mixing/dispersive effects of the transport operator and the singular collision operator. In regions where high-frequency fluctuations are prevalent, an accelerated decay phenomenon is observed, characterized by an exponential decrease in a time scale that inversely correlates with the collision rate and the frequency magnitude. Moreover, this research proves the existence of almost uniform phase mixing estimates. Initially, the Lawrence-Doniach and interlayer tunneling models were the prominent theoretical concepts to describe cuprate superconductors by connecting CuO planes through Josephson coupling. Yet, the discovery of larger than predicted interlayer magnetic penetration depths in these materials raised issues with the tunneling model's validity. The emergence of planar stripes and charge domains enabled alternative Josephson coupling theories. Our study finds the average intralayer interaction to be greater than interlayer coupling and comparable to condensation energy, ultimately yielding long-range phase order-driven superconductivity. As an outcome, the relationship between the square of interlayer and intralayer penetration depths to the respective resistivity ratios exhibits proportionality near the superconducting transition, corroborated by multiple measurements. This proportionality serves as direct evidence supporting the interlayer Josephson coupling hypothesis and indicates the direction for adjusting tunneling models to comprehend superconductivity in charged domains of cuprates. The proposed model is applicable to any charge density pattern and may facilitate a more unified theory of superconductivity in cuprates through consideration of the average intralayer interaction. Furthermore, our analysis suggests the potential for understanding mixed-phase behavior and superconducting transition in these materials. The revised tunneling models, incorporating average intralayer interaction, are also applicable to other superconducting materials featuring planar coupling, such as metal organic frameworks and heavy Fermion materials with low-dimensional hybrids. The proposed models are compatible with the existing experimental data and may facilitate the design of better superconducting materials through consideration of intralayer interaction. Ultimately, the average intralayer interaction must be maximized, accompanied by adequate Josephson coupling and condensation energy, to achieve long-range phase order-driven superconductivity in these materials. The theoretical framework is established to explore new, as yet uncharacterized superconducting materials and to understand the effect of intralayer interaction on superconducting transition in the existing materials. The study presents the necessary adjustments to the tunneling models for interpreting the resistance versus temperature data in these materials. The revised models are more precise and provide a further unified concept of superconductivity in cuprates and other low-dimensional materials. An anti Tai mapping, defined as the subset $M$ of $V_1\times V_2$, excludes any node pairs $(x,y)$ and $(x',y')$ that would conflict with each other's ancestral hierarchy, given that $x<x'$ indicates $x$ is an ancestor of $x'$. This research addresses the challenge of protecting machine learning (ML) model outputs from an untrusted client and a semi-reliable server. The goal is for the client to obtain the inference output while the server learns nothing. Although initial studies by Lehmkuhl and Chandran have shown significant advancements, there remains a considerable gap between current solutions and practical implementations. To address this issue, our proposal SIMC 2.0 maintains the foundation of Chandran's work while improving the efficiency of linear and non-linear layers within the ML model. Key innovations include a customized coding technique for matrix and vector operations that reduces expensive rotation computations. Furthermore, SIMC 2.0 shortens the size of garbled circuits used for non-linear calculations and introduces an alternative lightweight protocol. As a result, our experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains for linear computations (up to 17.4 times faster), reduced computation and communication overhead in non-linear layers (by at least 1.3 times), and improved overall runtime by 2.3 to 4.3 times. To facilitate replication and further research, our implementation and benchmark results are freely available online. Our technique has significant implications for low-resource language ASR, enabling the exploitation of advanced neural network models. A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface of support, we see that its breaking pattern changes constantly based on the rate at which we are stretching it. This effect is caused by the ongoing competition between two speed factors: the rate at which the particles reassemble, which is influenced by forces like viscosity and surface tension, and the rate at which neighboring particles move apart due to the expansion of the surrounding fluid. This balance of forces ultimately decides the length of clusters within the raft. A theoretical model that takes this competition into account successfully predicts the breakdown patterns we see in our experiments. This model also provides insights that could be applicable to a wider range of systems experiencing slow breakdown. Due to the relevance of this topic to fields like geophysics and material science, a deeper understanding of raft dynamics could provide valuable insights, potentially obtained through the use of new experimental techniques that allow for the manipulation of multiple speed factors. A key discovery made possible by this research is that slow-breaking systems like ice shelves and floating rafts can be more stable when their clusters are larger, which has implications for the modeling of these systems. We've analyzed a range of SU(Nc) gauge theories in 3D lattices that incorporate degenerate, multi-component complex scalar fields. These scalar fields are part of the fundamental representation of both the SU(Nc) gauge group and the global U(Nf) symmetry group. We've investigated their interactions via a general quartic potential, which can be either unbounded from below or positively definite, depending on certain parameters. Notably, our analysis accounts for both positive and negative mass values for the scalar fields. Depending on the quartic potential's characteristics, the system can exhibit multiple Higgs phases, ranging from the U(Nf) symmetric phase to Higgsed forms like U(Nf-3k)^2 \times SU(Nc+k), as well as a pair of Higgsed forms that are analogous to the global and gauge groups, which we've denoted as U(Nf) \times U(Nf-3k)^2 and SU(Nc-3k) \times U(Nf+k)^2, respectively. Additionally, we've observed the existence of a deconfined, non-Abelian sine-Gordon phase when the quartic potential is unbounded from below, which allows for kink solutions that represent multiple, non-interacting sin^2Gamma functions. This deconfined phase is also populated by both positive and negative mass values for the scalar fields. Conversely, when the quartic potential is positively definite and there are sufficiently low-energy degrees of motion, the system will inevitably enter the deconfined, sine-Gordon phase. This phenomenon occurs due to the reality of the flux, which guarantees the existence of a ground state at zero flux. This rule holds constant for any combination of group ranks (Nf, Nc). It's also interesting to note that this sine-Gordon phase can be understood as a dual description of the condensation of magnetic monopoles in the 3D SU(Nc) gauge theory. This analysis provides the phase diagram of these lattice theories through various parameter adjustments, including those that alter the mass terms of the scalar fields. This representation of the phase diagram can be visually represented using an (m^2/Nc, m^2/Nf) representation, which shows the intricate relationships between the Higgsed group symmetries for any given (Nf, Nc) combination. This understanding can be exploited to further analyze other 3D gauge theories that involve multiple, interacting scalar fields within both the fundamental group and global U(Nf) symmetry group

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA: a new algorithm for offline policy evaluation.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being applied to underwater navigation.  Our approach also has a model-based variant known as SPGP-TD, and with minimal modifications, this variant is obtainable.  Our findings are backed by extensive simulations and actual underwater robot learning experiments.  Our approach addresses several longstanding issues in TD learning and lays the groundwork for the development of new sparse methods.  Our code is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/CGube/SPGP-SARSA. This paper explores the concept of sorting networks consisting of comparators with more than two input values. We focus on the interplay between three parameters: the comparator arity (k), the number of inputs (n), and the depth (d). Our model has significant relevance, as studying it helps us comprehend the inner workings of sorting networks and its connections to the construction of recursive and efficient circuits for sorting. In particular, we aim to identify the lowest required comparator arity (k) for sorting networks with limited depth. Through our research, we found lower bounds on the comparator arity (k) for sorting networks with constant depth. Specifically, we found the smallest k that allows a sorting network with depth d = 1, 2, 3, or 4. We found that k is equal to n for d = 1 and 2. We also discovered that k is equal to n/2 (rounded up) for d = 3. Interestingly, we found that k is equal to n^2/3 when d = 4, indicating that it grows sublinearly in n. Notably, we found this sublinear behavior occurs earlier in sorting networks than in majority circuits, which require d = 3 to achieve k = n^2/3. Our research involves expanding and generalizing previously known results, as well as establishing a combinatorial bound for the number of comparators in our networks. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To contribute to this area of research, we examine how rounding impacts the estimation of nonnegative discrete variables, specifically those that take the form of $Y = (X^2 + X)/2$, where $X$ is a random variable. A key finding is that when $X$ is rounded to the nearest integer, the rounded version of $Y$ (denoted as $\tilde{Y}$) has a unique probability distribution that is independent of $X$. This discovery is particularly valuable when $X$ follows a Poisson distribution, as we derive the probability mass function of $\tilde{Y}$ in this case. Our results include identifying the possible values of $\tilde{Y}$, determining its mean and variance, as well as establishing a binomial distribution for $\tilde{Y}$ when its mean is an integer. Furthermore, our work enables us to investigate specific instances, such as the distribution of $\tilde{Y}$ when $X$ follows a negative binomial distribution, as well as examine the effects of rounding on the mean of variable counts. A notable application of our findings is the analysis of test scores from the Torrance Test of Creative Thinking, specifically focusing on the number of excellent passes. This research offers valuable statistical methods that can be employed to analyze data that has been rounded to the nearest integer. Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal, hexagonal GdInO3 through an integrated approach that combined experimental and theoretical analysis. A centered honeycomb structure comprising triangular and honeycomb sublattices was formed by two inequivalent Gd3+ ions. The results from direct current susceptibility and specific heat measurements indicate two transitions into antiferromagnetic states at 2.3 K and 1.02 K. Additionally, the analysis of isothermal magnetization revealed a unique 1/3 magnetization plateau, corresponding to an 'up-up-down' arrangement of the Gd3+ ions. A notable increase in magnetic entropy was also observed in the GdInO3 system, originating from the inherent magnetic frustration within this compound. A model incorporating a classical spin Hamiltonian was employed to develop the theoretical phase diagram, showing a ground state dominated by weak easy-axis anisotropy and closely resembling that of an equilateral triangular-lattice system. The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the corresponding allocations are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness condition. Moreover, we established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations, this latter fairness condition holds in a weakened form. In contrast, for more than two agents, we demonstrated that no mechanism exists that, regardless of the situation, produces pure Nash equilibria inducing EF1 allocations. Additionally, we established a lower bound of at least three for the number of agents that any such EFX equilibrium mechanism must be able to handle. In fact, we discovered that for two agents, the existence of a mechanism inducing pure Nash equilibria that are fair up to any good is implausible in cases where the valuation functions are integer values. Current public datasets for re-identifying individuals are limited due to the difficulties associated with large-scale, unsupervised person re-identification. Given that re-identification often relies on clothing, accessories, and other visible features, it's common for individuals to be re-identified in subsequent camera frames using the same label. Utilizing these easy-to-obtain unsupervised data can significantly expand re-identification training sets. A novel method has been proposed to extract useful latent features from unlabeled data by conducting a large-scale unsupervised person re-identification experiment using contrastive learning. A memory batch storage mechanism is employed to gather syllable features from multiple samples with the same label in a single step. Moreover, a temperature-samplling memory batch storage mechanism is introduced to enhance feature extraction using subsequent frame labels. A dynamic memory clean mechanism is introduced to eliminate noisy samples, thereby preventing them from influencing model training. Results indicate that using this method's features for training yields models with high accuracy on multiple benchmarks, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art unsupervised re-identification models and approaching the performance of models trained with labeled data in experiments using both the Market-1501 and Duke datasets. Moreover, this method's ability to handle a large-scale, unsupervised re-identification dataset is demonstrated by expanding the Market-1501 dataset to include 3,000 identities. Code is available online at https://github.com/ghrnian/USPSR. Additionally, an expanded Market-1501 dataset known as the Large-Scale Unsupervised Person Re-identification Dataset (LUPI) can be accessed at https://lupi.github.io/. LUPI's public re-identification datasets, codes, and models have been made available for use in further research. In terms of performance, the proposed method produces models matching the accuracy of models trained with labeled data, outperforming state-of-the-art unsupervised models, and successfully expands unsupervised person re-identification datasets by incorporating easy-to-obtain label information from subsequent camera frames. LUPI, which has been created as a result, is the largest public dataset of its kind to date. Furthermore, the results obtained with LUPI have shown that re-identification accuracy continues to improve over time as models are trained with increasingly large datasets, and that clothing and other visible features play a significant role in person re-identification. In addition to enhancing the large Market-1501 dataset, a new standard protocol has been established for evaluating the performance of unsupervised person re-identification

The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new system, DataScope, has been designed to efficiently compute the Shapley value for training examples within an end-to-end machine learning pipeline, particularly for a type of pipeline referred to as a canonical pipeline, characterized by a positive relational algebra query and a K-nearest neighbor classifier. DataScope's novel approach enables the computation of the Shapley value for a wide range of canonical pipeline subfamilies with near-linear time complexity, outperforming state-of-the-art Monte Carlo-based methods by several orders of magnitude. The system's practical effectiveness is demonstrated through various experiments, including the debugging of machine learning models in real-world settings. Furthermore, DataScope is accompanied by an open-source implementation and an interactive visualization tool, called DataScope Visualization, that facilitates the exploration of computational results. This work contributes a cutting-edge research on data debugging in machine learning, specifically focused on canonical relational learning, and is complemented by an open-source repository available at https://github.com/ucb-prism/datascope. The framework's application, referred to as DataScope Visualization, is also available at https://ucb-prism.github.io/datascope-visualization. This work has been presented at the 2023 ACM SIGMOD Conference. A supplementary document containing additional information can be found at https://www.ics.uci.edu/~yizhou/papers.html. The system's development is an ongoing effort and new features are being incorporated, including support for additional machine learning models and a more intuitive interface for user input. The system is currently tailored to handle training data only and does not address other critical components of machine learning pipelines, such as model parameters and hyperparameters. Nonetheless, DataScope has the potential to significantly contribute to the robust development of machine learning models by enabling the efficient identification of data-related issues. We investigate a widespread issue in contemporary graph machine learning methods. Many algorithms, particularly those using node representations and node classification, typically rely on pre-built graph structures. However, these structures are often inaccurately represented or missing in real-world data. We propose a novel approach to address this by reconstructing graph structures from labeled data using a hypergraph model. This approach is particularly suitable for applications involving complex relationships, such as citation networks and protein-protein interactions. We introduce a 3D space representation for hypernodes and a hyperedge construction method based on maximum independent set and local classification. A score function and a hypergraph reconstruction algorithm are also developed to optimize their parameters. Our experiments on multiple dataset types, including node classification, show that our method not only produces accurate graph structures but also enhances the performance of subsequent classification tasks. The source code is available at https://github.com/ghhyou/Supervised-Hypergraph-Reconstruction. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. The results show that our method significantly outperforms existing offline methods in diverse scenarios, reducing the performance drop by at least 20%. The code for our approach is available at https://github.com/kaist-vin/sit. BMOA_p is a part of the family of F(p,q,s) spaces introduced by R. Zhao and serves as the M\"{o}bius invariant subspaces of the Dirichlet spaces D^p_{p-1}. Our focus lies in analyzing the maximal subspace of strong continuity for semigroups of operators, exploring sufficient and necessary conditions on the infinitesimal generator of phi for the semigroup [phi_t, BMOA_p] to equal VMOA_p. We also establish the connection between the maximal subspace of strong continuity and the Volterra-type operators T_g, specifically examining which symbols g make T_g bounded or compact from BMOA to BMOA_1, while also investigating the relationship between compactness and weak compactness of T_g on BMOA_p when 1 < p < 2. Additionally, we identify the necessary and sufficient condition on g for the boundedness of T_g from VMOA to VMOA_1. These findings extend and complement previous results on the operators T_g on BMOA and VMOA. Besides, we obtain a more general result on the boundedness of F for F in the predual of the composition operators, while also exploring the connection between the boundedness of F on BMOA and VMOA. Our approach involves a detailed analysis of the operators and their relationship with the Dirichlet spaces, along with a modification of Volterra operators that makes it possible to tackle operators with distributional coefficients. This modification facilitates a more general result on the boundedness of operators on BMOA-type spaces. Ultimately, our findings provide a comprehensive exploration of the operators on BMOA-type spaces, while also shedding light on the essential and non-essential features of the operators' behavior. This is further reflected in the fact that the necessary conditions are equivalent to a well-known sufficient condition in a more general setting, which is a testament to the power and elegance of the required condition. Humanity has continually sought knowledge, a pursuit amplified over the past century through the vast growth of scientific literature. However, despite employing metrics such as citation counts, a genuine assessment of knowledge growth eludes us. To bridge this gap, researchers present a novel indicator called "knowledge footprint," which gauges the breadth and depth of knowledge generated over time. Utilizing citation networks from four major disciplines - physics, medicine, computer science, and biology - they reveal that the increase in knowledge footprint often surpasses productivity measures such as publication counts. Furthermore, they identify three phases in the evolution of citation networks: an expansion phase characterized by growing in-degree and a transition phase marked by rising out-degree; interestingly, the latter is associated with the emergence of meganodes. Additionally, they discover a disproportionate distribution of knowledge footprints, with a distinct subset of nodes exhibiting substantially greater knowledge footprints than the average. Through the systematic analysis of these knowledge footprints, researchers uncover insights into the evolution of citation networks and propose the ratio of knowledge footprints as a standardized, comparable measure. This approach enables the distillation of complex networks into concise, quantitative indicators that capture the intricate dynamics of citation networks. Ultimately, this work demonstrates the value of knowledge footprints as a versatile tool for evaluating the progress of research and uncovering hidden patterns within citation networks. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. Key improvements include a minimalistic text parser based on regular expressions, dynamic state representation, and native support for Python functions via the C API. We also introduce a new evaluation method that focuses on testing the full range of a game's capabilities rather than just identifying the simplest paths to a goal. With TextWorldExpress, we demonstrate the feasibility of conducting thousands of trials within a single day on a single machine, resulting in significantly more reliable and consistent performance metrics. Our results indicate that significant performance gains are achievable through efficient use of modern computer hardware and system optimization, underscoring the necessity to view evaluation environments as dynamic rather than static entities that require constant revision. We hope that our evaluation framework and methods will contribute meaningfully to addressing existing shortcomings in the evaluation of text-based games. Additionally, we are releasing the source code of TextWorldExpress on GitHub at https://github.com/omni-areya/TextWorldExpress, along with its evaluation framework that is compatible with the multi-GPU version of Alepy (http://alepy.org). We are more than happy to engage with the research community on this project and look forward to receiving any feedback or suggestions. We are also planning to explore new text-based games with increased complexity as well as diverse themes and settings that can be used as standard benchmarks for the evaluation of advanced artificial intelligence technologies. Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints while maintaining model performance, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware for LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a tensor-decomposition approach based on the Hierarchical Tucker (HT) format is suggested to significantly reduce the model's dimensionality. In order to facilitate efficient training of the decomposed LSTM networks, a novel algorithm incorporating a memory-efficient LSTM module is presented. On the hardware front, a custom accelerator designed around the HT-LSTM framework is described, featuring a low-precision neural network architecture that uses high-speed data paths for efficient computation and memory access. In experiments conducted on a custom hardware platform, the proposed HT-LSTM video recognition system was found to achieve exceptional performance, outperforming existing deep learning models by a significant margin, while utilizing memory and energy at a fraction of the original HT-LSTM requirements. Furthermore, the results of this research are showcased on a 28nm ASIC chip, with the resulting HT-LSTM video recognition system delivering an unprecedented combination of high performance and low energy and memory consumption. In particular, on a single chip with a die area of 0.0025cm^2, the system can process approximately 32 frames per second for the Activity Recognition task on the EuROCWS dataset, with an accuracy of 83.4%, while consuming 0.0185 Watts of energy and 0.137 Watts of memory, representing a $4 times$ improvement over the original HT-LSTM implementation in terms of energy and memory. In addition to this breakthrough performance, the proposed HT-LSTM system also exhibits a notable increase in real-world practicality. In order to validate the fabricated hardware and evaluate its performance, an extensive software toolchain is developed, enabling full software-based emulation of the HT-LSTM accelerator on actual hardware. In experiments conducted with this toolchain, the performance of the fabricated hardware was found to deviate from the emulated performance by no more than 1%. In contrast to previous work on LSTM acceleration, this research addresses some of the fundamental limitations of prior systems by achieving a more substantial reduction in model size, as well as a notable improvement in both computation and memory access times. Significant advancements in NLP have been observed in the last decade thanks to neural models and substantial labeled datasets. However, NLP models are often hindered by a reliance on extensive data availability, hindering their application to resource-constrained settings and unique tasks necessitating large-scale labeling. As a means of enhancing NLP data efficiency, data augmentation techniques have been investigated in recent years. A systematic examination of data augmentation in NLP under low-labeled data settings has been lacking until now, resulting in difficulty in comprehending the efficacy of diverse methods in various contexts. This study provides a comprehensive survey of data augmentation in NLP under low-labeled data settings, encompassing an overview of methods such as token-level and sentence-level augmentations, along with experiments conducted on 11 datasets across topics/news classification, inference, paraphrasing, and single-sentence tasks. Our research enables the formulation of recommendations to guide practitioners in selecting suitable augmentations tailored to different settings and highlights the current limitations and potential future pathways for NLP under low-labeled data settings. Our empirical findings, alongside a comprehensive framework that integrates context, operation level, and evaluation metrics, provide a valuable reference for further exploring the potential of data augmentation in NLP. This survey is an ongoing effort that can be adapted to address novel questions and methodologies in this domain. Another approach posits its fundamental expression is tied to the self-repulsive properties of a specific particle in long-range interactions. A new, closely related formulation suggests it could be formulated in terms of a particle's self-binding energy, which must remain non-negative. This new interpretation becomes particularly insightful within anti-de Sitter space due to its association with a conformal field theory, where a relationship involving the dimension of an operator exists and forms a convex function of the operator's charge under a U(1) symmetry. The novelty of this formulation's structure allows it to bypass any allusion to the theory's holographic duality and spacetime locality. Consequently, it's hypothesized that the property of a convex spectrum of charges should apply broadly to all conformal field theories that are unitary. The proposed conjecture of Charge Convexity, which encompasses not just the U(1) case, can be validated by testing the property of a convex spectrum of charges across a range of models where the dimensions of operators are analytically derivable through perturbation theory, expansions in N, and semi-classical approximations. To stabilize the estimation of ground and excited states on a quantum computer, we modify the quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) to utilize the model space. This model-space QITE method iteratively expands the model space while maintaining its orthogonality, enabling simultaneous description of multiple states. We enhance model-space QITE by integrating the quantum Lanczos algorithm, which boosts its convergence rate. In simulations, our approach outperforms both standard quantum Lanczos and the folded-spectrum QITE in calculating excited states. We show that spin contamination can be mitigated through an imaginary time propagator shift, efficiently obtaining excited states with specific spin properties without descending into lower-energy states with mixed spins. Additionally, we examine how the degree of unitary approximation within MSQITE influences its results. Our results suggest that, for small systems, MSQITE performs comparably to exact diagonalization, demonstrating its potential as a reliable quantum algorithm for studying multiple states in small, interacting systems. As such, it may effectively showcase the capabilities of quantum processors through benchmarking with well-studied models. Furthermore, we explore its applicability to researching multi-state phenomena in systems with non-interacting components, using the example of Dirac fermions in a holographic setup. Here, we demonstrate that MSQITE can efficiently analyze non-interacting systems by only requiring the imaginary time evolution of a single system unit, significantly improving the method's efficiency for these cases. Ultimately, our improvements position MSQITE as a leading candidate for a hybrid quantum-classical approach, combining the strengths of unitary quantum processing and imaginary time evolution while addressing the challenges of stabilizing ground and excited state calculations on quantum computers. We anticipate this algorithm to play a pivotal role in developing applications of quantum computers that leverage their ability to handle multiple states. We also emphasize the practical usefulness of this algorithm, given that its implementation based on superconducting qubits and a digital-analog interface is currently being prototyped in our research group. This implementation is expected to serve as a demonstration of large-scale quantum processing, building on the existing development of a high-fidelity diagonalization algorithm and extending its capabilities to multiple states. In the context of near-term quantum computing, we outline a strategy for implementing MSQITE that leverages the current capabilities of quantum processors, incorporating an hybrid approach that combines unitary processing and parameterized gates. These criteria make use of a specific polynomial and its coefficient. Additionally, we provide a lower bound for the tight Hilbert function that extends a previous result from Goto and Nakamura, which specifically holds true in equidimensional excellent local rings. If the ring has a specific dimension, we demonstrate the connection between the tight Hilbert function and its lower bound, achieving this condition implies that the ring is $F$-rational. Based on the ring's properties and test elements, we find formulas to compute various coefficients, which are in turn used to establish the relationship between $F$-rationality and these coefficients, ultimately leading to the condition for $F$-rationality as depth $R \geq 2$ and a specific equality of these coefficients. Unfortunately, evaluations and policy advice concerning ancillary services and market structures lack methods for examining the intricate interplay between markets and services. Consequently, this study presents an open-source agent-based model to evaluate design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA Python toolset for Power System Analysis. This model offers adjustable market parameters, agent-specific tactics, and thorough clearing algorithms for the day-ahead market, continuous intra-day trading, redispatch, and imbalance management. Furthermore, the model includes multiple policy performance indicators, including a novel pricing multiplier and new redispatch performance indicators. The results from a stylized simulation scenario validated against actual electricity data highlight the intricate character of electricity markets and the diversity of trading outcomes generated by different model parameters and agent behavior settings. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model is an adaptable policy tool that can be employed to explore a wide range of design options for electricity markets and ancillary services. The model is open-source and is available at https://github.com/agent-based-europe/Ancillary-Services-Acquisition-Model. The model is part of the agent-based models for the European electricity sector developed within the scope of the Agent-Based Europe project. These models are an initiative of the agent-based modeling community in Europe, and they are being employed for policy advice and evaluation of design options for the European electricity sector. The model is currently being applied to analyze market interactions and services in the European electricity sector. R.W.K. Odoni initially established the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the symmetric group in fields of characteristic zero. A generalization to fields of positive characteristic was achieved by Juul. Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients. When a generic monic polynomial Phi is composed with F, resulting in a new polynomial with coefficients (a0, a1,...), we identify the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate. The structure of this Galois group mirrors the (m-folded) iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_(nd) for n > 0, where n represents the polynomial's degree. In the case of large finite fields, the Galois group is instead isomorphic to the infinite iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_n, providing a connection between the geometry of an affine variety and its flock. This connection is utilized to analyze the number of components in an affine variety defined by a binary Diophantine equation over a finite field of large size. Additionally, this equation's solutions are linked to an infinite iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_n, specifically through the structure of an affine variety defined by a specific binary Diophantine equation over a finite field of large size, which is in turn related to an infinite iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_n. This structure is then employed to devise an unsolved problem related to an infinite iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_n, specifically focusing on whether its sequence of dual extension modules forms a monoid under the operation of direct sum. This problem is applied to an affine variety defined by a specific binary Diophantine equation over a finite field of large size, which is in turn linked to an infinite iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_n. Ultimately, our study provides an answer to this unsolved problem in the case when its sequence of dual extension modules forms a monoid under the operation of direct sum. Additionally, this solution is utilized to devise an answer to an unsolved problem regarding an affine variety defined by a specific binary Diophantine equation over a finite field of large size. This solution involves a novel application of Galois theory in an algebraic setting, specifically focusing on an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients.

Specifically, our analysis focuses on final states with two leptons and assesses the effectiveness of separating signal and background for experimental conditions representative of the ATLAS and CMS experiments during LHC Run 2, leveraging the DELPHES simulation package. As a result, we were able to achieve a $0.26\%$ top quark pair background suppression, corresponding to a $35\%$ Higgs boson pair signal efficiency. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the dominant irreducible background accounts for approximately $86\%$ of the total two-lepton top quark pair background. To achieve this level of separation, we employed a multi-step selection procedure, combining geometric and kinematic discriminants to distinguish the Higgs boson pair signal from the dominant irreducible top quark pair background. Ultimately, our study provides valuable insights for further research aimed at fully optimizing Higgs boson pair production analysis using the matrix element method. Additionally, we have made our implementation publicly available through an publicly accessible repository. This publicly accessible code can serve as a starting point for which more advanced analysis strategies may be developed, taking into consideration more refined detector information and potential extensions of the Higgs boson pair production process. Additionally, given the current state of research, our study results may be applicable to the search for Higgs boson pair production in final states involving hadronic decays of the W and Z bosons. However, more comprehensive studies are needed to fully assess the effectiveness of the matrix element method for this type of analysis. Nonetheless, our study lays the groundwork for further research aimed at fully optimizing Higgs boson pair production analysis using the matrix element method in all possible final state channels. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. Our findings reveal that even seemingly well-behaved models can exhibit unusual behavior when analyzed through Bayes factor analysis, underscoring the importance of rigorously testing the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates before drawing conclusions. Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction approach is used on top of pre-trained BERT models for 1500 semantically connected sentence pairs, resulting in a distribution of predicted indicators that reflects existing discourse indicators in a normalized form. This distribution serves as a normalized frequency map of discourse indicators by relation. Researchers adopted this approach in DiscSense, an open-source tool that enables researchers to produce such frequency maps for any defined discourse indicator set. It is currently available on GitHub at the address listed. To validate the frequency maps, an initial examination of the predicted indicators for 1500 semantically connected sentence pairs was conducted. The diversity of indicators assigned to each relation was analyzed using a well-known classification metric, followed by a comparison with the results obtained from an independent evaluation of a specially fine-tuned discourse detection model. Moreover, an exploratory study on the results of a multiple correspondence analysis was conducted to reveal the internal structure of the frequency maps. These frequency maps are potentially useful for designing machine learning models that consider discourse indicators, for developing datasets with diverse indicators, and for applying techniques from natural language generation to generate indicators between semantically connected sentences. Finally, due to the automatic nature of this approach, it is now feasible to create datasets with diverse indicators from existing classification datasets by running DiscSense on those datasets.
